paragraphs: This paper treats image segmentation as a classification decision for each pixel. The application comes from combustion research and forms part of developing a system for real-time image processing. Supervised examples of the pixel-labeling task provide the basis for deriving classifiers, so the segmentation problem becomes a comparison of learned decision methods.

The study evaluates a connectionist method alongside Gaussian maximum likelihood classification and polynomial classifiers of first, second, and third degree. Applying these approaches to the same practical problem creates a direct setting for assessing their suitability. The different polynomial degrees also make the comparison broader than a single neural-versus-statistical pairing.

Performance is measured on the training data and on three separate complete test images. This distinguishes behavior on the examples used to derive the classifiers from behavior on entire additional images. The abstract describes the comparative evaluation without identifying a winning method. Its contribution is the application-focused assessment design, which connects classifier choice to the actual pixel classification task faced by the segmentation system.
summary.tldr: The study compares neural, Gaussian, and polynomial pixel classifiers on a combustion-imaging segmentation task.

title: Comparing the Performance of Connectionist and Statistical Classifiers on an Image Segmentation Problem

abstract: We interpret the time interval data obtained from periodically stimulated sensory neurons in terms of two simple dynamical systems driven by noise with an embedded weak periodic function called the signal: 1) a bistable system defined by two potential wells separated by a barrier, and 2) a Fit(cid:173) zHugh-Nagumo system. The implementation is by analog simulation: elec(cid:173) tronic circuits which mimic the dynamics. For a given signal frequency, our simulators have only two adjustable parameters, the signal and noise intensi(cid:173) ties. We show that experimental data obtained from the periodically stimu(cid:173) lated mechanoreceptor in the crayfish tail fan can be accurately approximated by these simulations. Finally, we discuss stochastic resonance in the two models.

paragraphs: The paper interprets the intervals between responses of periodically stimulated sensory neurons using simple noisy dynamical systems. Both models receive noise together with a weak periodic signal. One model has two stable potential wells separated by a barrier; the other is a FitzHugh-Nagumo system.

The authors implement these models as electronic circuits that reproduce their dynamics. For a fixed signal frequency, only the signal intensity and noise intensity are adjustable. This provides a compact way to investigate whether changing the balance between periodic stimulation and noise can reproduce the timing patterns seen in biological recordings.

The simulations accurately approximate experimental interval data from a mechanoreceptor in the crayfish tail fan. This result connects a biological response distribution to two relatively simple dynamical descriptions. The paper also discusses stochastic resonance in both models, linking the interpretation of response timing to the interaction between weak periodic signals and noise. Its contribution combines statistical agreement with an explicit dynamical account.
summary.tldr: Two simple noisy dynamical models reproduce sensory-neuron interval data using adjustable signal and noise intensities.

title: Statistical and Dynamical Interpretation of ISIH Data from Periodically Stimulated Sensory Neurons

abstract: Each year people spend a huge amount of time typing. The text people type typically contains a tremendous amount of redundancy due to predictable word usage patterns and the text's structure. This paper describes a neural network system call AutoTypist that monitors a person's typing and predicts what will be entered next. AutoTypist displays the most likely subsequent word to the typist, who can accept it with a single keystroke, instead of typing it in its entirety. The multi-layer perceptron at the heart of Auto'JYpist adapts its predictions of likely subsequent text to the user's word usage pattern, and to the characteristics of the text currently being typed. Increases in typing speed of 2-3% when typing English prose and 10-20% when typing C code have been demonstrated using the system, suggesting a potential time savings of more than 20 hours per user per year. In addition to increasing typing speed, AutoTypist reduces the number of keystrokes a user must type by a similar amount (2-3% for English, 10- 20% for computer programs). This keystroke savings has the potential to significantly reduce the frequency and severity of repeated stress injuries caused by typing, which are the most common injury suffered in today's office environment.

paragraphs: AutoTypist aims to reduce typing by predicting the next word and letting the user accept it with one keystroke. The system takes advantage of repeated word choices and predictable text structure. Its interaction is straightforward: the user continues composing, while the network offers a likely continuation that can replace several individual keystrokes.

A multilayer perceptron generates the predictions. It adapts both to the user's word usage and to the characteristics of the text being written. This makes the prediction task sensitive to the person and the current material, rather than treating every writing situation as having the same likely vocabulary or sequence of words.

The authors report typing-speed improvements of 2–3% for English prose and 10–20% for C code, with comparable reductions in keystrokes. The larger programming gains show that the demonstrated benefit depends on the material. They also suggest annual time savings exceeding 20 hours per user and possible reductions in repetitive strain injuries; those are potential consequences of the measured typing savings.
summary.tldr: AutoTypist learns a user's typing patterns to suggest next words, producing larger demonstrated speed gains for C code than for English prose.

title: A Connectionist Technique for Accelerated Textual Input: Letting a Network Do the Typing

abstract: We propose a way of using boolean circuits to perform real valued computation in a way that naturally extends their boolean func(cid:173) tionality. The functionality of multiple fan in threshold gates in this model is shown to mimic that of a hardware implementation of continuous Neural Networks. A Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension and sample size analysis for the systems is performed giving best known sample sizes for a real valued Neural Network. Experimen(cid:173) tal results confirm the conclusion that the sample sizes required for the networks are significantly smaller than for sigmoidal networks.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way for Boolean circuits to perform real-valued computation while naturally extending their existing Boolean behavior. The construction connects discrete circuit elements with continuous neural computation. In particular, threshold gates receiving multiple inputs are shown to behave like a hardware implementation of continuous neural networks.

The authors analyze the resulting systems using Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension and sample-size bounds. This connects the expressive capacity of the model class to the amount of training data required for generalization. The analysis therefore addresses a statistical question alongside the circuit construction: what learning requirements follow from this particular way of implementing real-valued functions?

The paper reports sample-size results described as the best known for a real-valued neural network in its setting. Experiments support the conclusion that these networks require substantially fewer samples than sigmoidal networks. The contribution joins an implementation-oriented model with theoretical and experimental evidence about learning from data, showing how the choice of computational units can affect the amount of training evidence needed.
summary.tldr: A real-valued extension of Boolean circuits yields neural networks with favorable sample-size bounds and supporting experimental results.

title: Generalisation of A Class of Continuous Neural Networks

abstract: Recent experiments show that the neural codes at work in a wide range of creatures share some common features. At first sight, these observations seem unrelated. However, we show that these features arise naturally in a linear filtered threshold crossing (LFTC) model when we set the threshold to maximize the transmitted information. This maximization process requires neural adaptation to not only the DC signal level, as in conventional light and dark adaptation, but also to the statistical structure of the signal and noise distribu(cid:173) tions. We also present a new approach for calculating the mutual information between a neuron's output spike train and any aspect of its input signal which does not require reconstruction of the in(cid:173) put signal. This formulation is valid provided the correlations in the spike train are small, and we provide a procedure for checking this assumption. This paper is based on joint work (DeWeese [1], 1995). Preliminary results from the LFTC model appeared in a previous proceedings (DeWeese [2], 1995), and the conclusions we reached at that time have been reaffirmed by further analysis of the model.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether shared features of neural codes can follow from a common optimization principle. It studies a model that linearly filters an input and generates spikes through threshold crossings. When the threshold is chosen to maximize transmitted information, the model naturally produces features seen across a range of creatures.

This optimization requires adaptation to more than the average signal level. The neuron must also adapt to the statistical structure of both signals and noise. The result gives apparently separate coding observations a shared explanation: they can arise from adjusting a threshold to preserve information under the prevailing input conditions.

The authors also introduce a method for calculating mutual information between a spike train and a selected aspect of its input without reconstructing the input signal. The formulation assumes small correlations within the spike train, and they provide a procedure for checking that assumption. This analytical contribution complements the model by offering a way to quantify information while explicitly testing a condition required by the calculation.
summary.tldr: Maximizing transmitted information in a threshold-crossing neuron model explains shared coding features and requires adaptation to signal and noise statistics.

title: Optimization Principles for the Neural Code

abstract: A directed generative model for binary data using a small number of hidden continuous units is investigated. A clipping nonlinear(cid:173) ity distinguishes the model from conventional principal components analysis. The relationships between the correlations of the underly(cid:173) ing continuous Gaussian variables and the binary output variables are utilized to learn the appropriate weights of the network. The advantages of this approach are illustrated on a translationally in(cid:173) variant binary distribution and on handwritten digit images.
originalAbstract: A directed generative model for binary data using a small number of hidden continuous units is investigated. A clipping nonlinear(cid:173) ity distinguishes the model from conventional principal components analysis. The relationships between the correlations of the underly(cid:173) ing continuous Gaussian variables and the binary output variables are utilized to learn the appropriate weights of the network. The advantages of this approach are illustrated on a translationally in(cid:173) variant binary distribution and on handwritten digit images.

paragraphs: This paper investigates a generative model for binary observations that uses a small number of continuous hidden units. The model connects a compact continuous representation to outputs with only two possible values. Its design includes a clipping nonlinearity, which distinguishes the relationship between hidden variables and outputs from conventional principal component analysis.

Learning relies on the relationship between correlations among underlying continuous Gaussian variables and correlations among the resulting binary variables. The authors use those relationships to determine the network's weights. This gives the learning procedure a way to connect observable binary dependencies to the continuous structure assumed by the model.

The advantages of the approach are illustrated with a translationally invariant binary distribution and handwritten digit images. These examples show its application to both a specified binary distribution and image data. The central contribution is the combination of continuous hidden variables, nonlinear binary outputs, and correlation-based weight learning. Together, these elements provide a generative representation tailored to binary observations while retaining a small continuous hidden space.
summary.tldr: A compact continuous latent model learns binary data by relating Gaussian-variable correlations to correlations after nonlinear clipping.

title: Learning a Continuous Hidden Variable Model for Binary Data

abstract: The committee approach has been proposed for reducing model uncertainty and improving generalization performance. The ad(cid:173) vantage of committees depends on (1) the performance of individ(cid:173) ual members and (2) the correlational structure of errors between members. This paper presents an input grouping technique for de(cid:173) signing a heterogeneous committee. With this technique, all input variables are first grouped based on their mutual information. Sta(cid:173) tistically similar variables are assigned to the same group. Each member's input set is then formed by input variables extracted from different groups. Our designed committees have less error cor(cid:173) relation between its members, since each member observes different input variable combinations. The individual member's feature sets contain less redundant information, because highly correlated vari(cid:173) ables will not be combined together. The member feature sets con(cid:173) tain almost complete information, since each set contains a feature from each information group. An empirical study for a noisy and nonstationary economic forecasting problem shows that commit(cid:173) tees constructed by our proposed technique outperform committees formed using several existing techniques.

paragraphs: Combining prediction models is useful when the members perform well individually and do not make strongly correlated errors. This paper designs model committees by controlling which input variables each member receives. The goal is to preserve useful information while giving members different combinations of evidence.

The method groups input variables using mutual information, placing statistically similar variables together. Each member then receives variables drawn from different groups. This construction avoids combining highly redundant variables within a member's feature set, while including a feature from each information group is intended to retain almost complete information. Different selections across members also reduce the correlation of their errors.

The authors evaluate the technique on an economic forecasting problem with noisy data and changing statistical behavior. Committees constructed with this grouping method outperform committees built using several existing techniques in that empirical study. The result supports feature selection as a way to shape both individual model quality and diversity across a committee, rather than treating the choice of each member's inputs as incidental.
summary.tldr: Grouping related features and giving committee members different cross-group selections improves performance in the reported economic forecasting study.

title: Constructing Heterogeneous Committees Using Input Feature Grouping: Application to Economic Forecasting

abstract: This paper revisits the classical neuroscience paradigm of Hebbian learning. We find that a necessary requirement for effective as(cid:173) sociative memory learning is that the efficacies of the incoming synapses should be uncorrelated. This requirement is difficult to achieve in a robust manner by Hebbian synaptic learning, since it depends on network level information. Effective learning can yet be obtained by a neuronal process that maintains a zero sum of the in(cid:173) coming synaptic efficacies. This normalization drastically improves the memory capacity of associative networks, from an essentially bounded capacity to one that linearly scales with the network's size. It also enables the effective storage of patterns with heterogeneous coding levels in a single network. Such neuronal normalization can be successfully carried out by activity-dependent homeostasis of the neuron's synaptic efficacies, which was recently observed in cortical tissue. Thus, our findings strongly suggest that effective associa(cid:173) tive learning with Hebbian synapses alone is biologically implausi(cid:173) ble and that Hebbian synapses must be continuously remodeled by neuronally-driven regulatory processes in the brain.

paragraphs: The paper revisits whether Hebbian synaptic learning is sufficient for effective associative memory. The authors identify uncorrelated incoming synaptic efficacies as a necessary requirement in their analysis. Achieving that condition robustly through Hebbian changes is difficult because it depends on information at the network level.

They show that a neuronal process maintaining a zero sum across incoming synaptic efficacies can support effective learning. This normalization changes the reported scaling of memory capacity: an essentially bounded capacity becomes one that increases linearly with network size. It also allows a single network to store patterns with different coding levels, broadening the kinds of memories it can accommodate.

The authors connect this mechanism to activity-dependent homeostasis of synaptic efficacies, which the abstract identifies as observed in cortical tissue. Their findings strongly suggest that effective biological associative learning needs neuronal regulation alongside Hebbian plasticity. The biological conclusion is presented as an implication of the findings, while the capacity improvement and heterogeneous-pattern storage are stated outcomes of the normalization approach.
summary.tldr: Normalizing incoming synaptic strengths greatly improves associative-memory capacity and supports the need for neuronal regulation alongside Hebbian learning.

title: Effective Learning Requires Neuronal Remodeling of Hebbian Synapses

abstract: In kernel based learning the data is mapped to a kernel feature space of a dimension that corresponds to the number of training data points. In practice, however, the data forms a smaller submanifold in feature space, a fact that has been used e.g. by reduced set techniques for SVMs. We propose a new mathematical construction that permits to adapt to the in- trinsic dimension and to ﬁnd an orthonormal basis of this submanifold. In doing so, computations get much simpler and more important our theoretical framework allows to derive elegant kernelized blind source separation (BSS) algorithms for arbitrary invertible nonlinear mixings. Experiments demonstrate the good performance and high computational efﬁciency of our kTDSEP algorithm for the problem of nonlinear BSS.

paragraphs: Kernel methods work with a feature-space representation whose dimension can track the number of training examples. Yet the data may occupy a smaller submanifold within that space. This paper develops a mathematical construction that adapts to this intrinsic dimension and finds an orthonormal basis for the smaller structure.

Representing the relevant structure through such a basis simplifies computations. The authors also use the construction as a theoretical foundation for kernelized blind source separation, the task of recovering hidden sources from mixtures. Their framework allows them to derive algorithms for arbitrary invertible nonlinear mixing, with invertibility being an explicit condition on the mixing process.

The paper presents kTDSEP as an algorithm arising from this approach. Experiments demonstrate good nonlinear source-separation performance and high computational efficiency. The contribution links a more economical representation of kernel-space data with a concrete inference task: adapting to the structure actually occupied by the data both simplifies the mathematics and supports an effective source-separation method in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: An intrinsic-dimensional kernel representation simplifies computation and supports efficient blind separation of invertible nonlinear mixtures.

title: Kernel Feature Spaces and Nonlinear Blind Souce Separation

abstract: We present an automatic alignment procedure which maps the disparate internal representations learned by several local dimensionality reduction experts into a single, coherent global coordinate system for the original data space. Our algorithm can be applied to any set of experts, each of which produces a low-dimensional local representation of a highdimensional input. Unlike recent efforts to coordinate such models by modifying their objective functions [1, 2], our algorithm is invoked after training and applies an efficient eigensolver to post-process the trained models. The post-processing has no local optima and the size of the system it must solve scales with the number of local models rather than the number of original data points, making it more efficient than model-free algorithms such as Isomap [3] or LLE [4].

Our algorithm can be applied to any set of experts, each of which produces a low-dimensional local representation of a highdimensional input. paragraphs: Several dimensionality reduction models can each learn a useful local description of high-dimensional data while producing incompatible internal coordinates. This paper introduces an automatic procedure that aligns those descriptions into one coherent global coordinate system. The intended inputs are local experts, each producing a low-dimensional representation of part of the original input space.

Alignment takes place after the experts have been trained. The procedure therefore coordinates their representations through post-processing, using an efficient eigensolver, instead of modifying the objectives used to train them. The authors state that this post-processing has no local optima, separating its optimization behavior from possible difficulties in learning the individual experts.

The system solved during alignment grows with the number of local models rather than the number of original observations. That scaling is the basis for the authors' efficiency comparison with model-free methods such as Isomap and LLE. The contribution is a way to assemble local representations into a global one while making the alignment computation depend on the collection of models.
summary.tldr: An eigenvector-based post-processing procedure aligns trained local representations into global coordinates with computation that scales with the number of models.

title: Automatic Alignment of Local Representations

abstract: The extraction of a single high-quality image from a set of low(cid:173) resolution images is an important problem which arises in fields such as remote sensing, surveillance, medical imaging and the ex(cid:173) traction of still images from video. Typical approaches are based on the use of cross-correlation to register the images followed by the inversion of the transformation from the unknown high reso(cid:173) lution image to the observed low resolution images, using regular(cid:173) ization to resolve the ill-posed nature of the inversion process. In this paper we develop a Bayesian treatment of the super-resolution problem in which the likelihood function for the image registra(cid:173) tion parameters is based on a marginalization over the unknown high-resolution image. This approach allows us to estimate the unknown point spread function, and is rendered tractable through the introduction of a Gaussian process prior over images. Results indicate a significant improvement over techniques based on MAP (maximum a-posteriori) point optimization of the high resolution image and associated registration parameters.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution combines several low-resolution observations into one higher-quality image. This requires determining how the observations align and how the unknown image was transformed into each observation. The reconstruction is ill-posed, so additional structure is needed to resolve ambiguities in the possible high-resolution images.

The paper develops a Bayesian treatment in which the likelihood for alignment parameters averages over the unknown high-resolution image. This marginalization accounts for possible images when assessing registration parameters. A Gaussian process prior over images makes the calculation tractable, and the approach also permits estimation of the unknown point spread function, which describes the imaging blur.

The reported results indicate a significant improvement over methods that optimize a single maximum-a-posteriori estimate of both the image and registration parameters. The central methodological contribution is therefore the treatment of image uncertainty during registration. Rather than committing immediately to one reconstructed image, the method uses an average over possible images to support estimation of the transformations and blur.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian super-resolution method averages over unknown images when estimating alignment and can also infer blur, improving reported reconstruction results.

title: Bayesian Image Super-Resolution

abstract: We consider multi-agent systems whose agents compete for resources by striving to be in the minority group. The agents adapt to the environment by reinforcement learning of the preferences of the policies they hold. Diversity of preferences of policies is introduced by adding random bi- ases to the initial cumulative payoffs of their policies. We explain and provide evidence that agent cooperation becomes increasingly important when diversity increases. Analyses of these mechanisms yield excellent agreement with simulations over nine decades of data.

The agents adapt to the environment by reinforcement learning of the preferences of the policies they hold. Diversity of preferences of policies is introduced by adding random bi- ases to the initial cumulative payoffs of their policies. We explain and provide evidence that agent cooperation becomes increasingly important when diversity increases. Analyses of these mechanisms yield excellent agreement with simulations over nine decades of data.

paragraphs: The paper studies a population of agents competing for resources by trying to belong to the minority group. Each agent holds policies and adapts its preferences among them through reinforcement learning. This creates a setting in which the consequences of an agent's choices depend on the choices made throughout the population.

The authors introduce diversity by adding random biases to the initial cumulative payoffs associated with policies. Agents therefore begin with different policy preferences. This gives the study a specific way to vary diversity and investigate its relationship to the population's collective behavior as learning proceeds.

The paper explains and provides evidence that cooperation becomes increasingly important as this diversity increases. Its analysis of the underlying mechanisms agrees closely with simulations across nine decades of data, describing a broad numerical span rather than a historical period. The stated finding concerns the growing importance of cooperation within this modeled resource-competition setting, with agreement between analysis and simulation supporting the proposed explanation.
summary.tldr: Analysis and simulation indicate that cooperation becomes more important as initial policy-preference diversity increases in a minority-game population.

title: Multi-agent Cooperation in Diverse Population Games

abstract: A number of exact and approximate methods are available for inference calculations in graphical models. Many recent approximate methods for graphs with cycles are based on tractable algorithms for tree structured graphs. Here we base the approximation on a different tractable model, planar graphs with binary variables and pure interaction potentials (no external field). The partition function for such models can be calculated exactly using an algorithm introduced by Fisher and Kasteleyn in the 1960s. We show how such tractable planar models can be used in a decomposition to derive upper bounds on the partition function of non-planar models. The resulting algorithm also allows for the estimation of marginals. We compare our planar decomposition to the tree decomposition method of Wainwright et. al., showing that it results in a much tighter bound on the partition function, improved pairwise marginals, and comparable singleton marginals.

paragraphs: Inference in graphical models often requires quantities that are difficult to compute when the graph contains cycles. Many approximation methods use tractable tree models as building blocks. This paper explores a different building block: planar graphs, which can retain cycles while still supporting exact calculations under particular restrictions.

The tractable models have binary variables and interaction potentials without an external field. For this restricted class, an existing exact algorithm computes the partition function, the quantity that normalizes the model's probabilities. The authors use these planar models in a decomposition that produces upper bounds on the partition function of non-planar models. Their algorithm also estimates marginal probabilities for individual variables and pairs.

Compared with the tree decomposition method identified in the abstract, the planar decomposition gives a much tighter partition-function bound and better pairwise marginals, while singleton marginals are comparable. The findings distinguish improvements in joint relationships from estimates for individual variables. They show the value of using richer tractable components for approximation, within the stated restrictions on those components.
summary.tldr: Decomposing graphical models into tractable planar components yields tighter partition-function bounds and better pairwise marginals than the compared tree decomposition.

title: Approximate inference using planar graph decomposition

abstract: In the quest to make Brain Computer Interfacing (BCI) more usable, dry electrodes have emerged that get rid of the initial 30 minutes required for placing an electrode cap. Another time consuming step is the required individualized adaptation to the BCI user, which involves another 30 minutes calibration for assessing a subjects brain signature. In this paper we aim to also remove this calibration proceedure from BCI setup time by means of machine learning. In particular, we harvest a large database of EEG BCI motor imagination recordings (83 subjects) for constructing a library of subject-specific spatio-temporal filters and derive a subject independent BCI classifier. Our offline results indicate that BCI-na{i}ve users could start real-time BCI use with no prior calibration at only a very moderate performance loss."

paragraphs: The paper aims to reduce the setup time for an EEG-based brain-computer interface by removing individualized classifier calibration. It distinguishes this step from placing the electrode cap: dry electrodes can reduce physical preparation, but adapting the system to a user's brain signature introduces another substantial delay.

The authors use motor-imagination EEG recordings from 83 subjects to build a library of subject-specific spatio-temporal filters. From that library, they derive a subject-independent classifier. The approach uses recordings from previous participants to support decoding for a new user, rather than requiring a fresh calibration procedure before that person can begin.

Offline results indicate that users without prior BCI experience could potentially start real-time use without calibration while accepting only a very moderate performance loss. The distinction between offline evidence and the proposed real-time use is important to the finding. The work supports the feasibility of reducing a major setup burden through shared training data, with the usability benefit balanced against the reported decoding-performance reduction.
summary.tldr: A classifier built from 83 subjects' EEG recordings shows offline promise for BCI use without individual calibration at a moderate performance cost.

title: Subject independent EEG-based BCI decoding

abstract: In this paper, we examine the generalization error of regularized distance metric learning. We show that with appropriate constraints, the generalization error of regularized distance metric learning could be independent from the dimensionality, making it suitable for handling high dimensional data. In addition, we present an efficient online learning algorithm for regularized distance metric learning. Our empirical studies with data classification and face recognition show that the proposed algorithm is (i) effective for distance metric learning when compared to the state-of-the-art methods, and (ii) efficient and robust for high dimensional data.

We show that with appropriate constraints, the generalization error of regularized distance metric learning could be independent from the dimensionality, making it suitable for handling high dimensional data. In addition, we present an efficient online learning algorithm for regularized distance metric learning. Our empirical studies with data classification and face recognition show that the proposed algorithm is (i) effective for distance metric learning when compared to the state-of-the-art methods, and (ii) efficient and robust for high dimensional data.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning aims to learn how distances between examples should be measured for a task. The paper examines the generalization error of regularized metric learning: how well a learned distance rule performs beyond the data used to fit it. The central concern is whether high dimensionality must worsen the theoretical guarantee.

The authors show that, with appropriate constraints, the generalization error could be independent of dimensionality. This is a conditional result: the constraints are part of what makes dimension independence possible. It provides theoretical motivation for using regularized metric learning on high-dimensional data, where a guarantee that grows with dimension could become less useful.

The paper also introduces an efficient online learning algorithm and evaluates it on classification and face recognition. The empirical studies find it effective relative to state-of-the-art metric-learning methods and efficient and robust on high-dimensional data. The contribution therefore connects a conditional statistical result with an algorithm whose practical behavior is assessed on tasks that use learned distances.
summary.tldr: Appropriate constraints can make regularized metric-learning generalization independent of dimension, and an online algorithm performs effectively on high-dimensional tasks.

title: Regularized Distance Metric Learning:Theory and Algorithm

abstract: We present policy gradient results within the framework of linearly-solvable MDPs. For the first time, compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients are obtained by estimating the cost-to-go function, rather than the (much larger) state-action advantage function as is necessary in traditional MDPs. We also develop the first compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients for continuous-time stochastic systems.
originalAbstract: We present policy gradient results within the framework of linearly-solvable MDPs. For the first time, compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients are obtained by estimating the cost-to-go function, rather than the (much larger) state-action advantage function as is necessary in traditional MDPs. We also develop the first compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients for continuous-time stochastic systems.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve decision rules using information about how changes to the policy affect expected cost. This paper develops such results for linearly solvable Markov decision processes. Its central contribution concerns the quantity that must be estimated to construct compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients within that framework.

The authors obtain these constructions by estimating the cost-to-go function, which describes future cost from a state. The traditional formulation described in the abstract instead requires a much larger state-action advantage function. Working with cost-to-go therefore changes the estimation problem underlying the gradient calculation, taking advantage of the structure of linearly solvable processes.

The paper also develops compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients for continuous-time stochastic systems, presenting these as first results of their kind. The significance is a theoretical route to policy-gradient construction in both settings. The reduction to cost-to-go is specifically established within the linearly solvable framework, where the required structure makes that alternative possible.
summary.tldr: Linearly solvable MDPs allow natural policy gradients to be constructed from cost-to-go estimates rather than larger state-action advantage estimates.

title: Policy gradients in linearly-solvable MDPs

abstract: Recently, some variants of the $l_1$ norm, particularly matrix norms such as the $l_{1,2}$ and $l_{1,\infty}$ norms, have been widely used in multi-task learning, compressed sensing and other related areas to enforce sparsity via joint regularization. In this paper, we unify the $l_{1,2}$ and $l_{1,\infty}$ norms by considering a family of $l_{1,q}$ norms for $1 < q\le\infty$ and study the problem of determining the most appropriate sparsity enforcing norm to use in the context of multi-task feature selection. Using the generalized normal distribution, we provide a probabilistic interpretation of the general multi-task feature selection problem using the $l_{1,q}$ norm. Based on this probabilistic interpretation, we develop a probabilistic model using the noninformative Jeffreys prior. We also extend the model to learn and exploit more general types of pairwise relationships between tasks. For both versions of the model, we devise expectation-maximization~(EM) algorithms to learn all model parameters, including $q$, automatically. Experiments have been conducted on two cancer classification applications using microarray gene expression data.

We also extend the model to learn and exploit more general types of pairwise relationships between tasks. paragraphs: Multi-task feature selection uses related learning problems to guide which inputs are retained. The paper examines joint sparsity penalties from the l1,q family, bringing commonly used l1,2 and l1,infinity penalties into one framework. Its central question is how to determine the appropriate member of that family for the task.

The authors give these penalties a probabilistic interpretation through the generalized normal distribution. They then construct a model using the noninformative Jeffreys prior. This connects the choice of sparsity penalty to model parameters that can be learned, making the shape of the regularization part of the estimation problem.

An extended version learns and uses more general pairwise relationships between tasks. For both versions, expectation-maximization algorithms estimate all model parameters, including q, automatically. Experiments cover two cancer-classification applications using microarray gene-expression data. The methodological contribution is a probabilistic route to adapting both feature-selection regularization and, in the extended model, the relationships through which tasks share information.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model learns the sparsity penalty for multi-task feature selection and can also learn pairwise task relationships.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Task Feature Selection

abstract: We introduce PiCoDes: a very compact image descriptor which nevertheless allows high performance on object category recognition. In particular, we address novel-category recognition: the task of defining indexing structures and image representations which enable a large collection of images to be searched for an object category that was not known when the index was built. Instead, the training images defining the category are supplied at query time. We explicitly learn descriptors of a given length (from as small as 16 bytes per image) which have good object-recognition performance. In contrast to previous work in the domain of object recognition, we do not choose an arbitrary intermediate representation, but explicitly learn short codes. In contrast to previous approaches to learn compact codes, we optimize explicitly for (an upper bound on) classification performance. Optimization directly for binary features is difficult and nonconvex, but we present an alternation scheme and convex upper bound which demonstrate excellent performance in practice. PiCoDes of 256 bytes match the accuracy of the current best known classifier for the Caltech256 benchmark, but they decrease the database storage size by a factor of 100 and speed-up the training and testing of novel classes by orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: An image collection may need to support searches for object categories that were unknown when its index was created. In this setting, examples defining a new category arrive only at query time. PiCoDes addresses the need for an image representation that is compact enough for large collections and useful for learning these later categories.

The method explicitly learns short binary descriptors at a chosen length, including codes as small as 16 bytes per image. Its optimization uses a bound tied to classification performance, making recognition quality part of code learning. Because direct optimization over binary features is difficult and nonconvex, the authors introduce an alternating scheme and a convex upper bound.

On Caltech256, 256-byte PiCoDes match the accuracy of the best-known classifier reported in the paper. They also reduce database storage by a factor of 100 and accelerate training and testing for novel classes by orders of magnitude. These results demonstrate a favorable recognition, storage, and computation tradeoff in that evaluation.
summary.tldr: PiCoDes learns compact binary image codes that retain strong recognition accuracy while greatly reducing storage and novel-category computation.

title: PiCoDes: Learning a Compact Code for Novel-Category Recognition

abstract: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) and Single Index Models (SIMs) provide powerful generalizations of linear regression, where the target variable is assumed to be a (possibly unknown) 1-dimensional function of a linear predictor. In general, these problems entail non-convex estimation procedures, and, in practice, iterative local search heuristics are often used. Kalai and Sastry (2009) provided the first provably efficient method, the \emph{Isotron} algorithm, for learning SIMs and GLMs, under the assumption that the data is in fact generated under a GLM and under certain monotonicity and Lipschitz (bounded slope) constraints. The Isotron algorithm interleaves steps of perceptron-like updates with isotonic regression (fitting a one-dimensional non-decreasing function). However, to obtain provable performance, the method requires a fresh sample every iteration. In this paper, we provide algorithms for learning GLMs and SIMs, which are both computationally and statistically efficient. We modify the isotonic regression step in Isotron to fit a Lipschitz monotonic function, and also provide an efficient $O(n \log(n))$ algorithm for this step, improving upon the previous $O(n^2)$ algorithm. We provide a brief empirical study, demonstrating the feasibility of our algorithms in practice.

paragraphs: Generalized linear and single-index models relate a target to a one-dimensional function of a linear predictor. Learning that function and predictor can lead to non-convex estimation. The paper develops efficient learning algorithms by building on Isotron, which alternates perceptron-like predictor updates with isotonic regression, a procedure for fitting a non-decreasing function.

The earlier Isotron guarantee assumed data generated under a generalized linear model, together with monotonicity and bounded-slope conditions, and required fresh samples at every iteration. The authors modify the regression step so that it explicitly fits a function that is both monotonic and Lipschitz, meaning its slope is bounded. They present algorithms described as computationally and statistically efficient.

They also make this constrained regression step faster, reducing its running time from O(n²) to O(n log n). This improvement matters because the step is part of the iterative learning procedure. A brief empirical study demonstrates practical feasibility. The contribution combines a more structured function-fitting step with efficient computation for models whose response depends on a learned linear index.
summary.tldr: A Lipschitz-constrained isotonic regression step supports efficient learning of generalized linear and single-index models.

title: Efficient Learning of Generalized Linear and Single Index Models with Isotonic Regression

abstract: We consider an adversarial online learning setting where a decision maker can choose an action in every stage of the game. In addition to observing the reward of the chosen action, the decision maker gets side observations on the reward he would have obtained had he chosen some of the other actions. The observation structure is encoded as a graph, where node i is linked to node j if sampling i provides information on the reward of j. This setting naturally interpolates between the well-known ``experts'' setting, where the decision maker can view all rewards, and the multi-armed bandits setting, where the decision maker can only view the reward of the chosen action. We develop practical algorithms with provable regret guarantees, which depend on non-trivial graph-theoretic properties of the information feedback structure. We also provide partially-matching lower bounds.
originalAbstract: We consider an adversarial online learning setting where a decision maker can choose an action in every stage of the game. In addition to observing the reward of the chosen action, the decision maker gets side observations on the reward he would have obtained had he chosen some of the other actions. The observation structure is encoded as a graph, where node i is linked to node j if sampling i provides information on the reward of j. This setting naturally interpolates between the well-known ``experts'' setting, where the decision maker can view all rewards, and the multi-armed bandits setting, where the decision maker can only view the reward of the chosen action. We develop practical algorithms with provable regret guarantees, which depend on non-trivial graph-theoretic properties of the information feedback structure. We also provide partially-matching lower bounds.

paragraphs: In some sequential decision problems, choosing an action reveals more than its own reward. It also reveals what would have happened for certain other actions. This paper studies such side observations in an adversarial online setting, where a decision maker repeatedly selects actions and learns from the feedback each selection makes available.

The authors represent the feedback structure with a graph. A connection from one action to another indicates that selecting the first reveals information about the second's reward. This representation covers intermediate cases between bandit feedback, where only the selected reward is visible, and expert feedback, where every reward can be observed.

The paper develops practical algorithms with provable regret guarantees that depend on graph-theoretic properties of this observation structure. It also gives lower bounds that partially match those guarantees. Together, these results characterize how the arrangement of available information affects learning difficulty. The significance is that side observations have a value determined by their structure, and that structure can be incorporated directly into algorithm design and analysis.
summary.tldr: Graph-based feedback models yield algorithms and partial lower bounds for learning from rewards of both chosen and indirectly observed actions.

title: From Bandits to Experts: On the Value of Side-Observations

abstract: We present a joint image segmentation and labeling model (JSL) which, given a bag of figure-ground segment hypotheses extracted at multiple image locations and scales, constructs a joint probability distribution over both the compatible image interpretations (tilings or image segmentations) composed from those segments, and over their labeling into categories. The process of drawing samples from the joint distribution can be interpreted as first sampling tilings, modeled as maximal cliques, from a graph connecting spatially non-overlapping segments in the bag, followed by sampling labels for those segments, conditioned on the choice of a particular tiling. We learn the segmentation and labeling parameters jointly, based on Maximum Likelihood with a novel Incremental Saddle Point estimation procedure. The partition function over tilings and labelings is increasingly more accurately approximated by including incorrect configurations that a not-yet-competent model rates probable during learning. We show that the proposed methodology matches the current state of the art in the Stanford dataset, as well as in VOC2010, where 41.7% accuracy on the test set is achieved.

The process of drawing samples from the joint distribution can be interpreted as first sampling tilings, modeled as maximal cliques, from a graph connecting spatially non-overlapping segments in the bag, followed by sampling labels for those segments, conditioned on the choice of a particular tiling. We learn the segmentation and labeling parameters jointly, based on Maximum Likelihood with a novel Incremental Saddle Point estimation procedure. The partition function over tilings and labelings is increasingly more accurately approximated by including incorrect configurations that a not-yet-competent model rates probable during learning. We show that the proposed methodology matches the current state of the art in the Stanford dataset, as well as in VOC2010, where 41.7% accuracy on the test set is achieved.

paragraphs: This paper models image segmentation and category labeling jointly. It begins with candidate figure-ground segments extracted at different image locations and scales, then assigns probabilities to compatible segment combinations and their labels. The model therefore represents uncertainty about both which regions form an image interpretation and what those regions depict.

Compatibility is encoded in a graph connecting segments that do not overlap spatially. Segmentations correspond to maximal cliques in that graph. Sampling can be understood as choosing a segmentation and then drawing labels conditional on it. The authors learn both sets of parameters together using maximum likelihood and an incremental saddle-point estimation procedure.

During training, the approximation to the partition function becomes more accurate by incorporating incorrect configurations that the developing model considers probable. This focuses the approximation on mistakes relevant to learning. The method matches the reported state of the art on the Stanford dataset and VOC2010, achieving 41.7% test accuracy on the latter. The results support learning compatible image regions and their category assignments within one probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A joint probabilistic model learns compatible image segments and their labels, matching reported state-of-the-art results on two datasets.

title: Probabilistic Joint Image Segmentation and Labeling

abstract: This paper discusses the problem of calibrating posterior class probabilities from partially labelled data. Each instance is assumed to be labelled as belonging to one of several candidate categories, at most one of them being true. We generalize the concept of proper loss to this scenario, establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a loss function to be proper, and we show a direct procedure to construct a proper loss for partial labels from a conventional proper loss. The problem can be characterized by the mixing probability matrix relating the true class of the data and the observed labels. An interesting result is that the full knowledge of this matrix is not required, and losses can be constructed that are proper in a subset of the probability simplex.

Each instance is assumed to be labelled as belonging to one of several candidate categories, at most one of them being true. We generalize the concept of proper loss to this scenario, establish a necessary and sufficient condition for a loss function to be proper, and we show a direct procedure to construct a proper loss for partial labels from a conventional proper loss. The problem can be characterized by the mixing probability matrix relating the true class of the data and the observed labels. An interesting result is that the full knowledge of this matrix is not required, and losses can be constructed that are proper in a subset of the probability simplex.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn calibrated class probabilities when training labels are ambiguous. Each example comes with several candidate categories, at most one of which is true. The goal is to obtain meaningful posterior probabilities despite this incomplete supervision, rather than treating the observed candidate set as a fully resolved class label.

The authors generalize proper losses to this setting. A proper loss aligns the learning objective with estimating the relevant probabilities. They establish a necessary and sufficient condition for propriety and give a direct construction that converts a conventional proper loss into one suitable for partial labels.

The analysis represents the relationship between true classes and observed labels through a mixing probability matrix. A notable result is that constructing useful proper losses does not require knowing that entire matrix. The authors also show that losses can be proper on a subset of the probability simplex. This qualification identifies a restricted region of class-probability distributions where the desired property holds.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes and constructs proper probability-estimation losses for ambiguous labels, including constructions that do not need the full label-mixing matrix.

title: Proper losses for learning from partial labels

abstract: This paper examines the possibility of a `reject option' in the context of least squares regression. It is shown that using rejection it is theoretically possible to learn `selective' regressors that can $\epsilon$-pointwise track the best regressor in hindsight from the same hypothesis class, while rejecting only a bounded portion of the domain. Moreover, the rejected volume vanishes with the training set size, under certain conditions. We then develop efficient and exact implementation of these selective regressors for the case of linear regression. Empirical evaluation over a suite of real-world datasets corroborates the theoretical analysis and indicates that our selective regressors can provide substantial advantage by reducing estimation error.
originalAbstract: This paper examines the possibility of a `reject option' in the context of least squares regression. It is shown that using rejection it is theoretically possible to learn `selective' regressors that can $\epsilon$-pointwise track the best regressor in hindsight from the same hypothesis class, while rejecting only a bounded portion of the domain. Moreover, the rejected volume vanishes with the training set size, under certain conditions. We then develop efficient and exact implementation of these selective regressors for the case of linear regression. Empirical evaluation over a suite of real-world datasets corroborates the theoretical analysis and indicates that our selective regressors can provide substantial advantage by reducing estimation error.

paragraphs: The paper asks what least-squares regression can gain by allowing a model to decline some predictions. This reject option produces a selective regressor: it predicts on part of the input domain and rejects elsewhere. The objective is to obtain stronger control over predictions where the model does choose to respond.

The authors show that rejection makes it theoretically possible to track, point by point within an epsilon tolerance, the best regressor in hindsight from the same hypothesis class. The rejected part of the domain has bounded volume. Under certain conditions, that volume tends to zero as the training set grows, so the theoretical benefit need not require permanently rejecting a fixed share of inputs.

For linear regression, the paper develops efficient, exact implementations of these selective regressors. Evaluation on real-world datasets supports the theoretical analysis and indicates substantial reductions in estimation error. The comparison target remains the best regressor within the chosen class. The result explains how selective prediction can trade coverage for more accurate estimation, with increasing data potentially reducing the amount of rejection required.
summary.tldr: Allowing regression to reject some inputs enables pointwise tracking guarantees and can reduce estimation error in practice.

title: Pointwise Tracking the Optimal Regression Function

abstract: We propose a new class of structured Schatten norms for tensors that includes two recently proposed norms (overlapped'' and "latent'') for convex-optimization-based tensor decomposition. Based on the properties of the structured Schatten norms, we mathematically analyze the performance of "latent'' approach for tensor decomposition, which was empirically found to perform better than the "overlapped'' approach in some settings. We show theoretically that this is indeed the case. In particular, when the unknown true tensor is low-rank in a specific mode, this approach performs as well as knowing the mode with the smallest rank. Along the way, we show a novel duality result for structures Schatten norms, which is also interesting in the general context of structured sparsity. We confirm through numerical simulations that our theory can precisely predict the scaling behaviour of the mean squared error. "

Based on the properties of the structured Schatten norms, we mathematically analyze the performance of "latent'' approach for tensor decomposition, which was empirically found to perform better than the "overlapped'' approach in some settings. We show theoretically that this is indeed the case. In particular, when the unknown true tensor is low-rank in a specific mode, this approach performs as well as knowing the mode with the smallest rank. Along the way, we show a novel duality result for structures Schatten norms, which is also interesting in the general context of structured sparsity. We confirm through numerical simulations that our theory can precisely predict the scaling behaviour of the mean squared error. "

paragraphs: A tensor can have different ranks depending on which mode, or dimension, is used to organize it as a matrix. This makes the choice of low-rank regularization consequential. The paper introduces a family of structured Schatten norms that places the existing overlapped and latent approaches to convex tensor decomposition within one framework.

Using properties of this family, the authors analyze why the latent approach can outperform the overlapped approach in some settings. In particular, when the true tensor has low rank in a specific mode, the latent method performs as well as an approach that already knows which mode has the smallest rank. The result explains a conditional advantage without claiming that the latent formulation is always superior.

The analysis also produces a duality result for structured Schatten norms that is relevant to structured sparsity more broadly. Numerical simulations show that the theory precisely predicts how mean squared error scales. Together, the mathematical and numerical results connect the choice of tensor regularizer with its expected recovery behavior.
summary.tldr: Structured Schatten norms explain when latent tensor decomposition can match performance obtained with prior knowledge of the lowest-rank mode.

title: Convex Tensor Decomposition via Structured Schatten Norm Regularization

abstract: Recursive Neural Networks have recently obtained state of the art performance on several natural language processing tasks. However, because of their feedforward architecture they cannot correctly predict phrase or word labels that are determined by context. This is a problem in tasks such as aspect-specific sentiment classification which tries to, for instance, predict that the word Android is positive in the sentence Android beats iOS. We introduce global belief recursive neural networks (GB-RNNs) which are based on the idea of extending purely feedforward neural networks to include one feedbackward step during inference. This allows phrase level predictions and representations to give feedback to words. We show the effectiveness of this model on the task of contextual sentiment analysis. We also show that dropout can improve RNN training and that a combination of unsupervised and supervised word vector representations performs better than either alone. The feedbackward step improves F1 performance by 3% over the standard RNN on this task, obtains state-of-the-art performance on the SemEval 2013 challenge and can accurately predict the sentiment of specific entities.
originalAbstract: Recursive Neural Networks have recently obtained state of the art performance on several natural language processing tasks. However, because of their feedforward architecture they cannot correctly predict phrase or word labels that are determined by context. This is a problem in tasks such as aspect-specific sentiment classification which tries to, for instance, predict that the word Android is positive in the sentence Android beats iOS. We introduce global belief recursive neural networks (GB-RNNs) which are based on the idea of extending purely feedforward neural networks to include one feedbackward step during inference. This allows phrase level predictions and representations to give feedback to words. We show the effectiveness of this model on the task of contextual sentiment analysis. We also show that dropout can improve RNN training and that a combination of unsupervised and supervised word vector representations performs better than either alone. The feedbackward step improves F1 performance by 3% over the standard RNN on this task, obtains state-of-the-art performance on the SemEval 2013 challenge and can accurately predict the sentiment of specific entities.

paragraphs: The paper addresses word and phrase labels that depend on surrounding context. In aspect-specific sentiment analysis, an entity's sentiment can depend on how the sentence compares it with another entity. A purely feedforward recursive network builds larger representations from smaller ones, but the paper identifies this architecture as inadequate for sending contextual information back to the words that need it.

Global belief recursive neural networks add one feedback step during inference. Phrase-level representations and predictions can then influence word-level representations and labels. This gives the model a way to use information assembled at the phrase level when deciding the sentiment attached to a particular word or entity.

On contextual sentiment analysis, the feedback step improves F1 by a reported 3% over the standard recursive network, and the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SemEval 2013 challenge. The authors also find that dropout improves training and that combining supervised and unsupervised word vectors works better than either alone. The results support contextual feedback as a useful addition for entity-specific sentiment prediction.
summary.tldr: Adding one phrase-to-word feedback step improves recursive neural networks' contextual sentiment predictions, with a reported 3% F1 gain.

title: Global Belief Recursive Neural Networks

abstract: Learning from a few examples remains a key challenge in machine learning. Despite recent advances in important domains such as vision and language, the standard supervised deep learning paradigm does not offer a satisfactory solution for learning new concepts rapidly from little data. In this work, we employ ideas from metric learning based on deep neural features and from recent advances that augment neural networks with external memories. Our framework learns a network that maps a small labelled support set and an unlabelled example to its label, obviating the need for fine-tuning to adapt to new class types. We then define one-shot learning problems on vision (using Omniglot, ImageNet) and language tasks. Our algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on ImageNet from 82.2% to 87.8% and from 88% accuracy to 95% accuracy on Omniglot compared to competing approaches. We also demonstrate the usefulness of the same model on language modeling by introducing a one-shot task on the Penn Treebank.

title: Matching Networks for One Shot Learning

abstract: Clustering is an important unsupervised learning problem in machine learning and statistics. Among many existing algorithms, kernel \km has drawn much research attention due to its ability to find non-linear cluster boundaries and its inherent simplicity. There are two main approaches for kernel k-means: SVD of the kernel matrix and convex relaxations. Despite the attention kernel clustering has received both from theoretical and applied quarters, not much is known about robustness of the methods. In this paper we first introduce a semidefinite programming relaxation for the kernel clustering problem, then prove that under a suitable model specification, both K-SVD and SDP approaches are consistent in the limit, albeit SDP is strongly consistent, i.e. achieves exact recovery, whereas K-SVD is weakly consistent, i.e. the fraction of misclassified nodes vanish. Also the error bounds suggest that SDP is more resilient towards outliers, which we also demonstrate with experiments.

paragraphs: Kernel clustering can identify groups separated by nonlinear boundaries, but the paper asks how robust its main algorithmic approaches are. It examines a spectral approach based on singular value decomposition of the kernel matrix and introduces a semidefinite programming relaxation. The comparison concerns both recovery of clusters and resilience to outliers.

Under a suitable model specification, both approaches are consistent as the problem grows, but the guarantees differ. The semidefinite approach achieves strong consistency, meaning exact recovery. The kernel SVD approach achieves weak consistency, meaning the proportion of incorrectly assigned points tends to zero. A vanishing error fraction is meaningful, but it does not require every assignment to be correct.

The error bounds also suggest that the semidefinite formulation is more resilient to outliers, and experiments demonstrate this advantage. The paper therefore distinguishes two questions often combined under accuracy: whether all assignments can be recovered and how performance responds to contamination. Its theoretical conclusions depend on the specified model, while the experimental evidence supports the suggested robustness difference.
summary.tldr: Under a suitable model, semidefinite kernel clustering achieves exact recovery, while kernel SVD achieves a vanishing error fraction.

title: On Robustness of Kernel Clustering

abstract: We introduce a semi-parametric Bayesian model for survival analysis. The model is centred on a parametric baseline hazard, and uses a Gaussian process to model variations away from it nonparametrically, as well as dependence on covariates. As opposed to many other methods in survival analysis, our framework does not impose unnecessary constraints in the hazard rate or in the survival function. Furthermore, our model handles left, right and interval censoring mechanisms common in survival analysis. We propose a MCMC algorithm to perform inference and an approximation scheme based on random Fourier features to make computations faster. We report experimental results on synthetic and real data, showing that our model performs better than competing models such as Cox proportional hazards, ANOVA-DDP and random survival forests.

The paper proposes a Bayesian model that starts from a parametric baseline hazard and uses a Gaussian process to represent departures from that baseline. The Gaussian process also captures dependence on covariates.

Combining a baseline with nonparametric variation gives the model both an initial structure and flexibility beyond it. The authors emphasize avoiding unnecessary restrictions on the hazard rate or survival function. Their framework also handles left, right, and interval censoring, accommodating observations that locate an event before a boundary, after a boundary, or within a time interval.

The paper supplies an MCMC inference algorithm and a random Fourier feature approximation to accelerate computation. Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than the compared Cox proportional hazards, ANOVA-DDP, and random survival forest models. These findings support the proposed combination of flexible event-time modeling and practical inference in the evaluated settings, rather than establishing universal superiority over those alternatives.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian survival model combines a baseline hazard with Gaussian-process flexibility, supports several censoring mechanisms, and outperforms compared models in experiments.

title: Gaussian Processes for Survival Analysis

abstract: DR-submodular continuous functions are important objectives with wide real-world applications spanning MAP inference in determinantal point processes (DPPs), and mean-field inference for probabilistic submodular models, amongst others. DR-submodularity captures a subclass of non-convex functions that enables both exact minimization and approximate maximization in polynomial time. In this work we study the problem of maximizing non-monotone DR-submodular continuous functions under general down-closed convex constraints. We start by investigating geometric properties that underlie such objectives, e.g., a strong relation between (approximately) stationary points and global optimum is proved. These properties are then used to devise two optimization algorithms with provable guarantees. Concretely, we first devise a "two-phase'' algorithm with 1/4 approximation guarantee. This algorithm allows the use of existing methods for finding (approximately) stationary points as a subroutine, thus, harnessing recent progress in non-convex optimization. Then we present a non-monotone Frank-Wolfe variant with 1/e approximation guarantee and sublinear convergence rate. Finally, we extend our approach to a broader class of generalized DR-submodular continuous functions, which captures a wider spectrum of applications. Our theoretical findings are validated on synthetic and real-world problem instances.

These objectives can be non-convex, yet their structure permits useful algorithmic guarantees. The focus is maximizing non-monotone functions, where increasing a variable need not improve the objective, under general down-closed convex constraints.

The authors first establish geometric relationships between approximately stationary points and the global optimum. These relationships make local optimization information useful for obtaining global approximation guarantees. These guarantees describe how much of the optimal objective value the algorithms can secure within the studied problem class. The paper also extends the approach to generalized DR-submodular functions and checks its theoretical findings on synthetic and real-world instances. Motivating applications include inference in determinantal point processes and probabilistic submodular models, connecting the optimization results to structured probabilistic reasoning.
summary.tldr: Geometric properties of continuous DR-submodular functions yield maximization algorithms with one-quarter and 1/e approximation guarantees.

title: Continuous DR-submodular Maximization: Structure and Algorithms

abstract: We propose Lomax delegate racing (LDR) to explicitly model the mechanism of survival under competing risks and to interpret how the covariates accelerate or decelerate the time to event. LDR explains non-monotonic covariate effects by racing a potentially infinite number of sub-risks, and consequently relaxes the ubiquitous proportional-hazards assumption which may be too restrictive. Moreover, LDR is naturally able to model not only censoring, but also missing event times or event types. For inference, we develop a Gibbs sampler under data augmentation for moderately sized data, along with a stochastic gradient descent maximum a posteriori inference algorithm for big data applications. Illustrative experiments are provided on both synthetic and real datasets, and comparison with various benchmark algorithms for survival analysis with competing risks demonstrates distinguished performance of LDR.

paragraphs: Survival analysis with competing risks models when an event occurs and which of several event types occurs. This paper introduces Lomax delegate racing to represent that competition explicitly. It also aims to make the influence of covariates interpretable in terms of accelerating or delaying the time to an event.

This construction can explain non-monotonic covariate effects and relaxes the proportional-hazards assumption, which may be too restrictive. It can also accommodate censoring, missing event times, and missing event types. These capabilities let the same framework represent flexible effects and multiple forms of incomplete outcome information.

The authors provide two inference approaches: a data-augmented Gibbs sampler for moderately sized datasets and stochastic gradient descent for maximum a posteriori inference in large-data applications. Experiments use synthetic and real datasets and report strong performance against competing-risks survival benchmarks. The contribution combines a flexible account of event competition with interpretation and inference methods aimed at different data scales.
summary.tldr: Lomax delegate racing models competing event risks with flexible covariate effects and support for censored or missing outcomes.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Lomax delegate racing for survival analysis with competing risks

abstract: Knowing when a classifier's prediction can be trusted is useful in many applications and critical for safely using AI. While the bulk of the effort in machine learning research has been towards improving classifier performance, understanding when a classifier's predictions should and should not be trusted has received far less attention. The standard approach is to use the classifier's discriminant or confidence score; however, we show there exists an alternative that is more effective in many situations. We propose a new score, called the {\it trust score}, which measures the agreement between the classifier and a modified nearest-neighbor classifier on the testing example. We show empirically that high (low) trust scores produce surprisingly high precision at identifying correctly (incorrectly) classified examples, consistently outperforming the classifier's confidence score as well as many other baselines. Further, under some mild distributional assumptions, we show that if the trust score for an example is high (low), the classifier will likely agree (disagree) with the Bayes-optimal classifier. Our guarantees consist of non-asymptotic rates of statistical consistency under various nonparametric settings and build on recent developments in topological data analysis.
