paragraphs: Graph few-shot learning uses a small number of labeled nodes to adapt to a new task. The paper identifies two reasons this can fail. A single filtering rule across an entire graph may overlook differences between local structures, while a tiny labeled support set may poorly represent the distribution of the query nodes the model must classify.

GRACE addresses both issues within one framework. Adaptive spectrum experts adjust the treatment of graph signals to local structural variation, rather than applying one predefined spectral operation everywhere. Cross-set distribution calibration addresses the mismatch between the support and query sets. The two components therefore target different sources of error: how graph structure is processed and how limited labels represent the prediction problem.

The authors provide a theoretical account of improved generalization through these adaptations and report consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines across a broad range of experimental settings. The findings support treating local graph heterogeneity and support-query mismatch as connected concerns in few-shot learning. Better adaptation requires attention both to the graph's varying structure and to what a small labeled sample can represent.
summary.tldr: GRACE improves graph few-shot learning by adapting spectral processing locally and calibrating differences between support and query distributions.

title: Graph Few-Shot Learning via Adaptive Spectrum Experts and Cross-Set Distribution Calibration

abstract: Semantic segmentation labels each pixel in an image with its corresponding class, and is typically evaluated using the Intersection over Union (IoU) and Dice metrics to quantify the overlap between predicted and ground-truth segmentation masks. In the literature, most existing methods estimate pixel-wise class probabilities, then apply argmax or thresholding to obtain the final prediction. These methods have been shown to generally lead to inconsistent or suboptimal results, as they do not directly maximize segmentation metrics. To address this issue, a novel consistent segmentation framework, RankSEG, has been proposed, which includes RankDice and RankIoU specifically designed to optimize the Dice and IoU metrics, respectively. Although RankSEG almost guarantees improved performance, it suffers from two major drawbacks. First, it is its computational expense—RankDice has a complexity of $\mathcal{O}(d \log d)$ with a substantial constant factor (where $d$ represents the number of pixels), while RankIoU exhibits even higher complexity $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$, thus limiting its practical application. For instance, in LiTS, prediction with RankSEG takes 16.33 seconds compared to just 0.01 seconds with the argmax rule. Second, RankSEG is only applicable to overlapping segmentation settings, where multiple classes can occupy the same pixel, which contrasts with standard benchmarks that typically assume non-overlapping segmentation. In this paper, we overcome these two drawbacks via a \textit{reciprocal moment approximation} (RMA) of RankSEG with the following contributions: (i) we improve RankSEG using RMA, namely RankSEG-RMA, reduces the complexity of both algorithms to $\mathcal{O}(d)$ while maintaining comparable performance; (ii) inspired by RMA, we develop a pixel-wise score function that allows efficient implementation for non-overlapping segmentation settings. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method across various datasets and state-of-the-art models. The code of our method is available in: \url{https://github.com/ZixunWang/RankSEG-RMA}.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns classes to image pixels, but evaluation usually measures overlap between whole predicted and reference masks. Choosing each pixel's most likely class does not directly optimize those overlap metrics. RankSEG addresses this mismatch through procedures targeting Dice and intersection over union, but its computational cost limits practical use.

This paper introduces a reciprocal moment approximation, producing RankSEG-RMA. It reduces the complexity of both metric-specific procedures to O(d), where d is the number of pixels, while retaining comparable performance. That replaces RankDice's O(d log d) computation with a substantial constant factor and RankIoU's O(d²) computation.

The authors also address RankSEG's restriction to overlapping segmentation, where a pixel may belong to several classes. A pixel-wise score inspired by the approximation enables efficient use when classes must be mutually exclusive, as in standard benchmarks. Evaluations across datasets and modern models demonstrate effectiveness. Together, the changes make metric-aware segmentation more computationally accessible and extend it to a common form of the task.
summary.tldr: RankSEG-RMA makes overlap-metric-aware segmentation linear in pixel count and extends it to mutually exclusive pixel classes.

title: RankSEG-RMA: An Efficient Segmentation Algorithm via Reciprocal Moment Approximation

abstract: Eye gaze offers valuable cues about attention, short-term intent, and future actions, making it a powerful signal for modeling egocentric behavior. In this work, we propose a gaze-regularized framework that enhances VLMs for two key egocentric understanding tasks: fine-grained future event prediction and current activity understanding. Unlike prior approaches that rely solely on visual inputs or use gaze as an auxiliary input signal , our method uses gaze only during training. We introduce a gaze-regularized attention mechanism that aligns model focus with human visual gaze. This design is flexible and modular, allowing it to generalize across multiple VLM architectures that utilize attention. Experimental results show that our approach improves semantic prediction scores by up to 11$\%$ for future event prediction and around 7$\%$ for current activity understanding, compared to the corresponding baseline models trained without gaze regularization. These results highlight the value of gaze-guided training in improving the accuracy and robustness of egocentric VLMs. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for using human gaze to enhance the predictive capabilities of VLMs in real-world scenarios like assistive robots and human-machine collaboration. Code and additional information is available at: https://github.com/anupampani/Gaze-VLM

paragraphs: Where a person looks provides clues about their attention, immediate intentions, and possible next actions. Gaze-VLM uses this information to train vision-language models for first-person understanding. The paper targets two tasks: describing the current activity and predicting fine-grained future events from an egocentric perspective.

The method introduces an attention regularizer that encourages the model's focus to align with human gaze during training. Gaze therefore shapes how the model learns to attend to visual information, without being required as an input at inference time. The mechanism is modular and can be used with multiple vision-language architectures that employ attention.

Compared with corresponding models trained without gaze regularization, the authors report semantic prediction-score improvements of up to 11% for future events and around 7% for current activities. These results support human gaze as a useful training signal for more accurate and robust first-person understanding. The work also motivates applications in assistive robotics and human-machine collaboration, where interpreting ongoing activity and anticipating what happens next can matter.
summary.tldr: Gaze-VLM uses human gaze during training to improve first-person activity understanding and future-event prediction.

title: Gaze-VLM: Bridging Gaze and VLMs through Attention Regularization for Egocentric Understanding

abstract: Many modeling tasks from disparate domains can be framed the same way, computing spherical signals from geometric inputs, for example, computing the radar response of different objects or navigating through an environment. This paper introduces G2Sphere, a general method for mapping object geometries to spherical signals. G2Sphere operates entirely in Fourier space, encoding geometric structure into latent Fourier features using equivariant neural networks and outputting the Fourier coefficients of the continuous target signal, which can be evaluated at any resolution. By utilizing a hybrid GNN-spherical CNN architecture, our method achieves much higher frequency output signal than comparable equivariant GNNs and avoids hand-engineered geometry features used previously by purely spherical methods. We perform experiments on various challenging domains including radar response modeling, aerodynamic drag prediction, and policy learning for manipulation and navigation. We find that G2Sphere outperforms competitive baselines in terms of accuracy and inference time, and we demonstrate that equivariance and Fourier features lead to improved sample efficiency and generalization.The source code is available at: https://github.com/ColinKohler/geometry2sphere.

G2Sphere provides a general architecture for this mapping, with applications ranging from object radar responses to navigation. Its design connects equivariant graph neural networks with spherical convolutional networks rather than requiring a separate geometric representation for each task.

The computation takes place entirely in Fourier space. An equivariant network encodes geometry into latent Fourier features, and the model predicts coefficients describing a continuous spherical output. That output can be evaluated at any resolution. The hybrid architecture supports substantially higher frequency signals than comparable equivariant graph networks while avoiding the hand-designed geometry features previously used by purely spherical approaches.

Experiments cover radar response modeling, aerodynamic drag prediction, and policy learning for manipulation and navigation. G2Sphere improves accuracy and inference time relative to competitive baselines in these evaluations. The authors also find that equivariance and Fourier features improve sample efficiency and generalization, supporting the value of combining geometric structure with a continuous signal representation.
summary.tldr: G2Sphere combines equivariant graph networks and spherical convolutions in Fourier space to efficiently predict detailed spherical signals from geometry.

title: Bridging Equivariant GNNs and Spherical CNNs for Structured Physical Domains

abstract: We consider Support Vector Machines (SVMs) learned together with linear transformations of the feature spaces on which they are applied. Under this scenario the radius of the smallest data enclosing sphere is no longer fixed. Therefore optimizing the SVM error bound by considering both the radius and the margin has the potential to deliver a tighter error bound. In this paper we present two novel algorithms: R-SVM_μ^+—a SVM radius-margin based feature selection algorithm, and R-SVM^+ — a metric learning-based SVM. We derive our algorithms by exploiting a new tighter approximation of the radius and a metric learning interpretation of SVM. Both optimize directly the radius-margin error bound using linear transformations. Unlike almost all existing radius-margin based SVM algorithms which are either non-convex or combinatorial, our algorithms are standard quadratic convex optimization problems with linear or quadratic constraints. We perform a number of experiments on benchmark datasets. R-SVM_μ^+ exhibits excellent feature selection performance compared to the state-of-the-art feature selection methods, such as L_1-norm and elastic-net based methods. R-SVM^+ achieves a significantly better classification performance compared to SVM and its other state-of-the-art variants. From the results it is clear that the incorporation of the radius, as a means to control the data spread, in the cost function has strong beneficial effects.

paragraphs: When an SVM is learned together with a linear transformation of its features, the transformation changes the spread of the data. Consequently, the radius of the smallest sphere enclosing the data is no longer fixed. The paper argues that accounting for both this radius and the classification margin has the potential to tighten the SVM error bound.

It introduces two algorithms: one for feature selection and another for metric learning. Both directly optimize a radius-margin error bound using linear transformations. Their construction combines a tighter approximation of the radius with a metric-learning interpretation of SVMs. The resulting optimization problems are convex quadratic problems with linear or quadratic constraints, unlike most existing radius-margin formulations.

Benchmark experiments report strong feature-selection performance against methods including L1 and elastic-net approaches. The metric-learning variant significantly improves classification relative to the compared SVM methods. These results support incorporating data spread into the learning objective, alongside the margin, in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Two convex SVM formulations jointly account for data radius and margin, improving feature selection and classification in benchmark experiments.

title: Convex formulations of radius-margin based Support Vector Machines

abstract: Human-generated lists are a form of non-iid data with important applications in machine learning and cognitive psychology. We propose a generative model - sampling with reduced replacement (SWIRL) - for such lists. We discuss SWIRL’s relation to standard sampling paradigms, provide the maximum likelihood estimate for learning, and demonstrate its value with two real-world applications: (i) In a ""feature volunteering"" task where non-experts spontaneously generate feature=>label pairs for text classification, SWIRL improves the accuracy of state-of-the-art feature-learning frameworks. (ii) In a ""verbal fluency"" task where brain-damaged patients generate word lists when prompted with a category, SWIRL parameters align well with existing psychological theories, and our model can classify healthy people vs. patients from the lists they generate.
originalAbstract: Human-generated lists are a form of non-iid data with important applications in machine learning and cognitive psychology. We propose a generative model - sampling with reduced replacement (SWIRL) - for such lists. We discuss SWIRL’s relation to standard sampling paradigms, provide the maximum likelihood estimate for learning, and demonstrate its value with two real-world applications: (i) In a ""feature volunteering"" task where non-experts spontaneously generate feature=>label pairs for text classification, SWIRL improves the accuracy of state-of-the-art feature-learning frameworks. (ii) In a ""verbal fluency"" task where brain-damaged patients generate word lists when prompted with a category, SWIRL parameters align well with existing psychological theories, and our model can classify healthy people vs. patients from the lists they generate.

paragraphs: Lists produced by people contain dependencies between entries, so treating every item as an independent draw can miss important structure. This paper introduces sampling with reduced replacement, called SWIRL, as a generative model for such lists. It relates the model to standard sampling schemes and provides a maximum-likelihood method for fitting it to observed data.

One application concerns people who spontaneously suggest associations between text features and labels. These volunteered pairs provide information for text classification even when the contributors are not experts. Incorporating SWIRL improves the accuracy of leading feature-learning frameworks in this task, showing that modeling how suggestions are generated can make the resulting supervision more useful.

The second application concerns verbal fluency: people generate words after receiving a category prompt. For lists from healthy participants and patients with brain damage, the learned parameters align well with existing psychological theories. The model can also distinguish the two groups from their lists. Together, the applications show how the same account of dependent list generation can support both predictive learning and psychologically meaningful analysis.
summary.tldr: SWIRL models dependencies in human-generated lists, improving volunteered-feature learning and supporting analysis of verbal-fluency responses.

title: Learning from Human-Generated Lists

abstract: Class imbalance situations, where one class is rare compared to the other, arise frequently in machine learning applications. It is well known that the usual misclassification error is ill-suited for measuring performance in such settings. A wide range of performance measures have been proposed for this problem, in machine learning as well as in data mining, artificial intelligence, and various applied fields. However, despite the large number of studies on this problem, little is understood about the statistical consistency of the algorithms proposed with respect to the performance measures of interest. In this paper, we study consistency with respect to one such performance measure, namely the arithmetic mean of the true positive and true negative rates (AM), and establish that some simple methods that have been used in practice, such as applying an empirically determined threshold to a suitable class probability estimate or performing an empirically balanced form of risk minimization, are in fact consistent with respect to the AM (under mild conditions on the underlying distribution). Our results employ balanced losses that have been used recently in analyses of ranking problems (Kotlowski et al., 2011) and build on recent results on consistent surrogates for cost-sensitive losses (Scott, 2012). Experimental results confirm our consistency theorems.

paragraphs: When one class is much rarer than the other, overall misclassification error can poorly reflect performance on the rare class. This paper studies the arithmetic mean of the true positive and true negative rates, called AM. This measure gives equal weight to correctly recognizing each class, regardless of their relative frequency.

The main question is whether practical learning procedures become optimal for AM as data accumulates. The guarantee is tied to AM and the stated distributional conditions, rather than extending automatically to every measure used for class imbalance.
summary.tldr: Under mild conditions, thresholding suitable probability estimates and balanced risk minimization are consistent for balanced classification accuracy.

title: On the Statistical Consistency of Algorithms for Binary Classification under Class Imbalance

abstract: Dual-tree algorithms are a widely used class of branch-and-bound algorithms. Unfortunately, developing dual-tree algorithms for use with different trees and problems is often complex and burdensome. We introduce a four-part logical split: the tree, the traversal, the point-to-point base case, and the pruning rule. We provide a meta-algorithm which allows development of dual-tree algorithms in a tree-independent manner and easy extension to entirely new types of trees. Representations are provided for five common algorithms; for k-nearest neighbor search, this leads to a novel, tighter pruning bound. The meta-algorithm also allows straightforward extensions to massively parallel settings.

paragraphs: Dual-tree algorithms are branch-and-bound methods, but developing them for different problems and tree structures can be burdensome. The paper addresses this design complexity by separating the pieces that are often intertwined. Its aim is to let algorithms be developed in a way that transfers more easily across tree types.

The proposed organization has four parts: the tree, the traversal, the point-to-point base case, and the pruning rule. A meta-algorithm combines these pieces. This separation distinguishes how data are organized and visited from the problem-specific computation and the conditions for skipping work, making extension to new trees easier.

The authors express five common algorithms within the framework. For k-nearest-neighbor search, the formulation leads to a new, tighter pruning bound. The framework also supports straightforward extensions to massively parallel settings. The contribution therefore includes both a reusable organization for algorithm development and a concrete improvement to one of the algorithms represented within it.
summary.tldr: A four-part framework makes dual-tree algorithms easier to reuse across trees and yields a tighter nearest-neighbor pruning bound.

title: Tree-Independent Dual-Tree Algorithms

abstract: We consider learning and planning in relational MDPs when object existence is uncertain and new objects may appear or disappear depending on previous actions or properties of other objects. Optimal policies actively need to discover objects to achieve a goal; planning in such domains in general amounts to a POMDP problem, where the belief is about the existence and properties of potential not-yet-discovered objects. We propose a computationally efficient extension of model-based relational RL methods that approximates these beliefs using discrete uncertainty predicates. In this formulation the belief update is learned using probabilistic rules and planning in the approximated belief space can be achieved using an extension of existing planners. We prove that the learned belief update rules encode an approximation of the exact belief updates of a POMDP formulation and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed approach successfully learns a set of relational rules appropriate to solve such problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies relational reinforcement learning when the agent is uncertain about which objects exist. Objects may appear or disappear depending on previous actions or properties of other objects. Achieving a goal can require actively discovering objects, so planning must consider potential objects that have not yet been observed.

An exact treatment generally leads to a partially observable Markov decision process, with beliefs about object existence and properties. The authors propose a computationally efficient approximation using discrete uncertainty predicates. Probabilistic rules learn how these approximate beliefs change, and an extension of existing planners supports planning in the resulting belief space.

The theoretical result connects the learned rules to the exact formulation: they encode an approximation of POMDP belief updates. Experiments show that the method learns relational rules appropriate for solving the studied problems. The contribution is therefore a representation and learning approach for object uncertainty, accompanied by a formal account of what its updates approximate. It enables discovery-related uncertainty to enter planning without claiming exact belief tracking.
summary.tldr: Discrete uncertainty predicates and learned probabilistic rules enable approximate relational planning when objects may be undiscovered, appear, or disappear.

title: Model-Based Relational RL When Object Existence is Partially Observable

abstract: Recently proposed distance dependent Chinese Restaurant Process (ddCRP) generalizes extensively used Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP) by accounting for dependencies between data points. Its posterior is intractable and so far only MCMC methods were used for inference. Because of very different nature of ddCRP no prior developments in variational methods for Bayesian nonparametrics are appliable. In this paper we propose novel variational inference for important sequential case of ddCRP (seqddCRP) by revealing its connection with Laplacian of random graph constructed by the process. We develop efficient algorithm for optimizing variational lower bound and demonstrate its efficiency comparing to Gibbs sampler. We also apply our variational approximation to CRP-equivalent seqddCRP-mixture model, where it could be considered as alternative to one based on truncated stick-breaking representation. This allowed us to achieve significantly better variational lower bound than variational approximation based on truncated stick breaking for Dirichlet process.

paragraphs: The distance-dependent Chinese Restaurant Process extends the Chinese Restaurant Process by accounting for dependencies between data points. Its posterior is intractable, and inference had relied on MCMC methods. This paper develops a variational alternative for the important sequential case, where existing variational techniques for Bayesian nonparametrics do not directly apply.

The key step is to reveal a connection between the sequential process and the Laplacian of a random graph generated by that process. This connection supports a new variational formulation. The authors develop an efficient algorithm for optimizing its lower bound and demonstrate its computational efficiency through comparison with a Gibbs sampler.

They also apply the approximation to a sequential-process mixture model equivalent to a Chinese Restaurant Process model. In this setting, it provides an alternative to variational inference based on truncated stick breaking for a Dirichlet process. The reported variational lower bound is significantly better than that alternative's, showing an improvement in the optimized bound for this comparison as well as a new inference route.
summary.tldr: A random-graph connection enables efficient variational inference for the sequential distance-dependent Chinese Restaurant Process and improves the reported bound in a CRP-equivalent application.

title: Variational Inference for Sequential Distance Dependent Chinese Restaurant Process

abstract: We propose the segmented iHMM (siHMM), a hierarchical infinite hidden Markov model (iHMM) that supports a simple, efficient inference scheme. The siHMM is well suited to segmentation problems, where the goal is to identify points at which a time series transitions from one relatively stable regime to a new regime. Conventional iHMMs often struggle with such problems, since they have no mechanism for distinguishing between high-and low-level dynamics. Hierarchical HMMs (HHMMs) can do better, but they require much more complex and expensive inference algorithms. The siHMM retains the simplicity and efficiency of the iHMM, but outperforms it on a variety of segmentation problems, achieving performance that matches or exceeds that of a more complicated HHMM.

paragraphs: The segmented infinite hidden Markov model addresses the problem of dividing a time series into relatively stable regimes. The key task is identifying when one regime gives way to another. Ordinary infinite hidden Markov models can struggle because they lack a mechanism for separating higher-level changes from lower-level dynamics within a regime.

Hierarchical hidden Markov models can represent these distinctions, but their inference procedures are more complex and expensive. The proposed segmented model introduces a hierarchical formulation while supporting a simple, efficient inference scheme. It is designed to retain the computational appeal of an infinite hidden Markov model while making it better suited to segmentation.

Across a variety of segmentation problems, the authors report that the segmented model outperforms the conventional infinite hidden Markov model. Its performance also matches or exceeds that of a more complicated hierarchical model. These findings support the proposed combination of hierarchy and efficient inference in the evaluated tasks, showing that additional segmentation structure can be useful without requiring the more elaborate inference of the compared hierarchical approach.
summary.tldr: The segmented iHMM adds hierarchy for time-series segmentation while retaining simple inference and achieving strong reported performance.

title: The Segmented iHMM: A Simple, Efficient Hierarchical Infinite HMM

abstract: Supervised learning on molecules has incredible potential to be useful in chemistry, drug discovery, and materials science. Luckily, several promising and closely related neural network models invariant to molecular symmetries have already been described in the literature. These models learn a message passing algorithm and aggregation procedure to compute a function of their entire input graph. At this point, the next step is to find a particularly effective variant of this general approach and apply it to chemical prediction benchmarks until we either solve them or reach the limits of the approach. In this paper, we reformulate existing models into a single common framework we call Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) and explore additional novel variations within this framework. Using MPNNs we demonstrate state of the art results on an important molecular property prediction benchmark; these results are strong enough that we believe future work should focus on datasets with larger molecules or more accurate ground truth labels.

paragraphs: The paper brings several related neural models for molecular prediction into a common framework. These models respect molecular symmetries and compute predictions from an input graph. Their shared approach is to learn how information passes through the graph and how that information is aggregated into a prediction for the whole molecule.

The authors call this framework Message Passing Neural Networks, or MPNNs. Expressing existing models in a shared form makes their common operations explicit and provides a basis for exploring new variants. The work combines that reformulation with an empirical search for particularly effective versions on molecular property prediction.

MPNNs achieve state-of-the-art results on an important benchmark in the reported experiments. The authors consider the results strong enough to recommend that future evaluation focus on larger molecules or more accurate ground-truth labels. That recommendation reflects their interpretation of the benchmark results, rather than a demonstration that molecular prediction in general is solved.
summary.tldr: MPNNs unify molecular graph networks through learned message passing and aggregation, achieving state-of-the-art molecular-property benchmark results.

title: Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry

abstract: While humans easily recognize relations between data from different domains without any supervision, learning to automatically discover them is in general very challenging and needs many ground-truth pairs that illustrate the relations. To avoid costly pairing, we address the task of discovering cross-domain relations given unpaired data. We propose a method based on a generative adversarial network that learns to discover relations between different domains (DiscoGAN). Using the discovered relations, our proposed network successfully transfers style from one domain to another while preserving key attributes such as orientation and face identity.
originalAbstract: While humans easily recognize relations between data from different domains without any supervision, learning to automatically discover them is in general very challenging and needs many ground-truth pairs that illustrate the relations. Using the discovered relations, our proposed network successfully transfers style from one domain to another while preserving key attributes such as orientation and face identity.

paragraphs: Learning a relationship between two data domains often relies on matched examples showing how one corresponds to the other. Collecting those pairs can be costly. This paper instead studies whether useful cross-domain relationships can be discovered from unpaired data, where examples from the two domains are available without explicit example-by-example correspondences.

The authors introduce DiscoGAN, a method based on a generative adversarial network. It learns relations between domains and uses them to transfer style. The important goal is more specific than producing an output that resembles the destination domain: the transformation should also preserve key attributes of the original example. The abstract identifies orientation and face identity as attributes preserved in the reported results.

These findings show that the proposed method can discover useful relationships without the paired supervision usually used to illustrate them. Preserving identity or orientation makes the transferred output meaningfully related to its input. The contribution therefore addresses both the cost of obtaining matched training examples and the need for cross-domain transformations that retain important content.
summary.tldr: DiscoGAN learns cross-domain style transfers from unpaired data while preserving key attributes such as orientation and face identity.

title: Learning to Discover Cross-Domain Relations with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: This paper proposes a method for multi-class classification problems, where the number of classes K is large. The method, referred to as Candidates vs. Noises Estimation (CANE), selects a small subset of candidate classes and samples the remaining classes. We show that CANE is always consistent and computationally efficient. Moreover, the resulting estimator has low statistical variance approaching that of the maximum likelihood estimator, when the observed label belongs to the selected candidates with high probability. In practice, we use a tree structure with leaves as classes to promote fast beam search for candidate selection. We further apply the CANE method to estimate word probabilities in learning large neural language models. Extensive experimental results show that CANE achieves better prediction accuracy over the Noise-Contrastive Estimation (NCE), its variants and a number of the state-of-the-art tree classifiers, while it gains significant speedup compared to standard O(K) methods.

paragraphs: Classification becomes computationally demanding when a model must consider a very large number of possible labels. Candidates vs. Noises Estimation, or CANE, divides this work between a small set of selected candidate classes and samples drawn from the remaining classes. The method uses this combination to estimate a classifier without the standard cost of processing every class.

The authors establish consistency and computational efficiency for the estimator. They also identify a condition for especially favorable statistical behavior: when the observed label falls among the selected candidates with high probability, the estimator's variance approaches that of maximum likelihood estimation. This makes the quality of candidate selection relevant to statistical precision as well as computation.

For practical selection, classes occupy the leaves of a tree searched with beam search. The authors also apply CANE to estimating word probabilities in neural language models. Their experiments report better prediction accuracy than Noise-Contrastive Estimation, its variants, and several leading tree classifiers, together with substantial speedups over methods whose cost grows linearly with the number of classes.
summary.tldr: CANE combines selected candidate labels with sampled alternatives to make large-class classification efficient while retaining strong statistical properties.

title: Candidates vs. Noises Estimation for Large Multi-Class Classification Problem

abstract: Building on the success of deep learning, two modern approaches to learn a probability model from the data are Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs). VAEs consider an explicit probability model for the data and compute a generative distribution by maximizing a variational lower-bound on the log-likelihood function. GANs, however, compute a generative model by minimizing a distance between observed and generated probability distributions without considering an explicit model for the observed data. The lack of having explicit probability models in GANs prohibits computation of sample likelihoods in their frameworks and limits their use in statistical inference problems. In this work, we resolve this issue by constructing an explicit probability model that can be used to compute sample likelihood statistics in GANs. In particular, we prove that under this probability model, a family of Wasserstein GANs with an entropy regularization can be viewed as a generative model that maximizes a variational lower-bound on average sample log likelihoods, an approach that VAEs are based on. This result makes a principled connection between two modern generative models, namely GANs and VAEs. In addition to the aforementioned theoretical results, we compute likelihood statistics for GANs trained on Gaussian, MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10 and LSUN datasets. Our numerical results validate the proposed theory.

This prevents direct computation of sample likelihoods within that formulation and limits statistical inference. VAEs take a different route, learning an explicit model through a lower bound on log likelihood.

Under this model, the authors prove that a family of entropy-regularized Wasserstein GANs maximizes a variational lower bound on average sample log likelihood. The contribution supplies a statistical interpretation and likelihood calculation framework, linking distribution matching to a likelihood-based view of generative learning.
summary.tldr: An explicit probability model connects entropy-regularized Wasserstein GANs to variational likelihood learning and enables sample likelihood statistics.

title: Entropic GANs meet VAEs: A Statistical Approach to Compute Sample Likelihoods in GANs

abstract: Many works have been proposed in the literature to capture the dynamics of diffusion in networks. While some of them define graphical Markovian models to extract temporal relationships between node infections in networks, others consider diffusion episodes as sequences of infections via recurrent neural models. In this paper we propose a model at the crossroads of these two extremes, which embeds the history of diffusion in infected nodes as hidden continuous states. Depending on the trajectory followed by the content before reaching a given node, the distribution of influence probabilities may vary. However, content trajectories are usually hidden in the data, which induces challenging learning problems. We propose a topological recurrent neural model which exhibits good experimental performances for diffusion modeling and prediction.

While some of them define graphical Markovian models to extract temporal relationships between node infections in networks, others consider diffusion episodes as sequences of infections via recurrent neural models. In this paper we propose a model at the crossroads of these two extremes, which embeds the history of diffusion in infected nodes as hidden continuous states. Depending on the trajectory followed by the content before reaching a given node, the distribution of influence probabilities may vary. However, content trajectories are usually hidden in the data, which induces challenging learning problems. We propose a topological recurrent neural model which exhibits good experimental performances for diffusion modeling and prediction.

paragraphs: The paper studies how content spreads through a network over time. Existing approaches described in the abstract either use graphical models to capture temporal relationships between infections or treat a diffusion episode as a sequence processed by a recurrent neural network. The proposed model brings these perspectives together by representing diffusion history inside the infected nodes.

Each infected node carries a hidden continuous state that encodes the history of the spread. This allows influence probabilities to depend on the route content followed before arriving at that node. Two arrivals therefore need not have the same implications simply because they reach the same place; their preceding trajectories can matter for what happens next.

A central learning difficulty is that these trajectories are usually absent from the observed data. The authors propose a topological recurrent neural model for this setting and report good experimental performance in diffusion modeling and prediction. The contribution is a way to make network diffusion sensitive to its history while retaining a recurrent neural representation.
summary.tldr: A recurrent diffusion model stores history in infected nodes so that influence can depend on the route content took through a network.

title: A Recurrent Neural Cascade-based Model for Continuous-Time Diffusion

abstract: Empirical risk minimization is an important class of optimization problems with many popular machine learning applications, and stochastic variance reduction methods are popular choices for solving them. Among these methods, SVRG and Katyusha X (a Nesterov accelerated SVRG) achieve fast convergence without substantial memory requirement. In this paper, we propose to accelerate these two algorithms by inexact preconditioning , the proposed methods employ fixed preconditioners, although the subproblem in each epoch becomes harder, it suffices to apply fixed number of simple subroutines to solve it inexactly, without losing the overall convergence. As a result, this inexact preconditioning strategy gives provably better iteration complexity and gradient complexity over SVRG and Katyusha X. We also allow each function in the finite sum to be nonconvex while the sum is strongly convex. In our numerical experiments, we observe an on average $8\times$ speedup on the number of iterations and $7\times$ speedup on runtime.

In this paper, we propose to accelerate these two algorithms by inexact preconditioning , the proposed methods employ fixed preconditioners, although the subproblem in each epoch becomes harder, it suffices to apply fixed number of simple subroutines to solve it inexactly, without losing the overall convergence. In our numerical experiments, we observe an on average $8\times$ speedup on the number of iterations and $7\times$ speedup on runtime.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to accelerate SVRG and Katyusha X, two optimization methods used to fit models by minimizing average training loss. Both already reduce the noise associated with stochastic optimization while keeping memory requirements modest. The proposed improvement changes the geometry of their optimization steps through fixed preconditioners.

Preconditioning makes the subproblem within each training epoch harder to solve. The central result is that these subproblems need not be solved exactly: a fixed number of simple computational routines is sufficient to preserve overall convergence. This makes the extra work compatible with provable improvements in both iteration complexity and gradient complexity.

The analysis permits individual terms in the training objective to be nonconvex, provided their sum is strongly convex. That distinction defines the scope of the result: the guarantee depends on the combined objective. In numerical experiments, the authors report average speedups of eightfold in iteration count and sevenfold in runtime, supporting the practical value of the inexact approach.
summary.tldr: Inexact preconditioning provably accelerates SVRG and Katyusha X while allowing their harder internal subproblems to be solved approximately.

title: Acceleration of SVRG and Katyusha X by Inexact Preconditioning

abstract: A key learning scenario in large-scale applications is that of federated learning, where a centralized model is trained based on data originating from a large number of clients. We argue that, with the existing training and inference, federated models can be biased towards different clients. Instead, we propose a new framework of agnostic federated learning, where the centralized model is optimized for any target distribution formed by a mixture of the client distributions. We further show that this framework naturally yields a notion of fairness. We present data-dependent Rademacher complexity guarantees for learning with this objective, which guide the definition of an algorithm for agnostic federated learning. We also give a fast stochastic optimization algorithm for solving the corresponding optimization problem, for which we prove convergence bounds, assuming a convex loss function and a convex hypothesis set. We further empirically demonstrate the benefits of our approach in several datasets. Beyond federated learning, our framework and algorithm can be of interest to other learning scenarios such as cloud computing, domain adaptation, drifting, and other contexts where the training and test distributions do not coincide.

We also give a fast stochastic optimization algorithm for solving the corresponding optimization problem, for which we prove convergence bounds, assuming a convex loss function and a convex hypothesis set. We further empirically demonstrate the benefits of our approach in several datasets. Beyond federated learning, our framework and algorithm can be of interest to other learning scenarios such as cloud computing, domain adaptation, drifting, and other contexts where the training and test distributions do not coincide.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model from data supplied by many clients. The paper argues that existing training and inference practices can favor some clients over others. It proposes an objective designed for target populations formed by mixtures of client distributions, so the model is not optimized solely around one particular balance of clients.

This agnostic formulation also produces a notion of fairness tied to performance across those mixtures. The authors provide data-dependent learning guarantees using Rademacher complexity, a measure used to relate a model class to its ability to fit data. These guarantees help guide the learning algorithm, connecting the proposed objective to an analysis of generalization.

The paper additionally develops a fast stochastic optimization algorithm and proves convergence bounds when both the loss and the hypothesis set are convex. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate benefits of the approach. Its broader relevance is to situations where training and deployment distributions differ: the mixture-based formulation offers a way to account for uncertainty about which populations a shared model will serve.
summary.tldr: Agnostic federated learning optimizes a shared model across mixtures of client populations, linking distributional robustness with fairness.

title: Agnostic Federated Learning

abstract: Capturing long-range dependencies in feature representations is crucial for many visual recognition tasks. Despite recent successes of deep convolutional networks, it remains challenging to model non-local context relations between visual features. A promising strategy is to model the feature context by a fully-connected graph neural network (GNN), which augments traditional convolutional features with an estimated non-local context representation. However, most GNN-based approaches require computing a dense graph affinity matrix and hence have difficulty in scaling up to tackle complex real-world visual problems. In this work, we propose an efficient and yet flexible non-local relation representation based on a novel class of graph neural networks. Our key idea is to introduce a latent space to reduce the complexity of graph, which allows us to use a low-rank representation for the graph affinity matrix and to achieve a linear complexity in computation. Extensive experimental evaluations on three major visual recognition tasks show that our method outperforms the prior works with a large margin while maintaining a low computation cost.

paragraphs: Visual recognition often requires relating features that lie far apart in an image. A fully connected graph neural network can represent these nonlocal relationships, but computing a dense matrix of affinities between features makes that strategy difficult to scale. LatentGNN addresses this computational obstacle while retaining the ability to represent context beyond nearby image regions.

The key idea is to introduce a latent space that reduces the complexity of the graph. This enables a low-rank representation of the affinity matrix and gives linear computational complexity. Instead of requiring the full dense representation, the method uses the latent structure to build an efficient and flexible account of relationships among visual features.

The paper evaluates the approach on three major visual recognition tasks and reports substantial improvements over prior work while maintaining low computational cost. These findings connect the representational goal with the efficiency goal: modeling long-range context can improve recognition without carrying the cost of the dense graph formulation considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: LatentGNN uses a latent, low-rank graph representation to capture long-range visual relationships with linear computational complexity.

title: LatentGNN: Learning Efficient Non-local Relations for Visual Recognition

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the composition of a smooth function (which can be nonconvex) and a smooth vector mapping, where both of them can be express as the average of a large number of components. We propose a composite randomized incremental gradient method by extending the SAGA framework. The gradient sample complexity of our method matches that of several recently developed methods based on SVRG in the general case. However, for structured problems where linear convergence rates can be obtained, our method can be much better for ill-conditioned problems. In addition, when the finite-sum structure only appear for the inner mapping, the sample complexity of our method is the same as that of SAGA for minimizing finite sum of smooth nonconvex functions, despite the additional outer composition and the stochastic composite gradients being biased in our case.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems with two nested layers: a smooth vector mapping feeds its output into a smooth outer function. Both layers can involve averages over many components, and the outer function may be nonconvex. This structure makes incremental optimization more complicated because information sampled inside the mapping must also support optimization of the outer function.

The authors extend the SAGA framework to create a composite randomized incremental gradient method. Their analysis measures gradient sample complexity: how much sampled gradient information the method needs. In the general setting, its complexity matches several recently developed approaches based on SVRG. For structured problems admitting linear convergence, however, the proposed method can have a substantial advantage when the problem is ill-conditioned.

A separate result concerns problems where only the inner mapping has a finite-sum structure. Here the method matches SAGA's sample complexity for ordinary smooth nonconvex finite-sum optimization. That result is notable because the outer composition remains present and the sampled composite gradients are biased. The additional structure therefore need not increase the stated sample complexity in this setting.
summary.tldr: A SAGA-based method handles nested finite-sum optimization with competitive sample complexity and potential advantages for structured, ill-conditioned problems.

title: A Composite Randomized Incremental Gradient Method

abstract: The accuracy of modern machine learning algorithms deteriorates severely on adversarially manipulated test data. Optimal adversarial risk quantifies the best error rate of any classifier in the presence of adversaries, and optimal adversarial classifiers are sought that minimize adversarial risk. In this paper, we investigate the optimal adversarial risk and optimal adversarial classifiers from an optimal transport perspective. We present a new and simple approach to show that the optimal adversarial risk for binary classification with 0 − 1 loss function is completely characterized by an optimal transport cost between the probability distributions of the two classes, for a suitably defined cost function. We propose a novel coupling strategy that achieves the optimal transport cost for several univariate distributions like Gaussian, uniform and triangular. Using the optimal couplings, we obtain the optimal adversarial classifiers in these settings and show how they differ from optimal classifiers in the absence of adversaries. Based on our analysis, we evaluate algorithm-independent fundamental limits on adversarial risk for CIFAR-10, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and SVHN datasets, and Gaussian mixtures based on them.

paragraphs: Adversarial risk measures classification error when an adversary can manipulate test inputs. This paper asks about the best error rate any classifier could achieve under such interference. That changes the focus from improving a particular defense to understanding limits imposed by the classification problem itself.

For binary classification with a zero–one loss, which counts predictions as either correct or incorrect, the authors characterize optimal adversarial risk through an optimal transport cost between the two class distributions. A suitably chosen transport cost makes this connection exact. They also introduce a coupling strategy that attains the transport optimum for several one-dimensional distributions, including Gaussian, uniform, and triangular distributions.

Those couplings let the authors derive optimal adversarial classifiers in the studied settings and examine how they differ from classifiers optimized without adversaries. The analysis also supports evaluations of algorithm-independent risk limits for several image datasets and related Gaussian mixtures. These results provide a way to study achievable robustness through the relationship between class distributions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal binary adversarial risk using optimal transport and derives optimal robust classifiers for several one-dimensional distributions.

title: Adversarial Risk via Optimal Transport and Optimal Couplings

abstract: Although group convolutional networks are able to learn powerful representations based on symmetry patterns, they lack explicit means to learn meaningful relationships among them (e.g., relative positions and poses). In this paper, we present attentive group equivariant convolutions, a generalization of the group convolution, in which attention is applied during the course of convolution to accentuate meaningful symmetry combinations and suppress non-plausible, misleading ones. We indicate that prior work on visual attention can be described as special cases of our proposed framework and show empirically that our attentive group equivariant convolutional networks consistently outperform conventional group convolutional networks on benchmark image datasets. Simultaneously, we provide interpretability to the learned concepts through the visualization of equivariant attention maps.

paragraphs: Group convolutional networks learn representations built around symmetry patterns. The authors identify a missing capability: these networks do not explicitly learn which relationships among those patterns are meaningful. Recognizing symmetry alone does not directly express whether particular relative positions or poses form a useful combination.

The paper introduces attentive group equivariant convolutions, which incorporate attention into the convolution operation itself. Attention emphasizes useful combinations of symmetry patterns and reduces the influence of combinations that are implausible or misleading. This generalizes group convolution while retaining the framework’s focus on symmetry. The authors also describe earlier visual attention approaches as special cases of the proposed formulation.

On benchmark image datasets, the resulting networks consistently outperform conventional group convolutional networks in the reported experiments. The method also produces equivariant attention maps that can be visualized to help interpret learned concepts. Together, these results support learning relationships among symmetry patterns as a useful addition to learning the patterns themselves, with attention providing both a modeling mechanism and a way to inspect what the network emphasizes.
summary.tldr: Adding attention within group convolutions improves reported image benchmark performance and makes relationships among learned symmetry patterns easier to inspect.

title: Attentive Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks

abstract: The goal of classification with rejection is to avoid risky misclassification in error-critical applications such as medical diagnosis and product inspection. In this paper, based on the relationship between classification with rejection and cost-sensitive classification, we propose a novel method of classification with rejection by learning an ensemble of cost-sensitive classifiers, which satisfies all the following properties: (i) it can avoid estimating class-posterior probabilities, resulting in improved classification accuracy. (ii) it allows a flexible choice of losses including non-convex ones, (iii) it does not require complicated modifications when using different losses, (iv) it is applicable to both binary and multiclass cases, and (v) it is theoretically justifiable for any classification-calibrated loss. Experimental results demonstrate the usefulness of our proposed approach in clean-labeled, noisy-labeled, and positive-unlabeled classification.

paragraphs: Classification with rejection lets a model decline to make a prediction when an error would be too costly. This paper develops that capability through cost-sensitive classification, where different mistakes receive different penalties. The motivation is to support decisions in settings such as diagnosis and inspection, where forcing a prediction can create avoidable risk.

The proposed method learns an ensemble of cost-sensitive classifiers. It can make rejection decisions without first estimating the probability of every class, which the authors connect to improved classification accuracy. The same approach accommodates binary and multiclass problems and permits a flexible selection of training losses, including non-convex ones, without complicated changes for each loss.

The theoretical justification applies to classification-calibrated losses, preserving a specific condition on the losses covered by the analysis. Experiments demonstrate usefulness with clean labels, noisy labels, and positive-unlabeled data. Together, these results position cost-sensitive learning as a flexible foundation for rejection, with both a theoretical rationale and evidence across several forms of supervision.
summary.tldr: An ensemble of cost-sensitive classifiers learns when to reject predictions without requiring class-probability estimates.

title: Classification with Rejection Based on Cost-sensitive Classification

abstract: We study the problem of learning conditional average treatment effects (CATE) from high-dimensional, observational data with unobserved confounders. Unobserved confounders introduce ignorance—a level of unidentifiability—about an individual’s response to treatment by inducing bias in CATE estimates. We present a new parametric interval estimator suited for high-dimensional data, that estimates a range of possible CATE values when given a predefined bound on the level of hidden confounding. Further, previous interval estimators do not account for ignorance about the CATE associated with samples that may be underrepresented in the original study, or samples that violate the overlap assumption. Our interval estimator also incorporates model uncertainty so that practitioners can be made aware of such out-of-distribution data. We prove that our estimator converges to tight bounds on CATE when there may be unobserved confounding and assess it using semi-synthetic, high-dimensional datasets.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave treatment effects partly unidentified when unobserved factors influence the relationships being studied. This paper addresses conditional average treatment effects, which describe average treatment differences for specified characteristics. Hidden confounding can bias these estimates and leave several effect values compatible with the available evidence.

The authors propose a parametric interval estimator for high-dimensional data. Given a predefined bound on the strength of hidden confounding, it estimates a range of possible treatment-effect values. The method also incorporates model uncertainty to account for cases poorly represented in the study or affected by violations of overlap, where relevant treatment comparisons lack adequate support.

The paper proves convergence to tight bounds on conditional average treatment effects when hidden confounding may be present, and evaluates the estimator on semi-synthetic, high-dimensional datasets. The resulting intervals represent more than uncertainty from fitting a model: they also express ignorance tied to the supplied confounding bound. Incorporating model uncertainty additionally helps alert practitioners when a queried case lies outside the data’s reliable coverage.
summary.tldr: A treatment-effect interval estimator combines a specified hidden-confounding bound with model uncertainty to represent causal ignorance in high-dimensional observational data.

title: Quantifying Ignorance in Individual-Level Causal-Effect Estimates under Hidden Confounding

abstract: Deep domain adaptation (DDA) approaches have recently been shown to perform better than their shallow rivals with better modeling capacity on complex domains (e.g., image, structural data, and sequential data). The underlying idea is to learn domain invariant representations on a latent space that can bridge the gap between source and target domains. Several theoretical studies have established insightful understanding and the benefit of learning domain invariant features; however, they are usually limited to the case where there is no label shift, hence hindering its applicability. In this paper, we propose and study a new challenging setting that allows us to use a Wasserstein distance (WS) to not only quantify the data shift but also to define the label shift directly. We further develop a theory to demonstrate that minimizing the WS of the data shift leads to closing the gap between the source and target data distributions on the latent space (e.g., an intermediate layer of a deep net), while still being able to quantify the label shift with respect to this latent space. Interestingly, our theory can consequently explain certain drawbacks of learning domain invariant features on the latent space. Finally, grounded on the results and guidance of our developed theory, we propose the Label Matching Deep Domain Adaptation (LAMDA) approach that outperforms baselines on real-world datasets for DA problems.

paragraphs: Deep domain adaptation often learns an internal representation that makes source and target data distributions look similar. This can help transfer a model between domains, but much of the supporting theory assumes there is no label shift. The paper studies a setting that explicitly includes label shift, broadening the analysis beyond that restriction.

The authors use Wasserstein distance both to measure data shift and to define label shift. Their theory shows that minimizing the distance associated with data shift closes the gap between source and target distributions in the latent representation. At the same time, it retains a way to quantify label shift relative to that representation.

This joint treatment explains certain drawbacks of learning domain-invariant features: bringing representations together must be understood alongside what happens to label shift. Guided by the theory, the authors develop Label Matching Deep Domain Adaptation, or LAMDA. It outperforms baselines on real-world domain adaptation datasets, providing empirical support for incorporating label matching into the adaptation approach.
summary.tldr: LAMDA uses a Wasserstein-based treatment of data and label shift to guide deep domain adaptation and improve performance over evaluated baselines.

title: LAMDA: Label Matching Deep Domain Adaptation

abstract: Adder neural network (AdderNet) is a new kind of deep model that replaces the original massive multiplications in convolutions by additions while preserving the high performance. Since the hardware complexity of additions is much lower than that of multiplications, the overall energy consumption is thus reduced significantly. To further optimize the hardware overhead of using AdderNet, this paper studies the winograd algorithm, which is a widely used fast algorithm for accelerating convolution and saving the computational costs. Unfortunately, the conventional Winograd algorithm cannot be directly applied to AdderNets since the distributive law in multiplication is not valid for the l1-norm. Therefore, we replace the element-wise multiplication in the Winograd equation by additions and then develop a new set of transform matrixes that can enhance the representation ability of output features to maintain the performance. Moreover, we propose the l2-to-l1 training strategy to mitigate the negative impacts caused by formal inconsistency. Experimental results on both FPGA and benchmarks show that the new method can further reduce the energy consumption without affecting the accuracy of the original AdderNet.

paragraphs: AdderNet reduces computation's energy cost by replacing the many multiplications in convolution with additions while maintaining high predictive performance. This paper investigates whether the Winograd algorithm, commonly used to accelerate convolution, can further reduce AdderNet's hardware overhead. The challenge is that the standard algorithm's algebra does not directly carry over.

Conventional Winograd computation relies on multiplication's distributive law, which does not hold for AdderNet's L1-norm operation. The authors replace element-wise multiplication in the Winograd equation with additions and design new transform matrices. These matrices are intended to preserve the expressive ability of output features despite the changed computation.

The paper also introduces an L2-to-L1 training strategy to reduce the negative effects of the formal inconsistency. Evaluations on FPGA hardware and benchmarks show further energy reductions without reducing the original AdderNet's accuracy in the reported experiments. The contribution combines a revised computational transform with a supporting training strategy, making acceleration compatible with a network whose basic operation differs from standard convolution.
summary.tldr: A modified Winograd computation and L2-to-L1 training strategy further reduce AdderNet energy use while preserving accuracy in reported experiments.

title: Winograd Algorithm for AdderNet

abstract: We perform a rigorous study of private matrix analysis when only the last $W$ updates to matrices are considered useful for analysis. We show the existing framework in the non-private setting is not robust to noise required for privacy. We then propose a framework robust to noise and use it to give first efficient $o(W)$ space differentially private algorithms for spectral approximation, principal component analysis (PCA), multi-response linear regression, sparse PCA, and non-negative PCA. Prior to our work, no such result was known for sparse and non-negative differentially private PCA even in the static data setting. We also give a lower bound to demonstrate the cost of privacy in the sliding window model.

paragraphs: When matrix data arrives over time, an analysis may need to use only the most recent W updates. This sliding window requirement makes older information expire while new information enters. The paper studies how to perform useful matrix computations in this setting while also providing differential privacy.

The authors show that an existing framework for analysis without privacy does not withstand the noise needed for privacy. They develop a framework that tolerates this noise and use it to construct efficient private algorithms for spectral approximation, principal component analysis, multi-response linear regression, sparse PCA, and non-negative PCA. These algorithms use o(W) space, meaning that their memory grows more slowly than the window length.

The contribution covers several matrix tasks within one framework. The authors state that comparable results for private sparse and non-negative PCA were previously unavailable even for static data. They also establish a lower bound that identifies a cost of privacy in the sliding window setting, complementing their algorithmic results.
summary.tldr: A noise-robust framework enables differentially private matrix analysis using memory that grows sublinearly with the sliding window length.

title: A Framework for Private Matrix Analysis in Sliding Window Model

abstract: While unbiased machine learning models are essential for many applications, bias is a human-defined concept that can vary across tasks. Given only input-label pairs, algorithms may lack sufficient information to distinguish stable (causal) features from unstable (spurious) features. However, related tasks often share similar biases – an observation we may leverage to develop stable classifiers in the transfer setting. In this work, we explicitly inform the target classifier about unstable features in the source tasks. Specifically, we derive a representation that encodes the unstable features by contrasting different data environments in the source task. We achieve robustness by clustering data of the target task according to this representation and minimizing the worst-case risk across these clusters. We evaluate our method on both text and image classifications. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm is able to maintain robustness on the target task for both synthetically generated environments and real-world environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/YujiaBao/Tofu.

paragraphs: Input-label pairs may not contain enough information to distinguish stable predictive features from spurious ones. This paper explores how related tasks can provide additional guidance. Its starting observation is that tasks often share similar biases, so information about unstable features in a source task may help train a more robust target classifier.

The method first contrasts different data environments in the source task to learn a representation that encodes unstable features. It then uses that representation to cluster examples in the target task. Training minimizes the worst-case risk across these clusters, directing attention to performance across the groups created by the transferred representation.

The distinctive transfer is therefore knowledge of instability: the source task helps expose divisions relevant to robust target training. Evaluations on text and image classification show that the method maintains target-task robustness in both synthetically generated and real-world environments. These results support using shared bias information across related tasks, while the motivation depends on the relevance of source-task instabilities to the target setting.
summary.tldr: Transferring representations of unstable source-task features helps organize target data for robust worst-case training.

title: Learning Stable Classifiers by Transferring Unstable Features

abstract: Computational antibody design seeks to automatically create an antibody that binds to an antigen. The binding affinity is governed by the 3D binding interface where antibody residues (paratope) closely interact with antigen residues (epitope). Thus, the key question of antibody design is how to predict the 3D paratope-epitope complex (i.e., docking) for paratope generation. In this paper, we propose a new model called Hierarchical Structure Refinement Network (HSRN) for paratope docking and design. During docking, HSRN employs a hierarchical message passing network to predict atomic forces and use them to refine a binding complex in an iterative, equivariant manner. During generation, its autoregressive decoder progressively docks generated paratopes and builds a geometric representation of the binding interface to guide the next residue choice. Our results show that HSRN significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art on paratope docking and design benchmarks.

paragraphs: Designing an antibody requires considering how its binding region fits against an antigen in three dimensions. The antibody's interacting residues form the paratope, while the corresponding antigen region is the epitope. Because their interface governs binding affinity, predicting how these regions come together is central to generating a suitable antibody binding region.

The proposed Hierarchical Structure Refinement Network, or HSRN, connects docking with sequence design. For docking, a hierarchical message-passing network predicts atomic forces and repeatedly uses them to refine the binding complex. Its updates are equivariant, meaning that the geometric refinement respects changes in the coordinate frame used to represent the structure.

During generation, an autoregressive decoder chooses residues progressively. It docks the partially generated paratope and builds a geometric representation of its interface with the antigen, using that representation to guide the next residue choice. Geometry therefore informs the developing sequence throughout generation. The reported results show significant improvements over prior leading methods on paratope docking and design benchmarks, supporting this integration of structural refinement and residue selection.
summary.tldr: HSRN improves antibody docking and design by repeatedly refining binding geometry and using that geometry to guide residue generation.

title: Antibody-Antigen Docking and Design via Hierarchical Structure Refinement

abstract: While mixture of linear regressions (MLR) is a well-studied topic, prior works usually do not analyze such models for prediction error. In fact, prediction and loss are not well-defined in the context of mixtures. In this paper, first we show that MLR can be used for prediction where instead of predicting a label, the model predicts a list of values (also known as list-decoding ). The list size is equal to the number of components in the mixture, and the loss function is defined to be minimum among the losses resulted by all the component models. We show that with this definition, a solution of the empirical risk minimization (ERM) achieves small probability of prediction error. This begs for an algorithm to minimize the empirical risk for MLR, which is known to be computationally hard. Prior algorithmic works in MLR focus on the realizable setting, i.e., recovery of parameters when data is probabilistically generated by a mixed linear (noisy) model. In this paper we show that a version of the popular expectation minimization (EM) algorithm finds out the best fit lines in a dataset even when a realizable model is not assumed, under some regularity conditions on the dataset and the initial points, and thereby provides a solution for the ERM. We further provide an algorithm that runs in polynomial time in the number of datapoints, and recovers a good approximation of the best fit lines. The two algorithms are experimentally compared.
originalAbstract: While mixture of linear regressions (MLR) is a well-studied topic, prior works usually do not analyze such models for prediction error. In fact, prediction and loss are not well-defined in the context of mixtures. In this paper, first we show that MLR can be used for prediction where instead of predicting a label, the model predicts a list of values (also known as list-decoding ). The list size is equal to the number of components in the mixture, and the loss function is defined to be minimum among the losses resulted by all the component models. We show that with this definition, a solution of the empirical risk minimization (ERM) achieves small probability of prediction error. This begs for an algorithm to minimize the empirical risk for MLR, which is known to be computationally hard. Prior algorithmic works in MLR focus on the realizable setting, i.e., recovery of parameters when data is probabilistically generated by a mixed linear (noisy) model. In this paper we show that a version of the popular expectation minimization (EM) algorithm finds out the best fit lines in a dataset even when a realizable model is not assumed, under some regularity conditions on the dataset and the initial points, and thereby provides a solution for the ERM. We further provide an algorithm that runs in polynomial time in the number of datapoints, and recovers a good approximation of the best fit lines. The two algorithms are experimentally compared.

This paper defines prediction as returning a list with one value from each component. Its loss is the smallest loss among those component predictions, giving a concrete objective for evaluating the mixture.

Under this definition, a solution to empirical risk minimization has a small probability of prediction error. Finding such a solution is computationally difficult, however. The authors move beyond the usual realizable setting, where data are assumed to have been generated by a mixture of noisy linear models, and instead study fitting a dataset without that assumption.

They show that a version of expectation maximization finds the best-fitting lines under regularity conditions on the data and starting points. They also provide an algorithm whose runtime is polynomial in the number of data points and that approximates the best-fitting lines. An experimental comparison accompanies these results, connecting the prediction formulation to algorithms for fitting mixtures.
summary.tldr: The paper defines list-based prediction for regression mixtures and develops fitting guarantees beyond mixture-generated data, subject to stated conditions.

title: On Learning Mixture of Linear Regressions in the Non-Realizable Setting

abstract: Large pre-trained language models (LMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generating long, fluent text; however, there is little to no analysis on their ability to maintain entity coherence and consistency. In this work, we focus on the end task of narrative generation and systematically analyse the long-range entity coherence and consistency in generated stories. First, we propose a set of automatic metrics for measuring model performance in terms of entity usage. Given these metrics, we quantify the limitations of current LMs. Next, we propose augmenting a pre-trained LM with a dynamic entity memory in an end-to-end manner by using an auxiliary entity-related loss for guiding the reads and writes to the memory. We demonstrate that the dynamic entity memory increases entity coherence according to both automatic and human judgment and helps preserving entity-related information especially in settings with a limited context window. Finally, we also validate that our automatic metrics are correlated with human ratings and serve as a good indicator of the quality of generated stories.
