paragraphs: Fluent storytelling requires keeping track of the entities mentioned throughout a narrative. This paper studies whether large pretrained language models maintain that information coherently and consistently over long stretches of generated text. It introduces automatic measures of entity usage and uses them to quantify shortcomings in existing models.

To address those shortcomings, the authors add a dynamic entity memory to a pretrained language model. The system is trained end to end, with an auxiliary entity-related objective guiding what the model writes to memory and what it retrieves. This makes entity information an explicit part of the generation process.

Both automatic evaluation and human judgment show improved entity coherence with the memory mechanism. It is especially helpful for preserving entity information when the model’s context window is limited. The proposed automatic measures also correlate with human ratings and indicate story quality. The paper therefore contributes both a way to assess long-range entity handling and a memory-based method for improving it.
summary.tldr: A dynamic entity memory improves consistency in generated stories, while new automatic metrics track human judgments of entity coherence.

title: Towards Coherent and Consistent Use of Entities in Narrative Generation

abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (RL) methods can meta-train policies that adapt to new tasks with orders of magnitude less data than standard RL, but meta-training itself is costly and time-consuming. If we can meta-train on offline data, then we can reuse the same static dataset, labeled once with rewards for different tasks, to meta-train policies that adapt to a variety of new tasks at meta-test time. Although this capability would make meta-RL a practical tool for real-world use, offline meta-RL presents additional challenges beyond online meta-RL or standard offline RL settings. Meta-RL learns an exploration strategy that collects data for adapting, and also meta-trains a policy that quickly adapts to data from a new task. Since this policy was meta-trained on a fixed, offline dataset, it might behave unpredictably when adapting to data collected by the learned exploration strategy, which differs systematically from the offline data and thus induces distributional shift. We propose a hybrid offline meta-RL algorithm, which uses offline data with rewards to meta-train an adaptive policy, and then collects additional unsupervised online data, without any reward labels to bridge this distribution shift. By not requiring reward labels for online collection, this data can be much cheaper to collect. We compare our method to prior work on offline meta-RL on simulated robot locomotion and manipulation tasks and find that using additional unsupervised online data collection leads to a dramatic improvement in the adaptive capabilities of the meta-trained policies, matching the performance of fully online meta-RL on a range of challenging domains that require generalization to new tasks.

Experiments on simulated robot locomotion and manipulation show dramatic improvements in adaptation compared with prior offline meta-reinforcement learning methods. Across a range of challenging domains requiring new-task generalization, the approach matches fully online meta-learning performance. The result supports combining rewarded offline experience with reward-free online collection; the successful procedure includes that additional interaction.
summary.tldr: Reward-free online experience bridges distribution shift in offline meta-reinforcement learning and substantially improves adaptation in simulated robotics tasks.

title: Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Online Self-Supervision

abstract: The acquisition function, a critical component in Bayesian optimization (BO), can often be written as the expectation of a utility function under a surrogate model. However, to ensure that acquisition functions are tractable to optimize, restrictions must be placed on the surrogate model and utility function. To extend BO to a broader class of models and utilities, we propose likelihood-free BO (LFBO), an approach based on likelihood-free inference. LFBO directly models the acquisition function without having to separately perform inference with a probabilistic surrogate model. We show that computing the acquisition function in LFBO can be reduced to optimizing a weighted classification problem, which extends an existing likelihood-free density ratio estimation method related to probability of improvement (PI). By choosing the utility function for expected improvement (EI), LFBO outperforms the aforementioned method, as well as various state-of-the-art black-box optimization methods on several real-world optimization problems. LFBO can also leverage composite structures of the objective function, which further improves its regret by several orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses what to evaluate next using an acquisition function that expresses the value of a potential evaluation. Often, computing this function requires averaging a utility under a probabilistic surrogate model. Keeping that calculation manageable can restrict both the surrogate and the kinds of utility the optimization procedure can use.

The authors show that acquisition computation can be formulated as a weighted classification problem. This generalizes an existing density-ratio estimation approach associated with probability of improvement and permits other utility choices within the same framework.

Using expected improvement as its utility, LFBO outperforms that earlier approach and several leading black-box optimization methods on the reported real-world problems. The method can also exploit composite structure in an objective, yielding further regret improvements of several orders of magnitude. The contribution connects a broader acquisition-function design space to a classification-based learning procedure.
summary.tldr: LFBO learns acquisition functions through weighted classification, broadening Bayesian optimization beyond separately fitted probabilistic surrogates.

title: A General Recipe for Likelihood-free Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Pretrained language models have become the standard approach for many NLP tasks due to strong performance, but they are very expensive to train. We propose a simple and efficient learning framework, TLM, that does not rely on large-scale pretraining. Given some labeled task data and a large general corpus, TLM uses task data as queries to retrieve a tiny subset of the general corpus and jointly optimizes the task objective and the language modeling objective from scratch. On eight classification datasets in four domains, TLM achieves results better than or similar to pretrained language models (e.g., RoBERTa-Large) while reducing the training FLOPs by two orders of magnitude. With high accuracy and efficiency, we hope TLM will contribute to democratizing NLP and expediting its development.

paragraphs: Large pretrained language models perform well on many language tasks, but their training can be expensive. It still requires labeled task examples and access to a large general corpus.

The key design choice is to concentrate learning on retrieved text connected to the task, integrating language learning with task learning instead of relying on a separate large-scale pretraining stage.

On eight classification datasets spanning four domains, TLM matches or exceeds the results of pretrained language models, including RoBERTa-Large, while reducing training floating-point operations by two orders of magnitude. These findings support a substantially cheaper training route for the classification settings evaluated. The framework’s efficiency comes from task-directed data selection and joint optimization, with the reported comparison focused on training computation.
summary.tldr: TLM trains from scratch on task data and retrieved text, matching or exceeding pretrained models on evaluated classification tasks with far less training computation.

title: NLP From Scratch Without Large-Scale Pretraining: A Simple and Efficient Framework

abstract: Bilevel optimization recently has received tremendous attention due to its great success in solving important machine learning problems like meta learning, reinforcement learning, and hyperparameter optimization. Extending single-agent training on bilevel problems to the decentralized setting is a natural generalization, and there has been a flurry of work studying decentralized bilevel optimization algorithms. However, it remains unknown how to design the distributed algorithm with sample complexity and convergence rate comparable to SGD for stochastic optimization, and at the same time without directly computing the exact Hessian or Jacobian matrices. In this paper we propose such an algorithm. More specifically, we propose a novel decentralized stochastic bilevel optimization (DSBO) algorithm that only requires first order stochastic oracle, Hessian-vector product and Jacobian-vector product oracle. The sample complexity of our algorithm matches the currently best known results for DSBO, while our algorithm does not require estimating the full Hessian and Jacobian matrices, thereby possessing to improved per-iteration complexity.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves linked optimization problems, with one level depending on the solution of another. Such structures arise in meta learning, reinforcement learning, and hyperparameter optimization. This paper considers the decentralized setting, where multiple agents participate in training, and asks how to obtain strong convergence and sample efficiency without expensive matrix computations.

The proposed decentralized stochastic bilevel optimization algorithm uses stochastic first-order information together with Hessian-vector and Jacobian-vector products. These products provide information about how derivatives act along particular directions. The algorithm therefore avoids computing or estimating the complete Hessian and Jacobian matrices while still using the derivative information needed by its updates.

The authors report sample complexity matching the best known results for this decentralized problem class, alongside improved computation per iteration. The distinction matters: an algorithm can require relatively few samples yet still make each update costly. This work addresses that computational burden while retaining competitive sample complexity and the stated convergence properties.
summary.tldr: A decentralized bilevel optimizer matches leading sample-complexity results while reducing update costs by avoiding full Hessian and Jacobian estimation.

title: Decentralized Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Improved per-Iteration Complexity

abstract: The learnware paradigm aims to build a learnware market containing numerous learnwares, each of which is a well-performing machine learning model with a corresponding specification to describe its functionality so that future users can identify useful models for reuse according to their own requirements. With the learnware paradigm, model developers can spontaneously submit models to the market without leaking data privacy, and users can leverage models in the market to accomplish different machine learning tasks without having to build models from scratch. Recent studies have attempted to realize the model specification through Reduced Kernel Mean Embedding (RKME). In this paper, we make an attempt to improve the effectiveness of RKME specification for heterogeneous label spaces, where the learnware market does not contain a model that has the same label space as the user’s task, by considering a class-specific model specification explicitly, along with a class-wise learnware identification method. Both theoretical and empirical analyses show that our proposal can quickly and accurately find useful learnwares that satisfy users’ requirements. Moreover, we find that for a specific task, reusing a small model identified via the specification performs better than directly reusing a pre-trained generic big model.

paragraphs: A learnware market stores trained models together with specifications describing what they can do. Users can search these descriptions to find reusable models, while developers can contribute models without disclosing their training data. This paper addresses a difficult case: none of the available models has exactly the label space needed by the user.

The authors improve specifications based on Reduced Kernel Mean Embedding by explicitly describing models at the class level. They pair these class-specific descriptions with a class-wise identification method. This makes the search sensitive to relevant individual classes, allowing useful models to be identified even when their overall labeling tasks differ from the requested one.

Theoretical and empirical analyses support fast, accurate identification of models meeting user requirements. The authors also find that, for a specific task, a small model selected through its specification performs better than directly reusing a generic pretrained large model. This result highlights the value of matching a model’s capabilities to the task, rather than treating model size as sufficient evidence of usefulness.
summary.tldr: Class-specific model descriptions help users find reusable models even when available models have different label spaces.

title: Identifying Useful Learnwares for Heterogeneous Label Spaces

abstract: We consider the problem of constructing small coresets for $k$-Median in Euclidean spaces. Given a large set of data points $P\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, a coreset is a much smaller set $S\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, so that the $k$-Median costs of any $k$ centers w.r.t. $P$ and $S$ are close. Existing literature mainly focuses on the high-dimension case and there has been great success in obtaining dimension-independent bounds, whereas the case for small $d$ is largely unexplored. Considering many applications of Euclidean clustering algorithms are in small dimensions and the lack of systematic studies in the current literature, this paper investigates coresets for $k$-Median in small dimensions. For small $d$, a natural question is whether existing near-optimal dimension-independent bounds can be significantly improved. We provide affirmative answers to this question for a range of parameters. Moreover, new lower bound results are also proved, which are the highest for small $d$. In particular, we completely settle the coreset size bound for $1$-d $k$-Median (up to log factors). Interestingly, our results imply a strong separation between $1$-d $1$-Median and $1$-d $2$-Median. As far as we know, this is the first such separation between $k=1$ and $k=2$ in any dimension.

For k-median, this means a small representation can support comparison of candidate center sets. This paper investigates how small such representations can be when the data lives in a low-dimensional Euclidean space.

Much previous work emphasized guarantees that do not depend on dimension, especially for high-dimensional data. The authors ask whether knowing the dimension is small allows substantially better bounds. They answer affirmatively for a range of parameter settings and also prove new lower bounds, identifying limits on how far compression can go.

For one-dimensional k-median, the paper settles coreset size up to logarithmic factors. A particularly notable consequence is a strong separation between the one-center and two-center problems on a line. This means that allowing just one additional center can materially change the coreset-size requirement. The authors identify it as the first known separation of this kind between one and two centers in any dimension.
summary.tldr: Low-dimensional k-median admits improved coreset bounds, with the one-dimensional case settled up to logarithmic factors.

title: On Coresets for Clustering in Small Dimensional Euclidean spaces

abstract: Recent research shows that when Gradient Descent (GD) is applied to neural networks, the loss almost never decreases monotonically. Instead, the loss oscillates as gradient descent converges to its “Edge of Stability” (EoS). Here, we find a quantity that does decrease monotonically throughout GD training: the sharpness attained by the gradient flow solution (GFS)—the solution that would be obtained if, from now until convergence, we train with an infinitesimal step size. Theoretically, we analyze scalar neural networks with the squared loss, perhaps the simplest setting where the EoS phenomena still occur. In this model, we prove that the GFS sharpness decreases monotonically. Using this result, we characterize settings where GD provably converges to the EoS in scalar networks. Empirically, we show that GD monotonically decreases the GFS sharpness in a squared regression model as well as practical neural network architectures.

It examines the sharpness of the gradient-flow solution: the solution reached if training switched from its current parameters to infinitesimally small steps and continued until convergence.

This quantity concerns the curvature at that eventual solution, rather than simply the loss at the current training point. For scalar neural networks with squared loss, the authors prove that its sharpness decreases monotonically throughout gradient descent. They then use that result to characterize settings in which gradient descent provably approaches the edge of stability.

The authors also observe monotonic decreases in gradient-flow-solution sharpness in experiments with a squared regression model and practical neural-network architectures. The scope of the proof and the empirical observations are distinct: the formal analysis establishes the behavior in scalar networks, while the experiments show it in broader tested settings. The result offers a more orderly perspective on training dynamics whose observed loss can fluctuate.
summary.tldr: Gradient-flow-solution sharpness decreases monotonically in a proven scalar-network setting and in experiments with broader neural architectures.

title: Gradient Descent Monotonically Decreases the Sharpness of Gradient Flow Solutions in Scalar Networks and Beyond

abstract: Perturbative availability poisoning (PAP) adds small changes to images to prevent their use for model training. Current research adopts the belief that practical and effective approaches to countering such poisons do not exist. In this paper, we argue that it is time to abandon this belief. We present extensive experiments showing that 12 state-of-the-art PAP methods are vulnerable to Image Shortcut Squeezing (ISS), which is based on simple compression. For example, on average, ISS restores the CIFAR-10 model accuracy to 81.73%, surpassing the previous best preprocessing-based countermeasures by 37.97% absolute. ISS also (slightly) outperforms adversarial training and has higher generalizability to unseen perturbation norms and also higher efficiency. Our investigation reveals that the property of PAP perturbations depends on the type of surrogate model used for poison generation, and it explains why a specific ISS compression yields the best performance for a specific type of PAP perturbation. We further test stronger, adaptive poisoning, and show it falls short of being an ideal defense against ISS. Overall, our results demonstrate the importance of considering various (simple) countermeasures to ensure the meaningfulness of analysis carried out during the development of availability poisons.

summary.tldr: Simple compression counteracts twelve evaluated availability-poisoning methods, challenging claims that such perturbations reliably prevent image-based training.

title: Image Shortcut Squeezing: Countering Perturbative Availability Poisons with Compression

abstract: Finding the mode of a high dimensional probability distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is a fundamental algorithmic problem in statistics and data analysis. There has been particular interest in efficient methods for solving the problem when $\mathcal{D}$ is represented as a mixture model or kernel density estimate, although few algorithmic results with worst-case approximation and runtime guarantees are known. In this work, we significantly generalize a result of (LeeLiMusco:2021) on mode approximation for Gaussian mixture models. We develop randomized dimensionality reduction methods for mixtures involving a broader class of kernels, including the popular logistic, sigmoid, and generalized Gaussian kernels. As in Lee et al.’s work, our dimensionality reduction results yield quasi-polynomial algorithms for mode finding with multiplicative accuracy $(1-\epsilon)$ for any $\epsilon > 0$. Moreover, when combined with gradient descent, they yield efficient practical heuristics for the problem. In addition to our positive results, we prove a hardness result for box kernels, showing that there is no polynomial time algorithm for finding the mode of a kernel density estimate, unless $\mathit{P} = \mathit{NP}$. Obtaining similar hardness results for kernels used in practice (like Gaussian or logistic kernels) is an interesting future direction.

The paper develops algorithms with approximation and runtime guarantees for a broader collection of such distributions.

The authors extend earlier dimensionality-reduction results for Gaussian mixtures to kernels including logistic, sigmoid, and generalized Gaussian kernels. Their randomized reductions yield quasi-polynomial algorithms with multiplicative accuracy of one minus epsilon for any positive epsilon. Combining the reductions with gradient descent also produces practical heuristics, connecting the theoretical approach to a more directly usable search procedure.

The paper additionally proves a computational hardness result for box kernels: a polynomial-time mode-finding algorithm would imply that P equals NP. This result is specific to that kernel family. Establishing comparable hardness for commonly used Gaussian or logistic kernels remains an explicitly identified future direction. The contribution therefore includes both broader positive guarantees and a concrete boundary on efficient computation.
summary.tldr: Randomized dimensionality reduction extends guaranteed density-mode approximation to more kernels, while a separate result establishes hardness for box kernels.

title: Dimensionality Reduction for General KDE Mode Finding

abstract: In nonstationary bandit learning problems, the decision-maker must continually gather information and adapt their action selection as the latent state of the environment evolves. In each time period, some latent optimal action maximizes expected reward under the environment state. We view the optimal action sequence as a stochastic process, and take an information-theoretic approach to analyze attainable performance. We bound per-period regret in terms of the entropy rate of the optimal action process. The bound applies to a wide array of problems studied in the literature and reflects the problem’s information structure through its information-ratio.

paragraphs: In a changing bandit problem, a decision-maker repeatedly chooses actions while the environment evolves. The action with the highest expected reward can change with the hidden environment state. Learning therefore requires continuing to gather information while adapting decisions, rather than simply identifying one good action and keeping it.

This paper analyzes the sequence of optimal actions as a stochastic process. Its central quantity is the process's entropy rate, which captures the ongoing uncertainty in that sequence. The authors use this information-theoretic perspective to bound per-period regret, the reward shortfall relative to choosing the currently optimal action.

The bound also incorporates an information-ratio that reflects how the problem's observations relate to useful learning. This connects attainable performance to both the uncertainty introduced over time and the information available through decisions. The result applies across a broad collection of previously studied problems, providing a shared way to analyze adaptation through their information structure.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds regret in changing bandit problems using the entropy rate of optimal actions and the problem's information-ratio.

title: An Information-Theoretic Analysis of Nonstationary Bandit Learning

abstract: The wide application of pre-trained models is driving the trend of once-for-all training in one-shot neural architecture search (NAS). However, training within a huge sample space damages the performance of individual subnets and requires much computation to search for a optimal model. In this paper, we present PreNAS, a search-free NAS approach that accentuates target models in one-shot training. Specifically, the sample space is dramatically reduced in advance by a zero-cost selector, and weight-sharing one-shot training is performed on the preferred architectures to alleviate update conflicts. Extensive experiments have demonstrated that PreNAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art one-shot NAS competitors for both Vision Transformer and convolutional architectures, and importantly, enables instant specialization with zero search cost. Our code is available at https://github.com/tinyvision/PreNAS.

paragraphs: One-shot neural architecture search trains many candidate networks through shared weights. A very large candidate space can weaken individual subnetworks and make finding a suitable final model expensive. This paper introduces PreNAS, which focuses the shared training process on a smaller set of preferred architectures.

Before training, a zero-cost selector dramatically reduces the candidate space. Weight-sharing training then concentrates on those selected architectures, with the aim of reducing conflicts between their updates. This changes where the architecture-selection effort enters the process: preferred models are identified in advance so training can emphasize them and later specialization requires no search.

Experiments cover both vision transformer and convolutional architectures. The authors report that PreNAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art one-shot search competitors in those evaluations and enables instant specialization with zero search cost. That search-cost claim concerns specialization; the method still performs shared training. The contribution connects improved subnet performance with a more focused training space, while removing the subsequent search step used to choose a specialized model.
summary.tldr: PreNAS selects preferred architectures before shared training, improving reported performance and enabling specialization without a subsequent search.

title: PreNAS: Preferred One-Shot Learning Towards Efficient Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We study Pareto optimality in multi-objective multi-armed bandit by providing a formulation of adversarial multi-objective multi-armed bandit and defining its Pareto regrets that can be applied to both stochastic and adversarial settings. The regrets do not rely on any scalarization functions and reflect Pareto optimality compared to scalarized regrets. We also present new algorithms assuming both with and without prior information of the multi-objective multi-armed bandit setting. The algorithms are shown optimal in adversarial settings and nearly optimal up to a logarithmic factor in stochastic settings simultaneously by our established upper bounds and lower bounds on Pareto regrets. Moreover, the lower bound analyses show that the new regrets are consistent with the existing Pareto regret for stochastic settings and extend an adversarial attack mechanism from bandit to the multi-objective one.

paragraphs: Multi-objective bandits require learning which actions to take when rewards have several components. Combining those components into one score can obscure Pareto optimality, which concerns whether an outcome can be improved without sacrificing another objective. This paper defines Pareto regrets that avoid scalarization functions and apply in both stochastic and adversarial settings.

The authors formulate the adversarial multi-objective bandit problem and introduce algorithms for cases with and without prior information about the setting. They establish upper and lower bounds on the new regret measures. Together, these bounds show optimal performance in adversarial settings and near-optimal performance, within a logarithmic factor, in stochastic settings simultaneously.

The lower-bound analysis also connects the new definitions to existing Pareto regret in stochastic bandits, showing consistency with that earlier notion. It further extends an adversarial attack mechanism from ordinary bandits to the multi-objective case. The contribution is therefore a common evaluation framework and algorithms whose guarantees address multiple reward objectives without first reducing them to a single scalar score.
summary.tldr: New Pareto regret measures support multi-objective bandit algorithms with optimal adversarial and nearly optimal stochastic guarantees.

title: Pareto Regret Analyses in Multi-objective Multi-armed Bandit

abstract: The capability to generate responses with diversity and faithfulness using factual knowledge is paramount for creating a human-like, trustworthy dialogue system. Common strategies either adopt a two-step paradigm, which optimizes knowledge selection and response generation separately, and may overlook the inherent correlation between these two tasks, or leverage conditional variational method to jointly optimize knowledge selection and response generation by employing an inference network. In this paper, we present an end-to-end learning framework, termed Sequential Posterior Inference (SPI), capable of selecting knowledge and generating dialogues by approximately sampling from the posterior distribution. Unlike other methods, SPI does not require the inference network or assume a simple geometry of the posterior distribution. This straightforward and intuitive inference procedure of SPI directly queries the response generation model, allowing for accurate knowledge selection and generation of faithful responses. In addition to modeling contributions, our experimental results on two common dialogue datasets (Wizard of Wikipedia and Holl-E) demonstrate that SPI outperforms previous strong baselines according to both automatic and human evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: A knowledge-grounded dialogue system must choose relevant information and turn it into a response that remains faithful to that information. Optimizing these steps separately can overlook their dependence: the usefulness of a fact depends partly on the response it supports. This paper proposes Sequential Posterior Inference, or SPI, to learn the two tasks together.

This gives the generation model a direct role in evaluating knowledge choices within an end-to-end framework.

The authors connect this procedure to accurate knowledge selection and faithful response generation while targeting diversity as well. On Wizard of Wikipedia and Holl-E, SPI outperforms previous strong baselines according to both automatic measures and human evaluations. Those results support the value of jointly handling knowledge selection and response generation through the proposed posterior-inference procedure.
summary.tldr: SPI jointly selects knowledge and generates dialogue through approximate posterior sampling, improving evaluated response quality on two datasets.

title: Diverse and Faithful Knowledge-Grounded Dialogue Generation via Sequential Posterior Inference

abstract: SARSA, a classical on-policy control algorithm for reinforcement learning, is known to chatter when combined with linear function approximation: SARSA does not diverge but oscillates in a bounded region. However, little is known about how fast SARSA converges to that region and how large the region is. In this paper, we make progress towards this open problem by showing the convergence rate of projected SARSA to a bounded region. Importantly, the region is much smaller than the region that we project into, provided that the the magnitude of the reward is not too large. Existing works regarding the convergence of linear SARSA to a fixed point all require the Lipschitz constant of SARSA’s policy improvement operator to be sufficiently small; our analysis instead applies to arbitrary Lipschitz constants and thus characterizes the behavior of linear SARSA for a new regime.

paragraphs: SARSA is an on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm that can oscillate within a bounded region when used with linear function approximation. This behavior, called chattering, differs from settling at a single fixed point. The paper investigates two unresolved questions: how quickly the algorithm approaches that region and how large the region can be.

The analysis establishes a convergence rate for projected SARSA to a bounded region. Projection restricts the algorithm to a prescribed region, but the authors show that its eventual region can be much smaller than that imposed boundary. This stronger conclusion requires that the magnitude of the rewards is not too large.

The new analysis permits arbitrary Lipschitz constants, extending the range of behavior that theory can characterize. Its guarantee concerns reaching a bounded region, not convergence to one point. That distinction lets the analysis describe chattering while quantifying the approach to the region in which it occurs.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how quickly projected linear SARSA reaches a bounded region without requiring a small policy-improvement Lipschitz constant.

title: On the Convergence of SARSA with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Causal effect estimation under networked interference is an important but challenging problem. Available parametric methods are limited in their model space, while previous semiparametric methods, e.g., leveraging neural networks to fit only one single nuisance function, may still encounter misspecification problems under networked interference without appropriate assumptions on the data generation process. To mitigate bias stemming from misspecification, we propose a novel doubly robust causal effect estimator under networked interference, by adapting the targeted learning technique to the training of neural networks. Specifically, we generalize the targeted learning technique into the networked interference setting and establish the condition under which an estimator achieves double robustness. Based on the condition, we devise an end-to-end causal effect estimator by transforming the identified theoretical condition into a targeted loss. Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis of our designed estimator, revealing a faster convergence rate compared to a single nuisance model. Extensive experimental results on two real-world networks with semisynthetic data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed estimators.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects becomes more difficult when outcomes are connected through a network and interference must be accounted for. The paper focuses on bias caused by misspecified models in this setting. It argues that restricted parametric models and neural approaches fitting only one nuisance function can both face problems when the data-generating assumptions are inadequate.

The authors adapt targeted learning to neural-network training under networked interference. They first establish a condition for double robustness, then translate that condition into a targeted training loss. This produces an end-to-end estimator whose training objective is tied to the theoretical requirement, connecting the desired robustness property directly to how the estimator is fitted.

The theoretical analysis gives a faster convergence rate than an approach using a single nuisance model. Experiments on semisynthetic data built from two real-world networks support the proposed estimators’ effectiveness. The contribution is therefore both methodological and theoretical: a way to train causal estimators for network interference, together with an explicit condition governing their double robustness.
summary.tldr: A targeted neural-network loss enables doubly robust causal estimation under network interference, with theoretical and semisynthetic empirical support.

title: Doubly Robust Causal Effect Estimation under Networked Interference via Targeted Learning

abstract: Robustness is a vital aspect to consider when deploying deep learning models into the wild. Numerous studies have been dedicated to the study of the robustness of vision transformers (ViTs), which have dominated as the mainstream backbone choice for vision tasks since the dawn of 2020s. Recently, some large kernel convnets make a comeback with impressive performance and efficiency. However, it still remains unclear whether large kernel networks are robust and the attribution of their robustness. In this paper, we first conduct a comprehensive evaluation of large kernel convnets’ robustness and their differences from typical small kernel counterparts and ViTs on six diverse robustness benchmark datasets. Then to analyze the underlying factors behind their strong robustness, we design experiments from both quantitative and qualitative perspectives to reveal large kernel convnets’ intriguing properties that are completely different from typical convnets. Our experiments demonstrate for the first time that pure CNNs can achieve exceptional robustness comparable or even superior to that of ViTs. Our analysis on occlusion invariance, kernel attention patterns and frequency characteristics provide novel insights into the source of robustness. Code available at: https://github.com/Lauch1ng/LKRobust.

paragraphs: Large-kernel convolutional networks have shown strong performance and efficiency, but their robustness has been less well understood. This paper investigates how they compare with conventional small-kernel networks and vision transformers. The question is both practical and explanatory: how well do these models withstand challenging inputs, and what properties accompany that behavior?

The authors evaluate robustness on six diverse benchmark datasets. They then use quantitative and qualitative experiments to investigate differences between large-kernel networks and typical convolutional networks. Their analysis examines occlusion invariance, kernel attention patterns, and frequency characteristics as sources of insight into the observed robustness.

The experiments show that purely convolutional networks can achieve robustness comparable to, and sometimes greater than, that of vision transformers. This is an empirical finding about the evaluated models and benchmarks. It demonstrates that strong robustness is attainable within a convolutional architecture and motivates closer attention to kernel size and the associated representation properties when studying why vision models remain reliable under difficult input conditions.
summary.tldr: Large-kernel convolutional networks show robustness comparable to or better than vision transformers in a six-benchmark evaluation.

title: Revealing the Dark Secrets of Extremely Large Kernel ConvNets on Robustness

abstract: The human brain is a complex inter-wired system that emerges spontaneous functional fluctuations. In spite of tremendous success in the experimental neuroscience field, a system-level understanding of how brain anatomy supports various neural activities remains elusive. Capitalizing on the unprecedented amount of neuroimaging data, we present a physics-informed deep model to uncover the coupling mechanism between brain structure and function through the lens of data geometry that is rooted in the widespread wiring topology of connections between distant brain regions. Since deciphering the puzzle of self-organized patterns in functional fluctuations is the gateway to understanding the emergence of cognition and behavior, we devise a geometric deep model to uncover manifold mapping functions that characterize the intrinsic feature representations of evolving functional fluctuations on the Riemannian manifold. In lieu of learning unconstrained mapping functions, we introduce a set of graph-harmonic scattering transforms to impose the brain-wide geometry on top of manifold mapping functions, which allows us to cast the manifold-based deep learning into a reminiscent of MLP-Mixer architecture (in computer vision) for Riemannian manifold. As a proof-of-concept approach, we explore a neural-manifold perspective to understand the relationship between (static) brain structure and (dynamic) function, challenging the prevailing notion in cognitive neuroscience by proposing that neural activities are essentially excited by brain-wide oscillation waves living on the geometry of human connectomes, instead of being confined to focal areas.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the brain's relatively static wiring supports changing patterns of neural activity. Its starting point is that connections between distant regions give the brain a geometry that may help explain those fluctuations. The authors develop a physics-informed deep model to study the relationship between anatomical structure and dynamic function.

The model represents evolving functional activity on a Riemannian manifold and learns mappings that describe its underlying features. Those mappings are constrained by graph-harmonic scattering transforms, which incorporate brain-wide connection geometry. This produces an architecture resembling an MLP-Mixer adapted to manifold-based representations, tying the learned transformations to the structure of the brain's network.

As a proof of concept, the approach offers a neural-manifold perspective on structure–function coupling. The authors propose that brain-wide oscillatory waves on connectome geometry excite neural activity, challenging an account confined to focal regions. This is a proposed interpretation developed through the model, rather than an established universal explanation of cognition or behavior.
summary.tldr: A geometry-constrained neural model explores how brain-wide connectivity and oscillatory waves may link anatomical structure to changing neural activity.

title: Exploring the Enigma of Neural Dynamics Through A Scattering-Transform Mixer Landscape for Riemannian Manifold

abstract: The primary objective of room acoustics is to model the intricate sound propagation dynamics from any source to receiver position within enclosed 3D spaces. These dynamics are encapsulated in the form of a 1D room impulse response (RIR). Precisely measuring RIR is difficult due to the complexity of sound propagation encompassing reflection, diffraction, and absorption. In this work, we propose to learn a continuous neural room acoustics field that implicitly encodes all essential sound propagation primitives for each enclosed 3D space, so that we can infer the RIR corresponding to arbitrary source-receiver positions unseen in the training dataset. Our framework, dubbed DeepNeRAP, is trained in a self-supervised manner without requiring direct access to RIR ground truth that is often needed in prior methods. The key idea is to design two cooperative acoustic agents to actively probe a 3D space, one emitting and the other receiving sound at various locations. Analyzing this sound helps to inversely characterize the acoustic primitives. Our framework is well-grounded in the fundamental physical principles of sound propagation, including reciprocity and globality, and thus is acoustically interpretable and meaningful. We present experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating superior quality in RIR estimation against closely related methods.

DeepNeRAP learns a continuous representation of a room's acoustics so it can infer responses for source and receiver positions absent from training.

summary.tldr: DeepNeRAP learns room acoustics from cooperating sound-emitting and sound-receiving agents without requiring ground-truth impulse responses.

title: Deep Neural Room Acoustics Primitive

abstract: This paper proposes a new algorithm for learning accurate tree-based models while ensuring the existence of recourse actions. Algorithmic Recourse (AR) aims to provide a recourse action for altering the undesired prediction result given by a model. Typical AR methods provide a reasonable action by solving an optimization task of minimizing the required effort among executable actions. In practice, however, such actions do not always exist for models optimized only for predictive performance. To alleviate this issue, we formulate the task of learning an accurate classification tree under the constraint of ensuring the existence of reasonable actions for as many instances as possible. Then, we propose an efficient top-down greedy algorithm by leveraging the adversarial training techniques. We also show that our proposed algorithm can be applied to the random forest, which is known as a popular framework for learning tree ensembles. Experimental results demonstrated that our method successfully provided reasonable actions to more instances than the baselines without significantly degrading accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse seeks an executable change that turns an unfavorable model prediction into a favorable one while keeping the required effort reasonable. Such a change may not exist when a classifier is trained solely for predictive performance. This paper incorporates the availability of recourse into the process of learning tree-based models.

The authors formulate tree learning as an accuracy-focused task constrained to make reasonable actions available for as many instances as possible. They propose an efficient greedy algorithm that builds the tree from the top down using techniques from adversarial training. They also show how the approach can be applied to random forests, extending it from individual trees to ensembles.

Experiments find that the learned models provide reasonable actions for more instances than the baselines, without significantly reducing accuracy or computational efficiency. The goal is broader access to recourse, rather than a claim that every individual necessarily receives an action. The findings support considering the possibility of changing an outcome during model construction, when the decision rules themselves can still be shaped.
summary.tldr: Training trees with recourse constraints makes reasonable prediction-changing actions available to more instances while largely preserving accuracy and efficiency.

title: Learning Decision Trees and Forests with Algorithmic Recourse

abstract: Raw images offer unique advantages in many low-level visual tasks due to their unprocessed nature. However, this unprocessed state accentuates noise, making raw images challenging to compress effectively. Current compression methods often overlook the ubiquitous noise in raw space, leading to increased bitrates and reduced quality. In this paper, we propose a novel raw image compression scheme that selectively compresses the noise-free component of the input, while discarding its real noise using a self-supervised approach. By excluding noise from the bitstream, both the coding efficiency and reconstruction quality are significantly enhanced. We curate an full-day dataset of raw images with calibrated noise parameters and reference images to evaluate the performance of models under a wide range of input signal-noise ratios. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing compression techniques, achieving a more advantageous rate-distortion balance with improvements ranging from +2 to +10dB and yielding a bit saving of 2 to 50 times. The code will be released upon paper acceptance.

paragraphs: Raw images preserve unprocessed visual information, which makes them useful for low-level vision tasks but also leaves noise prominent. A compression system that encodes that noise can spend extra bits representing information that does not improve the desired image. This paper treats separating useful image content from real noise as part of the compression problem itself.

The proposed self-supervised scheme selectively compresses the clean component of a noisy raw input and discards the noise. Its central idea is to keep unwanted noise out of the bitstream, improving both coding efficiency and reconstruction quality. Compression and noise removal are therefore connected through the choice of what information the compressed representation preserves.

For evaluation, the authors curate a full-day raw-image dataset with calibrated noise parameters and reference images, covering a broad range of signal-to-noise ratios. Experiments report a better rate-distortion balance than existing compression techniques, with improvements ranging from 2 to 10 dB and bit savings by factors of 2 to 50. These ranges describe the reported experimental gains, rather than a single improvement shared by every input.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised raw-image compressor improves reconstruction and reduces bit use by encoding clean image content while discarding real noise.

title: Compress Clean Signal from Noisy Raw Image: A Self-Supervised Approach

abstract: We study robust Markov games (RMG) with $s$-rectangular uncertainty. We show a general equivalence between computing a robust Nash equilibrium (RNE) of a $s$-rectangular RMG and computing a Nash equilibrium (NE) of an appropriately constructed regularized MG. The equivalence result yields a planning algorithm for solving $s$-rectangular RMGs, as well as provable robustness guarantees for policies computed using regularized methods. However, we show that even for just reward-uncertain two-player zero-sum matrix games, computing an RNE is PPAD-hard. Consequently, we derive a special uncertainty structure called efficient player-decomposability and show that RNE for two-player zero-sum RMG in this class can be provably solved in polynomial time. This class includes commonly used uncertainty sets such as $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ ball uncertainty sets.
originalAbstract: We study robust Markov games (RMG) with $s$-rectangular uncertainty. We show a general equivalence between computing a robust Nash equilibrium (RNE) of a $s$-rectangular RMG and computing a Nash equilibrium (NE) of an appropriately constructed regularized MG. The equivalence result yields a planning algorithm for solving $s$-rectangular RMGs, as well as provable robustness guarantees for policies computed using regularized methods. However, we show that even for just reward-uncertain two-player zero-sum matrix games, computing an RNE is PPAD-hard. Consequently, we derive a special uncertainty structure called efficient player-decomposability and show that RNE for two-player zero-sum RMG in this class can be provably solved in polynomial time. This class includes commonly used uncertainty sets such as $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ ball uncertainty sets.

The connection yields a planning algorithm and provable robustness guarantees for policies obtained through regularized methods. However, converting the formulation does not make every instance easy to solve. The authors prove that finding a robust equilibrium is PPAD-hard even for two-player, zero-sum matrix games where only rewards are uncertain, establishing a substantial computational obstacle within a restricted setting.

They then identify an uncertainty structure called efficient player-decomposability. For two-player, zero-sum robust Markov games in this class, robust equilibria can be computed in polynomial time. title: Roping in Uncertainty: Robustness and Regularization in Markov Games

abstract: Existing text-to-image models struggle to follow complex text prompts, raising the need for extra grounding inputs for better controllability. In this work, we propose to decompose a scene into visual primitives - denoted as dense blob representations - that contain fine-grained details of the scene while being modular, human-interpretable, and easy-to-construct. Based on blob representations, we develop a blob-grounded text-to-image diffusion model, termed BlobGEN, for compositional generation. Particularly, we introduce a new masked cross-attention module to disentangle the fusion between blob representations and visual features. To leverage the compositionality of large language models (LLMs), we introduce a new in-context learning approach to generate blob representations from text prompts. Our extensive experiments show that BlobGEN achieves superior zero-shot generation quality and better layout-guided controllability on MS-COCO. When augmented by LLMs, our method exhibits superior numerical and spatial correctness on compositional image generation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Complex image prompts require a generator to coordinate objects, their details, and their positions. This paper introduces dense blob representations as an intermediate description of a scene. These visual primitives carry detailed information while remaining modular, interpretable to people, and straightforward to construct. They provide additional grounding for a text-to-image model beyond the prompt itself.

The authors build BlobGEN, a diffusion model that generates images using these representations. Its masked cross-attention module separates how different blob descriptions interact with visual features, supporting compositional control. They also introduce an in-context learning method that lets a large language model produce blob representations from text, connecting language-based scene planning to the image generator.

Experiments report better zero-shot generation quality and layout control on MS-COCO. With language-model assistance, the method also improves numerical and spatial correctness on compositional generation benchmarks. These findings support using an explicit scene representation to help a generator follow object counts and spatial arrangements, alongside producing visually strong images.
summary.tldr: BlobGEN uses interpretable scene primitives to improve text-to-image composition, layout control, and adherence to object counts and spatial relationships.

title: Compositional Text-to-Image Generation with Dense Blob Representations

abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) priors is a widely-used family of methods for solving imaging inverse problems by integrating physical measurement models with image priors specified using image denoisers. PnP methods have been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance when the prior is obtained using powerful deep denoisers. Despite extensive work on PnP, the topic of distribution mismatch between the training and testing data has often been overlooked in the PnP literature. This paper presents a set of new theoretical and numerical results on the topic of prior distribution mismatch and domain adaptation for the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) variant of PnP. Our theoretical result provides an explicit error bound for PnP-ADMM due to the mismatch between the desired denoiser and the one used for inference. Our analysis contributes to the work in the area by considering the mismatch under nonconvex data-fidelity terms and expansive denoisers. Our first set of numerical results quantifies the impact of the prior distribution mismatch on the performance of PnP-ADMM on the problem of image super-resolution. Our second set of numerical results considers a simple and effective domain adaption strategy that closes the performance gap due to the use of mismatched denoisers. Our results suggest the relative robustness of PnP-ADMM to prior distribution mismatch, while also showing that the performance gap can be significantly reduced with only a few training samples from the desired distribution.

A denoiser trained on one image distribution may not match the images encountered during reconstruction. This paper studies how that mismatch affects the ADMM version of Plug-and-Play reconstruction and whether adaptation can reduce its effects.

The theoretical contribution is an explicit error bound tied to the difference between the desired denoiser and the denoiser actually used. The analysis covers nonconvex data-fidelity terms and expansive denoisers, extending the treatment of mismatch to these settings. This connects a discrepancy in the image prior with a quantified reconstruction error bound.

Numerical experiments on image super-resolution first measure the consequences of mismatched priors, then examine a simple domain-adaptation strategy. The results suggest that PnP-ADMM is relatively robust to mismatch and that a few training samples from the desired distribution can substantially reduce the performance gap. This supports adaptation as a practical response to mismatch in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds denoiser-mismatch error in PnP-ADMM and shows that adaptation with a few target-distribution samples can substantially reduce the reported performance gap.

title: Prior Mismatch and Adaptation in PnP-ADMM with a Nonconvex Convergence Analysis

abstract: In this work, we introduce PIPER: Primitive-Informed Preference-based Hierarchical reinforcement learning via Hindsight Relabeling, a novel approach that leverages preference-based learning to learn a reward model, and subsequently uses this reward model to relabel higher-level replay buffers. Since this reward is unaffected by lower primitive behavior, our relabeling-based approach is able to mitigate non-stationarity, which is common in existing hierarchical approaches, and demonstrates impressive performance across a range of challenging sparse-reward tasks. Since obtaining human feedback is typically impractical, we propose to replace the human-in-the-loop approach with our primitive-in-the-loop approach, which generates feedback using sparse rewards provided by the environment. Moreover, in order to prevent infeasible subgoal prediction and avoid degenerate solutions, we propose primitive-informed regularization that conditions higher-level policies to generate feasible subgoals for lower-level policies. We perform extensive experiments to show that PIPER mitigates non-stationarity in hierarchical reinforcement learning and achieves greater than 50$\%$ success rates in challenging, sparse-reward robotic environments, where most other baselines fail to achieve any significant progress.

Since this reward is unaffected by lower primitive behavior, our relabeling-based approach is able to mitigate non-stationarity, which is common in existing hierarchical approaches, and demonstrates impressive performance across a range of challenging sparse-reward tasks. Since obtaining human feedback is typically impractical, we propose to replace the human-in-the-loop approach with our primitive-in-the-loop approach, which generates feedback using sparse rewards provided by the environment. paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning divides decisions between higher-level policies that choose subgoals and lower-level primitives that carry them out. A difficulty arises when changing primitive behavior makes the higher-level learning problem non-stationary. PIPER addresses this issue in environments where rewards are sparse and human preference feedback is impractical to obtain.

The method learns a reward model through preference-based learning and uses it to relabel stored higher-level experience. Because this reward is unaffected by lower-level primitive behavior, relabeling helps mitigate non-stationarity. PIPER generates feedback through a primitive-in-the-loop process using sparse environmental rewards, replacing the need for a human to provide those preferences.

A further regularizer informs the higher-level policy about the primitives so that it generates feasible subgoals and avoids degenerate solutions. Experiments report reduced non-stationarity and success rates above 50% in challenging sparse-reward robotic environments, where most evaluated baselines make little significant progress. The approach combines a more stable reward signal with constraints on what the lower-level policies can feasibly accomplish.
summary.tldr: PIPER uses primitive-generated preferences, reward relabeling, and feasible-subgoal regularization to improve hierarchical learning in sparse-reward robotic tasks.

title: PIPER: Primitive-Informed Preference-based Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning via Hindsight Relabeling

abstract: Discrete diffusion or flow models could enable faster and more controllable sequence generation than autoregressive models. We show that naive linear flow matching on the simplex is insufficient toward this goal since it suffers from discontinuities in the training target and further pathologies. To overcome this, we develop Dirichlet flow matching on the simplex based on mixtures of Dirichlet distributions as probability paths. In this framework, we derive a connection between the mixtures’ scores and the flow’s vector field that allows for classifier and classifier-free guidance. Further, we provide distilled Dirichlet flow matching, which enables one-step sequence generation with minimal performance hits, resulting in $O(L)$ speedups compared to autoregressive models. On complex DNA sequence generation tasks, we demonstrate superior performance compared to all baselines in distributional metrics and in achieving desired design targets for generated sequences. Finally, we show that our classifier-free guidance approach improves unconditional generation and is effective for generating DNA that satisfies design targets.

paragraphs: Generating discrete sequences through diffusion or flow models could offer speed and control advantages over generating one symbol at a time. This paper identifies a problem with a straightforward approach: linear flow matching on the simplex, the space of categorical probability vectors, creates discontinuous training targets and other pathologies.

The authors replace those linear paths with probability paths built from mixtures of Dirichlet distributions. They derive a relationship between the mixtures’ scores and the flow’s vector field, enabling both classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance. These mechanisms let generation respond to desired properties. A distilled version compresses generation into one step, with minimal reported performance loss and speedups that scale as O(L) relative to autoregressive generation for sequence length L.

On complex DNA generation tasks, the method surpasses all evaluated baselines in distributional metrics and in meeting requested design targets. The authors also find that their classifier-free guidance improves unconditional generation and helps produce DNA satisfying specified targets. The results connect the mathematical redesign of the flow paths to faster sampling and stronger control in the evaluated sequence-design tasks.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet flow matching enables guided DNA sequence generation and one-step sampling with minimal reported performance loss.

title: Dirichlet Flow Matching with Applications to DNA Sequence Design

abstract: Adam with decoupled weight decay, also known as AdamW, is widely acclaimed for its superior performance in language modeling tasks, surpassing Adam with $\ell_2$ regularization in terms of generalization and optimization. However, this advantage is not theoretically well-understood. One challenge here is that though intuitively Adam with $\ell_2$ regularization optimizes the $\ell_2$ regularized loss, it is not clear if AdamW optimizes a specific objective. In this work, we make progress toward understanding the benefit of AdamW by showing that it implicitly performs constrained optimization. More concretely, we show in the full-batch setting, if AdamW converges with any non-increasing learning rate schedule whose partial sum diverges, it must converge to a KKT point of the original loss under the constraint that the $\ell_\infty$ norm of the parameter is bounded by the inverse of the weight decay factor. This result is built on the observation that Adam can be viewed as a smoothed version of SignGD, which is the normalized steepest descent with respect to $\ell_\infty$ norm, and a surprising connection between normalized steepest descent with weight decay and Frank-Wolfe.

However, this advantage is not theoretically well-understood. One challenge here is that though intuitively Adam with $\ell_2$ regularization optimizes the $\ell_2$ regularized loss, it is not clear if AdamW optimizes a specific objective. In this work, we make progress toward understanding the benefit of AdamW by showing that it implicitly performs constrained optimization. paragraphs: AdamW applies weight decay separately from Adam's adaptive updates, but the optimization objective implied by that choice has been unclear. This paper provides a conditional theoretical characterization: AdamW can implicitly behave like an optimizer whose parameters are constrained in size, helping explain the meaning of its weight decay.

The result concerns full-batch optimization. If AdamW converges under a non-increasing learning-rate schedule whose cumulative sum diverges, its limit must be a KKT point of the original loss subject to an infinity-norm bound. That bound equals the inverse of the weight decay factor, so it restricts the largest absolute parameter value. A KKT point satisfies constrained first-order conditions; the result does not establish convergence or global optimality.

The argument views Adam as a smoothed version of sign-based gradient descent and connects normalized steepest descent with weight decay to Frank–Wolfe optimization. Together, these connections give a geometric interpretation of AdamW's behavior. The contribution advances understanding of the optimizer without claiming a complete explanation of its empirical advantages in language modeling.
summary.tldr: Under stated full-batch convergence and learning-rate conditions, AdamW approaches a KKT point of an infinity-norm-constrained optimization problem.

title: Implicit Bias of AdamW: $\ell_∞$-Norm Constrained Optimization

abstract: Watermarking generative models consists of planting a statistical signal (watermark) in a model’s output so that it can be later verified that the output was generated by the given model. A strong watermarking scheme satisfies the property that a computationally bounded attacker cannot erase the watermark without causing significant quality degradation. In this paper, we study the (im)possibility of strong watermarking schemes. We prove that, under well-specified and natural assumptions, strong watermarking is impossible to achieve. This holds even in the private detection algorithm setting, where the watermark insertion and detection algorithms share a secret key, unknown to the attacker. To prove this result, we introduce a generic efficient watermark attack; the attacker is not required to know the private key of the scheme or even which scheme is used. Our attack is based on two assumptions: (1) The attacker has access to a "quality oracle" that can evaluate whether a candidate output is a high-quality response to a prompt, and (2) The attacker has access to a "perturbation oracle" which can modify an output with a nontrivial probability of maintaining quality, and which induces an efficiently mixing random walk on high-quality outputs. We argue that both assumptions can be satisfied in practice by an attacker with weaker computational capabilities than the watermarked model itself, to which the attacker has only black-box access. Furthermore, our assumptions will likely only be easier to satisfy over time as models grow in capabilities and modalities. We demonstrate the feasibility of our attack by instantiating it to attack three existing watermarking schemes for large language models: Kirchenbauer et al. (2023), Kuditipudi et al. (2023), and Zhao et al. (2023), and include preliminary results on vision-language models. The same attack successfully removes the watermarks planted by all schemes, with only minor quality degradation.

The impossibility claim is conditional on the oracle assumptions, while the experiments demonstrate feasibility for the tested schemes.
summary.tldr: Under explicit quality and perturbation-oracle assumptions, strong watermarking is impossible even with secret-key detection.

title: Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Language Models

abstract: Likelihood approximations for images are not trivial to compute and can be useful in many applications. We examine the use of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) to assess the likelihood of images and captions. We introduce Whitened CLIP, a novel transformation of the CLIP latent space via an invertible linear operation. This transformation ensures that each feature in the embedding space has zero mean, unit standard deviation, and no correlation with all other features, resulting in an identity covariance matrix. We show that the whitened embedding statistics can be well approximated by a standard normal distribution, allowing log-likelihood to be estimated using the squared Euclidean norm in the whitened space. The whitening procedure is completely training-free and uses a precomputed whitening matrix, making it extremely fast. We present several preliminary experiments demonstrating the properties and applicability of these likelihood scores to images and captions. Our code is available at github.com/rbetser/W_CLIP/tree/main.

paragraphs: Assigning likelihood scores to images can be computationally difficult. This paper investigates whether CLIP representations can provide a convenient surrogate for assessing images and captions. Its proposed method transforms the existing embedding space so that simple statistical calculations become useful for estimating log-likelihood.

Whitened CLIP applies an invertible linear transformation that centers each feature, scales it to unit standard deviation, and removes correlations between features. The resulting covariance matrix is the identity. The authors show that the transformed embedding statistics can be approximated well by a standard normal distribution. Under that approximation, the squared Euclidean norm supplies an estimate of log-likelihood.

The whitening operation requires no training and uses a precomputed matrix, making it very fast. Preliminary experiments examine the resulting scores and their applicability to both images and captions. The contribution is a lightweight statistical transformation of a learned representation. Its interpretation as a likelihood surrogate rests on the reported distributional approximation, rather than an exact likelihood model of the original image or caption.
summary.tldr: Whitened CLIP transforms embeddings into approximately normal features, enabling fast, training-free likelihood surrogate scores for images and captions.

title: Whitened CLIP as a Likelihood Surrogate of Images and Captions

abstract: The Risk Difference (RD), an absolute measure of effect, is widely used and well-studied in both randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. Complementary to the RD, the Risk Ratio (RR), as a relative measure, is critical for a comprehensive understanding of intervention effects: RD can downplay small absolute changes, while RR can highlight them. Despite its significance, the theoretical study of RR has received less attention, particularly in observational settings. This paper addresses this gap by tackling the estimation of RR in observational data. We propose several RR estimators and establish their theoretical properties, including asymptotic normality and confidence intervals. Through analyses on simulated and real-world datasets, we evaluate the performance of these estimators in terms of bias, efficiency, and robustness to generative data models. We also examine the coverage and length of the associated confidence intervals. Due to the non-linear nature of RR, influence function theory yields two distinct efficient estimators with different convergence assumptions. Based on theoretical and empirical insights, we recommend, among all estimators, one of the two doubly-robust estimators, which, intriguingly, challenges conventional expectations.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can be expressed as an absolute difference in risk or as a ratio between risks. The ratio adds a relative perspective that can make small absolute changes more visible. This paper studies how to estimate risk ratios from observational data, a setting where their theoretical properties have received less attention.

The authors propose several estimators and establish properties including asymptotic normality and associated confidence intervals. They evaluate the estimators using simulated and real-world data, examining bias, efficiency, and robustness across data-generating models. They also assess whether the intervals cover the target value and how long those intervals are.

Because a risk ratio is nonlinear, influence-function analysis yields two distinct efficient estimators with different convergence assumptions. That distinction matters when selecting an estimator: similar efficiency goals can be reached through procedures whose theoretical requirements differ. Combining theory and empirical evidence, the authors recommend one of the two doubly robust estimators. Their recommendation challenges conventional expectations and emphasizes the need to study relative-effect estimation on its own terms.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates risk-ratio estimators for observational studies, identifying distinct efficient approaches with different convergence assumptions.

title: Quantifying Treatment Effects: Estimating Risk Ratios via Observational Studies

abstract: We perform Bayesian optimization using a Gaussian process perspective on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our BART Kernel (BARK) uses tree agreement to define a posterior over piecewise-constant functions, and we explore the space of tree kernels using a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach. Where BART only samples functions, the resulting BARK model obtains samples of Gaussian processes defining distributions over functions, which allow us to build acquisition functions for Bayesian optimization. Our tree-based approach enables global optimization over the surrogate, even for mixed-feature spaces. Moreover, where many previous tree-based kernels provide uncertainty quantification over function values, our sampling scheme captures uncertainty over the tree structure itself. Our experiments show the strong performance of BARK on both synthetic and applied benchmarks, due to the combination of our fully Bayesian surrogate and the optimization procedure.

Our BART Kernel (BARK) uses tree agreement to define a posterior over piecewise-constant functions, and we explore the space of tree kernels using a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach. Where BART only samples functions, the resulting BARK model obtains samples of Gaussian processes defining distributions over functions, which allow us to build acquisition functions for Bayesian optimization. Moreover, where many previous tree-based kernels provide uncertainty quantification over function values, our sampling scheme captures uncertainty over the tree structure itself. paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model and its uncertainty to decide which input to evaluate next. This paper develops BARK, a model that connects Bayesian Additive Regression Trees with Gaussian processes. The goal is to combine the structure of tree models with uncertainty information suitable for guiding optimization.

BARK defines its kernel through agreement between trees and explores possible tree kernels using Markov chain Monte Carlo. Instead of sampling only individual functions, it samples Gaussian processes, each of which describes a distribution over functions. Those distributions support acquisition functions, which guide the choice of subsequent evaluations. The sampling also accounts for uncertainty about the tree structure itself.

The tree-based construction enables global optimization over the surrogate model, including spaces containing mixed feature types. This matters because choosing the next evaluation requires optimizing the model's guidance as well as fitting the model. Experiments on synthetic and applied benchmarks report strong performance, attributed to the combination of the fully Bayesian surrogate and its optimization procedure. The global optimization claim concerns the surrogate used to guide the search.
summary.tldr: BARK combines tree kernels with Gaussian processes to guide black-box optimization while accounting for uncertainty in tree structure.

title: BARK: A Fully Bayesian Tree Kernel for Black-box Optimization

abstract: Neural processes (NPs) are a promising paradigm to enable skill transfer learning across tasks with the aid of the distribution of functions. The previous NPs employ the empirical risk minimization principle in optimization. However, the fast adaption ability to different tasks can vary widely, and the worst fast adaptation can be catastrophic in risk-sensitive tasks. To achieve robust neural processes modeling, we consider the problem of training models in a risk-averse manner, which can control the worst fast adaption cases at a certain probabilistic level. By transferring the risk minimization problem to a two-level finite sum minimax optimization problem, we can easily solve it via a double-looped stochastic mirror prox algorithm with a task-aware variance reduction mechanism via sampling samples across all tasks. The mirror prox technique ensures better handling of complex constraint sets and non-Euclidean geometries, making the optimization adaptable to various tasks. The final solution, by aggregating prox points with the adaptive learning rates, enables a stable and high-quality output. The proposed learning strategy can work with various NPs flexibly and achieves less biased approximation with a theoretical guarantee. To illustrate the superiority of the proposed model, we perform experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, and the results demonstrate that our approach not only helps to achieve more accurate performance but also improves model robustness.
