The previous NPs employ the empirical risk minimization principle in optimization. However, the fast adaption ability to different tasks can vary widely, and the worst fast adaptation can be catastrophic in risk-sensitive tasks. To achieve robust neural processes modeling, we consider the problem of training models in a risk-averse manner, which can control the worst fast adaption cases at a certain probabilistic level. By transferring the risk minimization problem to a two-level finite sum minimax optimization problem, we can easily solve it via a double-looped stochastic mirror prox algorithm with a task-aware variance reduction mechanism via sampling samples across all tasks. The mirror prox technique ensures better handling of complex constraint sets and non-Euclidean geometries, making the optimization adaptable to various tasks. The final solution, by aggregating prox points with the adaptive learning rates, enables a stable and high-quality output. The proposed learning strategy can work with various NPs flexibly and achieves less biased approximation with a theoretical guarantee. To illustrate the superiority of the proposed model, we perform experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, and the results demonstrate that our approach not only helps to achieve more accurate performance but also improves model robustness.

paragraphs: Neural processes support transfer across tasks by learning with distributions of functions. Their ability to adapt quickly can vary substantially between tasks, making poor adaptation especially concerning in risk-sensitive settings. This paper changes the training objective to control bad adaptation outcomes at a specified probabilistic level.

The authors reformulate risk-averse training as a two-level finite-sum minimax optimization problem. They solve it using a double-loop stochastic mirror-prox algorithm with task-aware variance reduction, drawing samples across tasks. Mirror prox supports complex constraints and non-Euclidean geometries. The final output combines intermediate prox points using adaptive learning rates to promote stability and solution quality.

The training strategy can be applied to various neural processes and has a theoretical guarantee for a less biased approximation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improvements in both accuracy and robustness. The contribution connects a probabilistic concern about poor adaptation with a concrete optimization procedure, making the distribution of outcomes across tasks an explicit part of model training.
summary.tldr: Risk-averse training improves neural-process accuracy and robustness by explicitly controlling poor fast-adaptation outcomes at a probabilistic level.

title: Learning Robust Neural Processes with Risk-Averse Stochastic Optimization

abstract: The diffusion-based adversarial purification methods attempt to drown adversarial perturbations into a part of isotropic noise through the forward process, and then recover the clean images through the reverse process. Due to the lack of distribution information about adversarial perturbations in the pixel domain, it is often unavoidable to damage normal semantics. We turn to the frequency domain perspective, decomposing the image into amplitude spectrum and phase spectrum. We find that for both spectra, the damage caused by adversarial perturbations tends to increase monotonically with frequency. This means that we can extract the content and structural information of the original clean sample from the frequency components that are less damaged. Meanwhile, theoretical analysis indicates that existing purification methods indiscriminately damage all frequency components, leading to excessive damage to the image. Therefore, we propose a purification method that can eliminate adversarial perturbations while maximizing the preservation of the content and structure of the original image. Specifically, at each time step during the reverse process, for the amplitude spectrum, we replace the low-frequency components of the estimated image’s amplitude spectrum with the corresponding parts of the adversarial image. For the phase spectrum, we project the phase of the estimated image into a designated range of the adversarial image’s phase spectrum, focusing on the low frequencies. Empirical evidence from extensive experiments demonstrates that our method significantly outperforms most current defense methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based purification tries to remove adversarial image perturbations by adding noise and then reconstructing a clean image. This can also damage meaningful image information. The paper examines that tradeoff in the frequency domain, separating images into amplitude and phase spectra to study where adversarial damage is concentrated.

The authors find that damage in both spectra tends to increase with frequency. Lower-frequency components can therefore retain useful content and structural information. For phase, it constrains the estimated values to a designated range around the input’s phase, emphasizing low frequencies. Extensive experiments show significant improvements over most current defenses. The findings support frequency-aware reconstruction as a way to remove perturbations while better preserving the information needed to recognize the original image.
summary.tldr: Preserving relatively intact low-frequency amplitude and phase information improves diffusion-based adversarial image purification.

title: Diffusion-based Adversarial Purification from the Perspective of the Frequency Domain

abstract: We present a principled and simplified design of the projector and loss function for non-contrastive self-supervised learning based on hyperdimensional computing. We theoretically demonstrate that this design introduces an inductive bias that encourages representations to be simultaneously decorrelated and clustered, without explicitly enforcing these properties. This bias provably enhances generalization and suffices to avoid known training failure modes, such as representation, dimensional, cluster, and intracluster collapses. We validate our theoretical findings on image datasets, including SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100. Our approach effectively combines the strengths of feature decorrelation and cluster-based self-supervised learning methods, overcoming training failure modes while achieving strong generalization in clustering and linear classification tasks.

paragraphs: Self-supervised representation learning needs to produce features that retain useful differences between examples. This paper addresses several ways that non-contrastive training can lose that structure, including representation, dimensional, cluster, and intracluster collapse. Its contribution is a simplified design for the projector and training loss, grounded in hyperdimensional computing.

The design introduces a preference for representations that are both decorrelated and clustered. These properties serve complementary purposes: the features avoid unnecessary dependence while still organizing examples into groups. The authors show that their construction encourages both properties without adding explicit requirements to enforce each one. Their theoretical analysis establishes improved generalization and shows that this bias suffices to avoid the named failure modes.

Experiments on SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 support the theoretical findings. The method achieves strong results in clustering and linear classification, testing whether the learned representations support both grouping and prediction. The paper’s main idea is to obtain the benefits of decorrelation and clustering through the learning design itself.
summary.tldr: A projector and loss based on hyperdimensional computing encourage clustered, decorrelated representations and provably avoid several forms of collapse.

title: Collapse-Proof Non-Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: We present a principled, per-instance approach to quantifying the difficulty of unlearning via fine-tuning. We begin by sharpening an analysis of noisy gradient descent for unlearning (Chien et al., 2024), obtaining a better utility–unlearning trade-off by replacing worst-case privacy loss bounds with per-instance privacy losses (Thudi et al., 2024), each of which bounds the (R ényi) divergence to retraining without an individual datapoint. To demonstrate the practical applicability of our theory, we present empirical results showing that our theoretical predictions are born out both for Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) as well as for standard fine-tuning without explicit noise. We further demonstrate that per-instance privacy losses correlate well with several existing data difficulty metrics, while also identifying harder groups of data points, and introduce novel evaluation methods based on loss barriers. All together, our findings provide a foundation for more efficient and adaptive unlearning strategies tailored to the unique properties of individual data points.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of particular training examples. This paper studies how difficult that removal is when performed through fine-tuning, treating difficulty as something that can vary between individual data points. Its central move is to replace worst-case privacy loss bounds with losses specific to each example.

Each per-instance loss bounds a Rényi divergence from retraining without that example. Using these quantities sharpens the analysis of noisy gradient descent and improves the theoretical tradeoff between model utility and unlearning. This provides a more individualized account of removal difficulty than a bound determined by the hardest possible case.

Experiments support the theoretical predictions for both Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics and ordinary fine-tuning without explicit noise. Per-instance privacy losses also correlate with existing data difficulty measures while identifying harder groups of examples. The authors introduce evaluations based on loss barriers as well. Together, these results provide a foundation for unlearning strategies that adapt effort to the properties of the data being removed.
summary.tldr: Per-instance privacy losses sharpen unlearning analysis and help identify which training examples are harder to remove through fine-tuning.

title: Leveraging Per-Instance Privacy for Machine Unlearning

abstract: Invisible watermarking is widely used to protect digital images from unauthorized use. Accurate assessment of watermarking efficacy is crucial for advancing algorithmic development. However, existing statistical metrics, such as PSNR, rely on access to original images, which are often unavailable in text-driven generative watermarking and fail to capture critical aspects of watermarking, particularly visibility. More importantly, these metrics fail to account for potential corruption of image content. To address these limitations, we propose WMarkGPT, the first multimodal large language model (MLLM) specifically designed for comprehensive watermarked image understanding, without accessing original images. WMarkGPT not only predicts watermark visibility but also generates detailed textual descriptions of its location, content, and impact on image semantics, enabling a more nuanced interpretation of watermarked images. Tackling the challenge of precise location description and understanding images with vastly different content, we construct three visual question-answering (VQA) datasets: an object location-aware dataset, a synthetic watermarking dataset, and a real watermarking dataset. We introduce a meticulously designed three-stage learning pipeline to progressively equip WMarkGPT with the necessary abilities. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real watermarking QA datasets demonstrate that WMarkGPT outperforms existing MLLMs, achieving significant improvements in visibility prediction and content description. The datasets and code are released at https://github.com/TanSongBai/WMarkGPT.

title: WMarkGPT: Watermarked Image Understanding via Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often excel in specific domains but fall short in others due to the limitations of their training. Thus, enabling LLMs to solve problems collaboratively by integrating their complementary knowledge promises to improve their performance across domains. To realize this potential, we introduce a novel Collaborative Speculative Decoding (CoSD) algorithm that enables efficient LLM knowledge fusion at test time without requiring additional model training. CoSD employs a draft model to generate initial sequences and an easy-to-learn rule or decision tree to decide when to invoke an assistant model to improve these drafts. CoSD not only enhances knowledge fusion but also improves inference efficiency, is transferable across domains, and offers greater explainability. Experimental results demonstrate that CoSD improves accuracy by up to 10% across benchmarks compared to existing methods, providing a scalable and effective solution for LLM-based applications. Our code has been released at https://github.com/ATP-1010/CoSD.

paragraphs: Language models can have complementary strengths because their training equips them differently across domains. This paper proposes combining that knowledge during generation, without additional training of the language models. The aim is to improve answers while keeping collaboration efficient enough to be useful at inference time.

Collaborative Speculative Decoding, or CoSD, begins with a draft model that generates initial sequences. An easy-to-learn rule or decision tree determines when an assistant model should be called to improve those drafts. This selection mechanism makes the decision to collaborate explicit and interpretable, while the draft-and-assistant structure provides a way to combine knowledge during decoding.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 10% over existing methods across benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency. The authors also report transferability across domains and greater explainability. The contribution places collaboration inside the generation procedure itself: the system decides when another model’s knowledge is useful for a draft. The stated benefit therefore includes both stronger predictions and a practical mechanism for managing model cooperation.
summary.tldr: CoSD selectively calls an assistant model to improve draft generations, combining model knowledge efficiently without further language-model training.

title: Speculate, then Collaborate: Fusing Knowledge of Language Models during Decoding

abstract: Pre-trained interatomic potentials have become a new paradigm for atomistic materials simulations, enabling accurate and efficient predictions across diverse chemical systems. Despite their promise, fine-tuning is often required for complex tasks to achieve high accuracy. Traditional parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches are effective in NLP and CV. However, when applied to SO(3) equivariant pre-trained interatomic potentials, these methods will inevitably break equivariance—a critical property for preserving physical symmetries. In this paper, we introduce ELoRA (Equivariant Low-Rank Adaptation), a novel fine-tuning method designed specifically for SO(3) equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), the backbones in multiple pre-trained interatomic potentials. ELoRA adopts a path-dependent decomposition for weights updating which offers two key advantages: (1) it preserves SO(3) equivariance throughout the fine-tuning process, ensuring physically consistent predictions, and (2) it leverages low-rank adaptations to significantly improve data efficiency. We prove that ELoRA maintains equivariance and demonstrate its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments. On the rMD17 organic dataset, ELoRA achieves a 25.5% improvement in energy prediction accuracy and a 23.7% improvement in force prediction accuracy compared to full-parameter fine-tuning. Similarly, across 10 inorganic datasets, ELoRA achieves average improvements of 12.3% and 14.4% in energy and force predictions, respectively. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/hyjwpk/ELoRA.

For models built around rotation-equivariant graph neural networks, adaptation must preserve how predictions respond to rotations. The paper argues that conventional parameter-efficient methods break this symmetry when applied to these networks.

ELoRA introduces low-rank adaptation specifically structured for SO(3)-equivariant networks. summary.tldr: ELoRA preserves rotational symmetry during low-rank fine-tuning of interatomic models and improves energy and force predictions in reported experiments.

title: ELoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation for Equivariant GNNs

abstract: Eliciting information to reduce uncertainty about a latent entity is a critical task in many application domains, e.g., assessing individual student learning outcomes, diagnosing underlying diseases, or learning user preferences. Though natural language is a powerful medium for this purpose, large language models (LLMs) and existing fine-tuning algorithms lack mechanisms for strategically gathering information to refine their own understanding of the latent entity. To harness the generalization power and world knowledge of LLMs in developing effective information-gathering strategies, we propose an adaptive elicitation framework that actively reduces uncertainty on the latent entity. Since probabilistic modeling of an abstract latent entity is difficult, our framework adopts a predictive view of uncertainty, using a meta-learned language model to simulate future observations and enable scalable uncertainty quantification over complex natural language. Through autoregressive forward simulation, our model quantifies how new questions reduce epistemic uncertainty, enabling the development of sophisticated information-gathering strategies to choose the most informative next queries. In experiments on the 20 questions game, dynamic opinion polling, and adaptive student assessment, our method consistently outperforms baselines in identifying critical unknowns and improving downstream predictions, illustrating the promise of strategic information gathering in natural language settings.

paragraphs: Asking useful questions requires more than producing fluent language: a system must choose questions that reduce uncertainty about something hidden, such as a student's knowledge or a person's preferences. This paper develops an adaptive elicitation framework that uses language models to decide what information to seek next.

Directly assigning probabilities to an abstract hidden entity can be difficult. The framework instead considers uncertainty about future observations. A meta-learned language model simulates possible observations through autoregressive forward simulation, allowing the system to estimate how a new question would reduce uncertainty caused by incomplete knowledge. Those estimates guide the choice of subsequent questions as information accumulates.

Experiments cover the 20 questions game, dynamic opinion polling, and adaptive student assessment. Across these settings, the method consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines at identifying important unknowns and improving downstream predictions. The findings support a predictive approach to information gathering: reasoning about possible future observations can help a language model ask questions strategically, even when the underlying entity is difficult to model directly.
summary.tldr: The framework simulates future observations to choose natural-language questions that most effectively reduce uncertainty.

title: Adaptive Elicitation of Latent Information Using Natural Language

abstract: Leveraging high-quality joint representations from multimodal data can greatly enhance model performance in various machine-learning based applications. Recent multimodal learning methods, based on the multimodal information bottleneck (MIB) principle, aim to generate optimal MIB with maximal task-relevant information and minimal superfluous information via regularization. However, these methods often set regularization weights in an ad hoc manner and overlook imbalanced task-relevant information across modalities, limiting their ability to achieve optimal MIB. To address this gap, we propose a novel multimodal learning framework, Optimal Multimodal Information Bottleneck (OMIB), whose optimization objective guarantees the achievability of optimal MIB by setting the regularization weight within a theoretically derived bound. OMIB further addresses imbalanced task-relevant information by dynamically adjusting regularization weights per modality, ensuring the inclusion of all task-relevant information. Moreover, we establish a solid information-theoretical foundation for OMIB’s optimization and implement it under the variational approximation framework for computational efficiency. Finally, we empirically validate the OMIB’s theoretical properties on synthetic data and demonstrate its superiority over the state-of-the-art benchmark methods in various downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal information bottleneck methods aim to keep information useful for a task while discarding unnecessary information from combined data sources. The paper identifies two obstacles: regularization weights are often chosen without theoretical guidance, and different modalities may contain unequal amounts of task-relevant information.

OMIB introduces an optimization objective for which an optimal multimodal information bottleneck is achievable when the regularization weight lies within a theoretically derived bound. It also adjusts regularization weights dynamically for individual modalities to account for unequal contributions and preserve all task-relevant information. These components connect the overall compression objective with the different informational roles of the input sources.

The authors provide an information-theoretic foundation and implement the framework using variational approximation for computational efficiency. Synthetic-data experiments validate its theoretical properties, while downstream evaluations report improvements over state-of-the-art benchmark methods. The theoretical claim is conditional on the specified weight bound and concerns achievability of the optimum. The empirical findings separately support the practical value of informed, modality-specific regularization when learning joint representations.
summary.tldr: OMIB combines theoretically bounded regularization with modality-specific adjustments to preserve useful information in multimodal representations.

title: Learning Optimal Multimodal Information Bottleneck Representations

abstract: Heterogeneity in sensors and actuators across environments poses a significant challenge to building large-scale pre-trained world models on top of this low-dimensional sensor information. In this work, we explore pre-training world models for heterogeneous environments by addressing key transfer barriers in both data diversity and model flexibility. We introduce UniTraj, a unified dataset comprising over one million trajectories from 80 environments, designed to scale data while preserving critical diversity. Additionally, we propose TrajWorld, a novel architecture capable of flexibly handling varying sensor and actuator information and capturing environment dynamics in-context. Pre-training TrajWorld on UniTraj yields substantial gains in transition prediction, achieves a new state-of-the-art for off-policy evaluation, and also delivers superior online performance of model predictive control. To the best of our knowledge, this work, for the first time, demonstrates the transfer benefits of world models across heterogeneous and complex control environments. Code and data are available at https://github.com/thuml/TrajWorld.

paragraphs: A world model predicts how an environment changes, but sharing one across environments becomes difficult when their sensors and actuators differ. This paper addresses that problem for low-dimensional sensor information. It tackles both the diversity of pretraining data and the architectural flexibility needed to use data from heterogeneous control environments.

The authors introduce UniTraj, a dataset containing more than one million trajectories from 80 environments. They pair it with TrajWorld, an architecture that accommodates varying sensor and actuator information and learns environment dynamics from context. The dataset supplies diverse experience, while the model is designed to handle differences in how environments are observed and controlled.

Pretraining TrajWorld on UniTraj improves transition prediction, establishes a reported state of the art for off-policy evaluation, and improves online model predictive control performance. These results connect predictive transfer with downstream evaluation and control benefits. The authors describe the work, to their knowledge, as the first demonstration of such transfer benefits across heterogeneous, complex control environments.
summary.tldr: UniTraj and TrajWorld enable world-model pretraining across differing sensors and actuators, improving reported prediction, policy evaluation, and control.

title: Trajectory World Models for Heterogeneous Environments

abstract: Many real-world applications, such as logistics, routing, scheduling, and production planning, involve dynamic systems that require continuous updates to solutions for new Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) problems. These systems often require rapid updates to their solutions to accommodate slight modifications in constraints or objectives introduced by evolving conditions. While reoptimization techniques have been explored for Linear Programming (LP) and certain specific MILP problems, their effectiveness in addressing general MILP is limited. In this work, we propose a two-stage reoptimization framework for efficiently identifying high-quality feasible solutions. Specifically, we first utilize the historical solving process information to predict a high confidence solution space for modified MILPs, which is likely to contain high-quality solutions. Building on the prediction results, we fix a part of variables within the predicted intervals and apply the Thompson Sampling algorithm to determine which variables to fix. This is done by updating the Beta distributions based on the solutions obtained from the solver. Extensive experiments across nine reoptimization datasets show that our VP-OR outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher-quality solutions under strict time limits.

Extensive experiments across nine reoptimization datasets show that our VP-OR outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher-quality solutions under strict time limits.

paragraphs: Planning tasks in logistics, routing, scheduling, and production often require solving a revised optimization problem after conditions change. Mixed Integer Linear Programs can encode these decisions, but even small changes to constraints or objectives can demand a rapid new solution. This paper proposes VP-OR, a two-stage framework that reuses information from earlier solving processes.

First, the framework predicts a region of the revised problem’s solution space that is likely to contain high-quality solutions. It then fixes some variables within the predicted intervals. Thompson Sampling selects which variables to fix, with Beta distributions updated using solutions returned by the solver. This creates an adaptive process in which solver feedback informs subsequent choices.

The predicted region is a high-confidence guide rather than a guarantee that the best solution lies inside it. The practical goal is to find high-quality feasible solutions within strict time limits. Across nine reoptimization datasets, VP-OR outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in solution quality, supporting reuse of historical solving information when problems change.
summary.tldr: VP-OR reuses previous solving information and adaptively fixes variables to find better MILP solutions under strict time limits.

title: Don’t Restart, Just Reuse: Reoptimizing MILPs with Dynamic Parameters

abstract: This paper examines the systemic risks posed by incremental advancements in artificial intelligence, developing the concept of `gradual disempowerment', in contrast to the abrupt takeover scenarios commonly discussed in AI safety. We analyze how even incremental improvements in AI capabilities can undermine human influence over large-scale systems that society depends on, including the economy, culture, and nation-states. As AI increasingly replaces human labor and cognition in these domains, it can weaken both explicit human control mechanisms (like voting and consumer choice) and the implicit alignments with human preferences that often arise from societal systems' reliance on human participation to function. Furthermore, AI systems may amplify existing misalignments with human preferences by optimizing these systems more powerfully. These distortions across domains may be mutually reinforcing: economic power shapes cultural narratives and political decisions, while cultural shifts alter economic and political behavior. We argue that this dynamic could lead to an effectively irreversible loss of human influence over crucial societal systems, precipitating an existential catastrophe through the permanent disempowerment of humanity. This analysis suggests the need for both technical research and governance approaches that specifically address the risk of incremental erosion of human influence across interconnected societal systems.

summary.tldr: Incremental AI advances could create existential risk by progressively and irreversibly weakening human influence over interconnected societal systems.

title: Position: Humanity Faces Existential Risk from Gradual Disempowerment

abstract: We study a learner who sequentially makes and broadcasts predictions of some underlying adversarially varying state. Many downstream decision makers with different goals and different long-term constraints consume these decisions to choose actions. In this setting we give the first algorithm that obtains simultaneous dynamic regret guarantees for all of the decision makers — where regret for each agent is measured against a potentially changing sequence of actions across rounds of interaction, while also ensuring vanishing constraint violation for each agent. We can promise these dynamic regret bounds not just marginally, but simultaneously on many different intersecting subsequences, which lets decision makers compete with strategies that adapt with both long-term drift and short-term variation. Our results do not require the decision makers to maintain any state, but just to react myopically to our predictions.

paragraphs: The paper studies a prediction service whose broadcasts guide many decision makers. Each consumer has its own goals and long-term constraints, while the underlying state can change adversarially. A useful shared service must therefore support different downstream objectives under changing conditions.

The authors give an algorithm with simultaneous dynamic-regret guarantees for all decision makers, together with vanishing constraint violation. Dynamic regret compares each agent with a sequence of actions that may change across rounds, making the comparison more demanding than one against a fixed action. These subsequence guarantees let decision makers compete with strategies responding to both gradual drift and shorter-term variation. The consumers themselves need not maintain state: they can react myopically to the current predictions. The contribution places the burden of producing these guarantees on the shared prediction service, showing how simple downstream responses can receive guarantees against adaptive comparison strategies while also meeting long-term constraints asymptotically.
summary.tldr: A shared prediction algorithm gives multiple constrained decision makers simultaneous dynamic-regret guarantees, even when they react without maintaining state.

title: Stronger Benchmarks for Prediction as a Service with Constraints

abstract: Offline zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn agents that optimize unseen reward functions without additional environment interaction. The standard approach to this problem trains task-conditioned policies by sampling task vectors that define linear reward functions over learned state representations. In most existing algorithms, these task vectors are randomly sampled, implicitly assuming this adequately captures the structure of the task space. We argue that doing so leads to suboptimal zero-shot generalization. To address this limitation, we propose extracting task vectors directly from the offline dataset and using them to define the task distribution used for policy training. We introduce a simple and general reward function extraction procedure that integrates into existing offline zero-shot RL algorithms. Across multiple benchmark environments and baselines, our approach improves zero-shot performance by an average of 20%, highlighting the importance of principled task sampling in offline zero-shot RL.

paragraphs: Offline zero-shot reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent for reward functions it has not seen, without collecting additional environment interactions. A common strategy trains a task-conditioned policy using vectors that specify linear rewards over learned state representations. How those task vectors are chosen determines which tasks shape training.

Existing methods commonly sample the vectors randomly. The authors argue that this can inadequately capture task-space structure and weaken generalization. Their alternative extracts task vectors directly from the offline dataset and uses those vectors to define the training task distribution. They introduce a simple reward-extraction procedure that can be integrated into existing offline zero-shot algorithms.

Across multiple benchmark environments and baselines, the approach improves zero-shot performance by an average of 20%. This is an aggregate empirical finding across the evaluated settings. The contribution centers on making task selection reflect the available behavioral data: improving the distribution of training objectives can improve later adaptation to unseen rewards without requiring more environment interaction.
summary.tldr: Extracting training tasks from offline behavior instead of sampling them randomly improves zero-shot reinforcement-learning performance by 20% on average in the reported evaluations.

title: Improving Zero-Shot Offline RL via Behavioral Task Sampling

abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to adapt in non-stationary environments, yet deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often struggle in such settings. Prior studies introduce non-stationarity through abrupt shifts in features or dynamics, whereas real-world environments often evolve gradually through continual drift. This distinction has important implications for the “stability-plasticity dilemma” in RL, as abrupt task changes may demand more plasticity than naturalistic settings. To address this, we modify existing 3D Miniworld and MuJoCo environments to incorporate naturalistic, continual non-stationarity, and use them to examine how stability and adaptation affect performance under continuous environmental change. We find that methods favoring stability, such as synaptic consolidation, outperform approaches focused on plasticity, such as parameters resetting. Motivated by this result, and prior evidence that Successor Features (SFs) reduce interference, we investigate whether SFs are better consolidation targets than Q-values. Across both environments, applying neuro-inspired synaptic consolidation to SFs yields superior performance on continually changing settings. Moreover, consolidation is most effective when SFs are stabilized across multiple timescales, which capture complementary aspects of gradual environmental change. Together, these results suggest that stability is more critical in continual learning when changes are gradual, and that multi-timescale consolidation of predictive representations is an effective approach.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents must adapt to change without losing useful knowledge. Many studies examine abrupt changes, but gradual drift may place different demands on this balance. The authors modify 3D Miniworld and MuJoCo environments to study continual change and compare approaches that emphasize preserving knowledge with those that emphasize rapid adaptation.

In these environments, stability-oriented methods such as synaptic consolidation outperform plasticity-oriented methods such as parameter resetting. Motivated by this result, the paper investigates consolidating successor features rather than Q-values. Successor features provide predictive representations, making them a possible place to preserve useful structure while the environment evolves.

Consolidating successor features improves performance across both environments, and stabilization across multiple timescales works best. Those timescales capture complementary aspects of gradual change, allowing different parts of the predictive representation to retain information over different durations. The results suggest that gradual drift can make stability especially important; they support multi-timescale consolidation in the tested continual-change settings rather than establishing that stability always dominates adaptation.
summary.tldr: Experiments with gradually changing environments favor stabilizing successor features across multiple timescales to balance retention and adaptation.

title: Balancing Plasticity and Stability with Fast and Slow Successor Features

abstract: Recovering multiple physical parameters from high-dimensional optical measurements remains challenging in computational optics. We present MMPD-Bench, a pioneering benchmark that reframes multi-polarimetric modalities decomposition from Mueller matrix observations as a modality fission problem under the multi-modal learning paradigm. By replacing iterative numerical inversion with deep surrogate models, MMPD-Bench provides data, standardized solutions and evaluations to address the multi-physics modalities generation challenge. We benchmark representative architectures to this problem, including state-space models, vision transformers, conditional diffusion models, and neural operators, under a multi-faceted evaluation protocol that jointly assesses perceptual fidelity, physical consistency, robustness, and computational efficiency. Our analysis reveals non-trivial trade-offs between accuracy and robustness in accelerated high-fidelity polarimetric decomposition, highlighting key limitations of existing surrogates. To support reproducible research, we open-source the full codebase, together with a large-scale dataset of 21,412 high-resolution Mueller matrix observations acquired through extensive polarimetric measurements. We invite the community to further advance the intersection of polarization optics and multimodal representation learning.

paragraphs: Computational optics often needs to recover several physical properties from complex measurements. MMPD-Bench studies this problem for Mueller matrix observations, framing the recovery of multiple polarimetric modalities as modality fission. The learning task separates one rich observation into several physically meaningful outputs, connecting polarimetric decomposition with multimodal representation learning.

The benchmark provides data, standardized solutions, and evaluation procedures for deep surrogate models that replace iterative numerical inversion. It compares state-space models, vision transformers, conditional diffusion models, and neural operators. Evaluation considers perceptual fidelity, physical consistency, robustness, and computational efficiency together, so that producing visually convincing outputs is only one part of the assessment.

The analysis finds substantial trade-offs between accuracy and robustness in accelerated decomposition, exposing limitations of existing surrogates. The released resources include the full codebase and 21,412 high-resolution Mueller matrix observations collected through polarimetric measurements. This contribution creates a shared basis for studying how quickly learned models can recover multiple physical quantities while retaining reliable behavior.
summary.tldr: MMPD-Bench evaluates neural surrogates for polarimetric decomposition, revealing accuracy–robustness trade-offs across multiple model families.

title: MMPD-Bench: Bridging Multimodal Fission with Multi-Polarimetric Modalities Decomposition

abstract: Open-vocabulary grounding requires accurate vision-language alignment under weak supervision, yet existing methods either rely on global sentence embeddings that lack fine-grained expressiveness or introduce token-level alignment with explicit supervision or heavy cross-attention designs. We propose ExpAlign, a theoretically grounded vision-language alignment framework built on a principled multiple instance learning formulation. ExpAlign introduces an Expectation Alignment Head that performs attention-based soft MIL pooling over token-region similarities, enabling implicit token and instance selection without additional annotations. To further stabilize alignment learning, we develop an energy-based multi-scale consistency regularization scheme, including a Top-K multi-positive contrastive objective and a Geometry-Aware Consistency Objective derived from a Lagrangian-constrained free-energy minimization. Extensive experiments show that ExpAlign consistently improves open-vocabulary detection and zero-shot instance segmentation, particularly on long-tail categories. Most notably, it achieves 36.2 AP$_r$ on the LVIS minival split, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods at comparable model scale, while remaining lightweight and inference-efficient.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary grounding requires linking language to image regions under weak supervision. Whole-sentence embeddings can miss fine distinctions, while explicit token-level alignment can demand extra annotations or expensive cross-attention. ExpAlign addresses this tension with a multiple instance learning formulation that learns which language tokens and visual regions should contribute to alignment.

Its Expectation Alignment Head applies attention-based soft pooling to token-region similarities. This allows implicit selection of relevant tokens and instances without additional annotations. To stabilize learning across scales, the framework adds energy-based consistency regularization, combining a Top-K objective with multiple positive matches and a geometry-aware objective derived from constrained free-energy minimization.

Experiments show consistent gains in open-vocabulary detection and zero-shot instance segmentation, particularly for long-tail categories. On LVIS minival, ExpAlign achieves 36.2 AP_r, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods at comparable model scale. The authors also report lightweight, efficient inference, indicating that finer alignment need not require the heavy designs motivating the work.
summary.tldr: ExpAlign learns fine-grained token-region alignment without extra annotations, improving open-vocabulary grounding while keeping inference lightweight.

title: ExpAlign: Expectation-Guided Vision–Language Alignment for Open-Vocabulary Grounding

abstract: Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) offers a promising approach to visual self-supervised learning through masked feature prediction. However with the inherent visual uncertainty at masked positions, feature prediction remains challenging and may fail to learn semantic representations. In this work, we propose Text-Conditional JEPA (TC-JEPA) that uses image captions to reduce the prediction uncertainty. Specifically, we modulate the predicted patch features using a fine-grained text conditioner that computes sparse cross-attention over input text tokens. With such conditioning, patch features become predictable as a function of text, thus are more semantically meaningful. We show TC-JEPA improves downstream performance and training stability, with promising scaling properties. TC-JEPA also offers a new vision-language pretraining paradigm based on feature prediction only, outperforming contrastive methods on diverse tasks, especially those requiring fine-grained visual understanding and reasoning.

paragraphs: Image-based joint-embedding prediction learns visual representations by predicting features at masked image locations. Those locations can be visually ambiguous, making prediction difficult and potentially weakening the semantic information learned. Text-Conditional JEPA uses image captions to reduce that uncertainty and make the predicted features more closely connected to meaning.

The method applies a fine-grained text conditioner to predicted patch features. Sparse cross-attention over caption tokens lets the conditioning use relevant parts of the text. With this additional information, patch features become predictable as a function of the caption, linking local visual predictions to the semantic content expressed in language.

The authors report improved downstream performance and training stability, together with promising scaling behavior. They also frame the method as a vision-language pretraining approach based entirely on feature prediction. In the evaluated tasks, it outperforms contrastive methods, with particular strength on fine-grained visual understanding and reasoning. The findings suggest that captions can improve the learning signal within a predictive visual objective.
summary.tldr: TC-JEPA conditions masked visual feature prediction on captions, improving semantic representations, training stability, and evaluated downstream performance.

title: Text-Conditional JEPA for Learning Semantically Rich Visual Representations

abstract: Training deep spiking neural networks (SNNs) remains challenging due to sharp loss landscapes and temporal inconsistency caused by surrogate gradients. To address these challenges, we propose a unified framework: adaptive and asymmetric surrogate gradients (A$^2$SG). The adaptive gradients adjust an effective window for spatio-temporal adaptation, reducing spatial gradient variation and maintaining directional consistency of gradients over time. The asymmetric gradients reflect neuronal dynamics by assigning larger gradients to neurons with higher membrane potentials, and we prove that they yield lower variation than symmetric surrogates. Our analysis further establishes a direct connection between local gradient variation and the curvature of the loss landscape, providing a principled explanation for how A$^2$SG promotes convergence to flatter minima and improves generalization. We conduct extensive experiments on diverse models, including CNN-based and Transformer-based SNNs, across various tasks such as image classification using both static and neuromorphic datasets, as well as segmentation. The results demonstrate that A$^2$SG consistently improves accuracy and energy efficiency, establishing it as a general and reliable solution for training deep SNNs.Our code is available at https://github.com/KIST-NCL/A2SG.git.

paragraphs: Training deep spiking neural networks depends on surrogate gradients, but these approximations can create unstable learning signals across layers and time. The paper connects these difficulties to sharp loss landscapes and proposes A²SG, a framework that changes both how gradients adapt and how they respond to neuronal state.

The adaptive component adjusts the effective gradient window across space and time. Its purpose is to reduce spatial variation while keeping gradient directions consistent over time. The asymmetric component gives larger gradients to neurons with higher membrane potentials. The authors prove that their asymmetric gradients have lower variation than symmetric surrogates.

The analysis also connects local gradient variation to loss curvature, explaining how the method promotes convergence toward flatter minima and better generalization. Experiments cover convolutional and Transformer-based spiking networks, static and neuromorphic image classification, and segmentation. Across these evaluations, the authors report improvements in accuracy and energy efficiency. The contribution combines a proposed explanation for training instability with a gradient design tested across several architectures and tasks.
summary.tldr: A²SG adapts surrogate gradients across space, time, and neuronal state to improve spiking-network training, accuracy, and energy efficiency.

title: A$^2$SG: Adaptive and Asymmetric Surrogate Gradients for Training Deep Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: We propose contrastive order learning (ConOrd), a contrastive learning framework for ordinal regression that integrates the strengths of contrastive learning and order learning. While contrastive learning effectively leverages all samples in a batch, it typically ignores the inherent ordering among rank labels. Conversely, order learning explicitly models label ordinality but often relies on local, margin-based comparisons, limiting its ability to capture global ordinal structure. ConOrd addresses these limitations by introducing a contrastive order loss with soft affinity and disparity weights based on rank differences, enabling fine-grained modeling of ordinal relationships across all sample pairs within a batch. Extensive experiments on a range of ordinal regression tasks, including facial age estimation, blind image quality assessment, and blind video quality assessment, demonstrate that ConOrd consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes well across diverse ordinal regression scenarios. The source code is available at https://github.com/cwlee00/ConOrd.

paragraphs: Ordinal regression predicts labels with an inherent order, so the relationships between ranks matter as well as the individual labels. This paper introduces ConOrd, a framework that combines contrastive learning with order learning. Its motivation is that contrastive learning uses samples throughout a training batch effectively, while conventional order learning explicitly captures ranking but often depends on local comparisons.

ConOrd brings rank information into the contrastive objective through soft affinity and disparity weights. These weights depend on differences between ranks, allowing relationships between examples to vary gradually with their ordinal separation. Applying the loss across all sample pairs in a batch gives the model access to a broader ordinal structure than local, margin-based comparisons alone.

The authors evaluate ConOrd on facial age estimation and blind image and video quality assessment. They report consistently state-of-the-art results and good generalization across the evaluated ordinal regression settings. The stated findings suggest that using batch-wide comparisons while respecting graded rank differences is a useful combination across several kinds of ordered prediction.
summary.tldr: ConOrd uses rank-sensitive contrastive comparisons across training batches to improve ordinal regression across age and visual quality tasks.

title: Contrastive Order Learning: A General Framework for Ordinal Regression

abstract: We propose a system for marking sensitive or copyrighted texts to detect their use in fine-tuning large language models under black-box access with statistical guarantees. Our method builds digital “marks” using invisible Unicode characters organized into (“cue”, “reply”) pairs. During an audit, prompts containing only “cue” fragments are issued to trigger regurgitation of the corresponding “reply”, indicating document usage. To control false positives, we compare against held-out counterfactual marks and apply a ranking test, yielding a verifiable bound on the false positive rate. Empirically, we obtain a true positive rate of 96.7% at 0% false positive rate and reply regurgitation rates exceeding 28% per document with only 40 (4%) watermarked documents. The approach is minimally invasive, scalable across many sources, robust to standard processing pipelines, and achieves high detection power even when marked data is a small fraction of the fine-tuning corpus.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how a text owner can detect whether marked documents were used to fine-tune a language model when only black-box access is available. Its approach inserts digital marks made from invisible Unicode characters, preserving the visible text while creating associations that an audit can later probe.

Each mark contains a cue and a corresponding reply. During auditing, the investigator submits prompts containing cue fragments and checks whether the model reproduces the associated replies. To distinguish evidence of document use from accidental matches, the method compares responses against held-out counterfactual marks. A ranking test provides a verifiable bound on the false-positive rate, giving the audit a statistical basis.

The reported experiments achieve a 96.7% true-positive rate with an observed 0% false-positive rate. With 40 marked documents, representing 4% of the fine-tuning corpus, reply reproduction exceeds 28% per document. The authors also report robustness to standard processing pipelines and scalability across sources. These findings support detection even when marked material forms a small share of training data.
summary.tldr: Invisible cue–reply marks enable statistically controlled black-box audits of whether documents were used to fine-tune a language model.

title: Data Provenance Auditing of Fine-Tuned Large Language Models with a Text-Preserving Technique

abstract: Neural operators have shown promise in accelerating PDE solvers, yet they remain unreliable for the sparse linear systems induced by discretization due to limited generalization across physical parameters and insufficient accuracy, and hybrid neural iterative schemes face stagnation as the residual distribution evolves over iterations. To address these limitations, we propose G-RANS (Generalizable Residual-Aware Neural Solver), a neuralized iterative paradigm that performs residual-aware subspace corrections by mapping the residual to the matrix graph, generating multi-scale correction subspaces via a residual-aware basis generator, and applying projected updates through a differentiable subspace projection. G-RANS is trained fully self-supervised via progressive bootstrap with multi-stage residual distributions. On sparse FEM systems from a representative suite of second-order elliptic PDEs (Poisson, advection–diffusion, reaction–diffusion, and Helmholtz), G-RANS is robust to severe coefficient shifts (up to $\pm70%$) and shows strong cross-equation generalization. G-RANS reaches relative residuals on the order of $10^{-5}$, substantially outperforming end-to-end neural operators, and attains the same target residual with $2$–$4\times$ less wall-clock time than classical Krylov solvers.

paragraphs: Discretizing physical equations produces sparse linear systems that require accurate numerical solutions. Neural methods can accelerate this work, but their accuracy and generalization may be insufficient, and hybrid solvers can stall as their remaining errors change. G-RANS addresses this by making each learned correction depend on the current residual, which measures how far the current solution is from satisfying the system.

The solver maps that residual onto the matrix graph and generates correction subspaces at multiple scales. A differentiable projection then computes updates within those subspaces. Training is fully self-supervised and progressively incorporates residual distributions from multiple stages, preparing the model for the changing errors encountered during iteration.

Tests cover sparse finite-element systems from Poisson, advection-diffusion, reaction-diffusion, and Helmholtz equations. G-RANS shows robustness to coefficient shifts up to ±70% and strong transfer across equations. It reaches relative residuals around 10^-5 and requires two to four times less wall-clock time than classical Krylov solvers to reach the same target residual in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: G-RANS learns residual-dependent correction spaces to solve sparse physical systems accurately and faster in the reported evaluations.

title: G-RANS: Generalizable Residual-Aware Neural Solvers for Sparse Systems

abstract: Multi-compartment Hodgkin–Huxley (HH) models provide a principled framework for predicting neural dynamics and responses to electrical stimulation. However, fitting HH biophysical parameters typically requires intracellular recordings, which are invasive and low-throughput, limiting the ability to capture the geometry and cell-specific properties of many neurons in a given neural circuit. Multi-electrode arrays (MEAs) offer a scalable alternative—high-density extracellular measurements from full neural populations—but HH model complexity has so far precluded reliable biophysical inference from extracellular data alone. Here, we introduce a framework to rapidly infer HH parameters from designed features of extracellular MEA measurements by leveraging differentiable biophysical simulation and simulation-based inference, unlocking a wide range of downstream applications. In this work, we focus on a central goal of translational neuroengineering: predicting neural spiking responses to candidate neurostimulation patterns that would take hours to measure clinically. To validate our approach, we collected hundreds of hours of stimulation and recording data from isolated macaque retina with a 30 $\bm{\mu}$m-pitch 512-electrode array. Our framework predicted previously unseen multi-electrode stimulation responses with 90.6% accuracy using HH models fit from only a few minutes of recording, replacing hours of stimulus testing.

title: Learning Biophysical Models of Large-Scale Multineuronal Data To Enable Precise Neurostimulation

abstract: We study robustness to agent malfunctions in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), a failure mode that is critical in practice yet underexplored in existing theory. We introduce MARTA, a plug-and-play robustness layer that augments standard MARL algorithms with a Switcher–Adversary mechanism which selectively induces malfunctions in performance-critical states. This formulation defines a fault-switching $(N+2)$-player Markov game in which the Switcher chooses when and which agent fails, and the Adversary controls the resulting faulty behaviour via random or worst-case policies. We develop a Q-learning-type scheme and show that the associated Bellman operator is a contraction, yielding existence and uniqueness of the minimax value, convergence to a Markov perfect equilibrium. MARTA integrates seamlessly with MARL algorithms without architectural modification and consistently improves robustness across Traffic Junction (TJ), Level-Based Foraging (LBF), MPE SimpleTag, and SMAC (v2). In these domains, MARTA achieves large gains in final performance of up to 116.7% in SMAC, 21.4% in MPE SimpleTag, and 44.6% in LBF, while significantly reducing failure rates under train–test mismatched fault regimes. These results establish MARTA as a theoretically grounded and practically deployable mechanism for fault-tolerant MARL.

This creates a Markov game with two additional players. The authors develop a Q-learning-style scheme and establish contraction of its Bellman operator, supporting a unique minimax value and convergence to a Markov perfect equilibrium.

summary.tldr: MARTA improves cooperative-agent robustness by learning when to induce malfunctions and how faulty agents should behave during training.

title: Learning Robust Multi-Agent Policies via Selective Adversarial Fault Induction

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now generate substantial production code, often for tasks with multiple valid algorithmic solutions. Incidental prompt cues—contextual words or metadata outside the task specification—can steer which algorithm the model selects, even when all outputs pass the same tests. Prompt sensitivity is well studied as a mechanism for improving output quality; here, we instead study output policy: algorithm choice under fixed correctness. We define algorithm steering as cue-induced shifts in algorithm-family distributions and run 46,535 controlled experiments across 11 tasks, 19 cue types (18 channels plus a memoization semantic-vs-surface ablation that preserves meaning while changing typography and punctuation), and 15 model configurations. We find large, systematic shifts in algorithm-family distributions (up to 100 percentage points, pp), largely consistent with cue semantics, including in applied tasks such as rate limiting. Direct algorithm naming is the most reliable mitigation we tested. These results reveal an “invisible lottery” in which accidental context alters downstream properties such as performance, security, and maintainability.

paragraphs: A coding task can have several correct algorithmic solutions, with different implications for performance, security, or maintainability. This paper asks whether incidental words and metadata influence which solution a language model chooses even when the generated programs pass the same tests. It studies algorithm choice while holding correctness fixed, treating the distribution of algorithm families as the outcome.

The authors conduct 46,535 controlled experiments across 11 tasks, 19 cue types, and 15 model configurations. The cues include 18 channels and a memoization comparison that preserves meaning while changing typography and punctuation. They measure algorithm steering as the shift in algorithm-family distributions caused by those cues.

The observed shifts are large and systematic, reaching 100 percentage points, and generally align with cue meaning. Effects also appear in applied tasks such as rate limiting. Explicitly naming the desired algorithm is the most reliable mitigation tested. These findings show why passing correctness tests may leave important implementation choices sensitive to accidental context in the prompt.
summary.tldr: Incidental prompt cues can strongly shift which correct algorithm an LLM chooses, while explicitly naming the algorithm is the most reliable tested mitigation.

title: The Invisible Lottery: How Subtle Cues Steer Algorithm Choice in LLM Code Generation

abstract: This paper concerns the question of how AI systems encode semantic structure into the geometric structure of their representation spaces. The motivating observation is that the natural geometry of these representation spaces should reflect the way models use representations to produce behavior. We focus on the important special case of representations that define softmax distributions. In this case, we argue that the natural geometry is information geometry. Our focus is on the role of information geometry on semantic encoding and the linear representation hypothesis. As an illustrative application, we develop dual steering, a method for robustly steering representations to exhibit a particular concept using linear probes. We prove that dual steering optimally modifies the target concept while minimizing changes to off-target concepts. Empirically, we find that dual steering enhances the controllability and stability of concept manipulation.

paragraphs: Understanding a model's internal geometry requires deciding what makes two representations meaningfully different. This paper argues that the answer should reflect how representations produce behavior. It focuses on representations that define softmax probability distributions, proposing information geometry as the natural framework for studying their semantic structure.

The analysis connects this geometry to semantic encoding and the linear representation hypothesis. Its practical application is dual steering, which uses linear probes to guide representations toward a target concept. The method links concept manipulation to the geometry of the distributions produced by the model, making behavioral consequences central to the intervention.

The authors prove that dual steering optimally modifies the target concept while minimizing changes to off-target concepts within their formulation. Empirically, it improves the controllability and stability of concept manipulation. The contribution therefore combines a proposed geometric account with an intervention grounded in that account. Its stated scope is the important case of softmax-defined representations, where changes in internal states can be understood through changes in output distributions.
summary.tldr: Dual steering uses the information geometry of softmax representations to target concepts while minimizing off-target changes.

title: The Information Geometry of Softmax: Probing and Steering

abstract: When organizations delegate text generation tasks to AI providers via pay-for-performance contracts, expected payments rise when evaluation is noisy. As evaluation methods become more elaborate, the economic benefits of decreased noise are often overshadowed by increased evaluation costs. In this work, we introduce adaptive contracts for AI delegation, which allow detailed evaluation to be performed selectively after observing an initial coarse signal in order to conserve resources. We make three sets of contributions: First, we provide efficient algorithms for computing optimal adaptive contracts under natural assumptions or when core problem dimensions are small, and prove hardness of approximation in the general unstructured case. We then formulate alternative models of randomized adaptive contracts and discuss their benefits and limitations. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the benefits of adaptivity over non-adaptive baselines using question-answering and code-generation datasets.

paragraphs: Paying an AI provider according to output quality creates an evaluation problem: noisy assessments increase expected payments, but more elaborate assessments cost money themselves. The paper studies how an organization can balance these costs when delegating text generation. Its central idea is to make the evaluation process adaptive, using an initial coarse signal to decide whether a more detailed assessment is worth performing.

The authors develop algorithms for finding optimal adaptive contracts when natural assumptions hold or when the main problem dimensions are small. They also prove that approximating the optimum is hard in the general unstructured setting. This distinguishes cases where selective evaluation can be optimized efficiently from cases where designing the contract itself becomes computationally difficult.

The work additionally considers randomized versions of adaptive contracts and examines their benefits and limitations. Experiments using question-answering and code-generation datasets demonstrate advantages over non-adaptive baselines. The stated contribution is therefore both economic and computational: selective evaluation can improve delegation efficiency, while the theory identifies conditions under which suitable contracts can be computed.
summary.tldr: Adaptive contracts selectively request detailed evaluations to improve the cost efficiency of delegating text generation to AI providers.

title: Adaptive Contracts for Cost-Effective AI Delegation

abstract: Surgical video datasets are essential for scene understanding, enabling procedural modeling and intra-operative support. However, these datasets are often heavily imbalanced, with rare actions and tools under-represented, which limits the robustness of downstream models. We address this challenge with SurgiFlowVid, a sparse and controllable video diffusion framework for generating surgical videos of under-represented classes. Our approach introduces a dual-prediction diffusion module that jointly denoises RGB frames and optical flow, providing temporal inductive biases to improve motion modeling from limited samples. In addition, a sparse visual encoder conditions the generation process on lightweight signals (e.g., sparse segmentation masks or RGB frames), enabling controllability without dense annotations. We validate our approach on three surgical datasets across tasks including action recognition, tool presence detection, and laparoscope motion prediction. Synthetic data generated by our method yields consistent gains of $10$–$20$% over competitive baselines, establishing SurgiFlowVid as a promising strategy to mitigate data imbalance and advance surgical video understanding methods.

paragraphs: Surgical video datasets contain many examples of common events but relatively few of rare actions and tools. This imbalance limits the robustness of models trained for surgical scene understanding. SurgiFlowVid tackles the problem by generating videos of underrepresented classes, aiming to supply useful training examples where the original data are sparse.

Its diffusion module jointly denoises RGB video frames and optical flow, which describes motion between frames. Modeling appearance and motion together introduces temporal structure that helps the system learn movement from limited samples. A sparse visual encoder also lets lightweight inputs, such as occasional segmentation masks or RGB frames, control generation without requiring dense annotations.

The authors evaluate the approach on three surgical datasets, with downstream tasks covering action recognition, tool presence detection, and laparoscope motion prediction. They report consistent gains of 10–20% over competitive baselines using the generated data. These findings support controllable video synthesis as a promising way to mitigate training-data imbalance and improve the evaluated surgical video understanding tasks.
summary.tldr: SurgiFlowVid jointly models video appearance and motion to generate underrepresented surgical examples, yielding reported downstream gains of 10–20% over competitive baselines.

title: Mitigating Surgical Data Imbalance with Dual-Prediction Video Diffusion Model

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been demonstrated to be powerful tools for analyzing structural graph data. However, most existing methods usually rely on fixed adjacency structures for information propagation, lacking strong adaptability to the latent semantic relationships that exist but are not explicitly connected in graph, especially in complementary high-pass and low-pass filtering views. To this end, this paper proposes a novel Dual-channel Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DCD-GNN), mainly consisting of parallel representation learning channels: a static structure-preserving channel and a dynamic adjacency-enhancing channel. The dynamic channel exploits both low-pass structural filtering and high-pass personalized detail via the self-attention adjacency learning and then integrates them for comprehensive semantic modeling, while the static channel maintains structural stability. Both channels employ a multi-scale representation fusion mechanism and a unified and discriminative node embedding representation is obtained by integrating them. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets verify the superiority of DCD-GNN in discriminative graph representation learning.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly exchange information along the connections already present in a graph. Those connections may omit meaningful relationships between nodes. DCD-GNN addresses this problem by learning through two parallel channels: one preserves the supplied graph structure, and the other learns an adaptive adjacency structure that can represent additional semantic relationships.

The dynamic channel uses self-attention to learn adjacency and combines two complementary views. Low-pass filtering captures shared structural information, while high-pass filtering preserves more individualized details. The static channel maintains structural stability alongside this adaptation. Both channels fuse representations across multiple scales, and their outputs are combined into a single node representation intended to distinguish nodes effectively.

The authors report superior discriminative graph-representation learning across several benchmark datasets. The approach matters because structural preservation and relationship discovery have separate roles within the same model. Its reported findings support combining the original graph with learned connections and complementary filtering views, rather than relying entirely on a fixed adjacency structure.
summary.tldr: DCD-GNN combines a structure-preserving graph channel with learned connections and complementary filters to improve node representations.

title: Dual-channel Dynamic Graph Neural Networks with Adaptive Adjacency Learning and Multi-scale Representation Fusion

abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of integrating Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) into flow matching models, particularly for text-to-image and text-to-video generation. However, we find that directly applying these techniques to image-to-video (I2V) models often fails to yield consistent reward improvements. To address this limitation, we present TAGRPO, a robust post-training framework for I2V models inspired by contrastive learning. Our approach is grounded in the observation that rollout videos generated from identical initial noise provide superior guidance for optimization. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel GRPO loss applied to intermediate latents, encouraging direct alignment with high-reward trajectories while maximizing distance from low-reward counterparts. Furthermore, we introduce a memory bank for rollout videos to enhance diversity and reduce computational overhead. Despite its simplicity, TAGRPO achieves significant improvements over DanceGRPO in I2V generation.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization has shown promise for training flow-matching image and video generators, but this paper finds that direct transfer to image-to-video generation does not consistently improve rewards. TAGRPO addresses that instability through a contrastive approach to post-training, using comparisons between better and worse generated video trajectories.

The contribution is a simple way to adapt reward-guided optimization to this generation setting: compare trajectories from matched initial noise, steer intermediate representations according to their rewards, and reuse rollout videos to make the process more efficient.
summary.tldr: TAGRPO improves image-to-video post-training by aligning intermediate latents with high-reward trajectories and separating them from low-reward counterparts.

title: TAGRPO: Boosting GRPO on Image-to-Video Generation with Direct Trajectory Alignment

abstract: Federated fine-tuning presents a promising avenue for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to downstream tasks while preserving data privacy. However, the prohibitive computational and communication overhead of LLM adaptation inhibits its deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. In this paper, we propose SmartFed, a resource-efficient framework that circumvents expensive training from scratch by intelligently reusing knowledge embedded in existing LoRA modules. To fully exploit this potential and ensure scalability, we introduce the Mixture of Rank-Wise Experts (MoRE). MoRE decomposes LoRA modules into fine-grained rank-level experts, which are selectively activated based on input semantics and resource budgets. Furthermore, to optimize resource utilization, we propose Elastic Expert Quota Allocation (EEQA), a strategy that adaptively distributes expert capacity across parameter matrices based on their contribution to model performance. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SmartFed significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both model performance and training efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/benmagnifico/SmartFed.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning lets participants adapt a language model while retaining their data locally, but adaptation can still demand substantial computation and communication. Those costs make participation difficult for devices with limited resources. SmartFed addresses this problem by reusing knowledge already stored in existing LoRA adaptation modules.

Its central mechanism, Mixture of Rank-Wise Experts, divides those modules into smaller experts at the level of individual ranks. The framework selectively activates these pieces according to the input’s meaning and the available resource budget. This creates a finer unit of selection than an entire adaptation module, allowing existing knowledge to be assembled more selectively.

A second mechanism, Elastic Expert Quota Allocation, distributes expert capacity across parameter matrices according to their contribution to model performance. Together, selective activation and adaptive allocation aim to spend limited resources where they are most useful. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both performance and training efficiency. The findings support reusing and reorganizing existing adaptation knowledge as an effective approach to resource-constrained federated fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: SmartFed reassembles fine-grained experts from existing LoRA modules to improve federated fine-tuning performance and efficiency.

title: Don’t Reinvent the Wheel, Just Realign the Spokes: Resource-Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning via Rank-Wise Expert Assembly

abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems commonly rely on natural-language prompts to specify agent behavior, yet optimizing these prompts remains challenging when agent roles and interaction structures are fixed by design. In such systems, behaviors emerge over long, noisy interaction trajectories, making it difficult to determine which prompt components are responsible for success or failure. As a result, outcome-level feedback alone is insufficient, while existing prompt optimization methods typically rely on final task scores or global prompt rewrites, limiting their ability to exploit trajectory evidence or support the localized updates. We propose Trajectory-based Rule Credit Estimation (TRUCE), a framework for prompt optimization in multi-agent systems that explicitly addresses this credit assignment challenge. TRUCE performs trajectory-aware attribution by linking outcome feedback to informative sub-trajectories and translating the resulting credit signals into unit-level edits over prompt-defined behavioral rules. By preserving agent roles and interaction structures, TRUCE enables prompt refinement through localized updates aggregated across tasks. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that TRUCE consistently improves task performance and efficiency over competitive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/bingo-w/TRUCE.
