paragraphs: In a multi-agent language-model system, prompts define how each agent should behave. When a long interaction succeeds or fails, the final score alone gives little guidance about which instruction contributed to the outcome. This paper tackles that credit-assignment problem in systems whose agent roles and interaction structures are fixed.

TRUCE links outcome feedback to informative portions of the interaction history. It then translates those credit signals into edits to individual behavioral rules in the prompts. Updates are aggregated across tasks, allowing the system to refine specific instructions while preserving the existing organization of agents. The interaction trajectory thus becomes evidence for deciding what to change.

Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements in task performance and efficiency over competitive baselines. The significance is that prompt optimization can work at the level of particular behavioral rules, using evidence from intermediate exchanges. This offers a focused way to improve an established multi-agent workflow without redesigning its roles or communication structure.
summary.tldr: TRUCE improves multi-agent prompts by tracing outcomes to informative interactions and editing the behavioral rules implicated by that evidence.

title: From Interaction Trajectories to Prompt Rules: Credit Assignment for Multi-Agent Prompt Optimization

abstract: Multimodal models like CLIP have gained significant attention due to their remarkable zero-shot performance across various tasks. However, studies have revealed that CLIP can inadvertently learn spurious associations between target variables and confounding factors. To address this, we introduce Locate-Then-Correct (LTC), a contrastive framework that identifies spurious attention heads in Vision Transformers via mechanistic insights and mitigates them through targeted ablation. Furthermore, LTC identifies salient, task-relevant attention heads, enabling the integration of discriminative features through orthogonal projection to improve classification performance. We evaluate LTC on benchmarks with inherent background and gender biases, achieving over a $>$ 50% gain in worst-group accuracy compared to non-training post-hoc baselines. Additionally, we visualize the representation of selected heads and find that the presented interpretation corroborates our contrastive mechanism for identifying both spurious and salient attention heads.

To address this, we introduce Locate-Then-Correct (LTC), a contrastive framework that identifies spurious attention heads in Vision Transformers via mechanistic insights and mitigates them through targeted ablation. Furthermore, LTC identifies salient, task-relevant attention heads, enabling the integration of discriminative features through orthogonal projection to improve classification performance. We evaluate LTC on benchmarks with inherent background and gender biases, achieving over a $>$ 50% gain in worst-group accuracy compared to non-training post-hoc baselines. Additionally, we visualize the representation of selected heads and find that the presented interpretation corroborates our contrastive mechanism for identifying both spurious and salient attention heads.

paragraphs: CLIP's strong zero-shot classification can coexist with reliance on misleading associations. A model may connect a target label with background or gender-related information that does not reliably identify the target. Locate-Then-Correct examines this problem at the level of attention heads inside the vision transformer, seeking specific internal contributors to those associations.

The method uses a contrastive framework to identify heads associated with spurious information and suppresses their influence through targeted ablation. It also identifies heads that carry salient information for the task. An orthogonal projection step incorporates discriminative features from those useful heads to improve classification, combining removal of misleading signals with use of relevant ones.

On benchmarks containing background and gender biases, the authors report more than a 50% gain in worst-group accuracy compared with non-training post-hoc baselines. They also visualize representations from selected heads and find support for the proposed identification mechanism. The results suggest that distinguishing useful and spurious heads can improve performance for the groups most poorly served by biased classification.
summary.tldr: Locate-Then-Correct identifies and suppresses spurious CLIP attention heads while incorporating task-relevant features to improve worst-group classification.

title: Locate then Correct: Debiasing Attention Heads in CLIP

abstract: Inference-time guided sampling steers state-of-the-art diffusion and flow models without fine-tuning by interpreting the generation process as a controllable trajectory. This provides a simple and flexible way to inject external constraints (e.g., cost functions or pre-trained verifiers) for controlled generation. However, existing methods often fail when composing multiple constraints simultaneously, which leads to deviations from the true data manifold. In this work, we identify root causes of this off-manifold drift and find that the approximation error scales severely with gradient misalignment. Building on these findings, we propose Conflict-Aware Additive Guidance ($g^\text{car}$), a lightweight and learnable method, which actively rectifies off-manifold drift by dynamically detecting and resolving gradient conflicts. We validate $g^\text{car}$ across diverse domains, ranging from synthetic datasets and image editing to generative decision-making for planning and control. Our results demonstrate that $g^\text{car}$ effectively rectifies off-manifold drift, surpassing baselines in generation fidelity while using light compute. Code is available at https://github.com/yuxuehui/CAR-guidance.

paragraphs: Guided sampling controls a generative model during inference by treating generation as a trajectory that can be redirected. External rewards or constraints provide steering signals without requiring fine-tuning of the generator. Trouble arises when several constraints are applied together: their combined influence can push generation away from the structure of the underlying data.

This paper analyzes that drift and finds that approximation error grows severely with misalignment between guidance gradients. In plain language, the directions favored by different constraints can interfere with one another. Conflict-Aware Additive Guidance addresses this interaction through a lightweight, learnable mechanism that dynamically detects gradient conflicts and resolves them while generation proceeds.

The authors evaluate the method on synthetic data, image editing, and generative planning and control. They report improved generation fidelity over baselines while using light computation and effectively correcting off-manifold drift. The contribution is a way to manage interactions among steering signals, making the composition of multiple objectives more reliable in the tested generative settings.
summary.tldr: Conflict-Aware Additive Guidance detects and resolves competing steering gradients to improve generation fidelity when multiple rewards are combined.

title: Conflict-Aware Additive Guidance for Flow Models under Compositional Rewards

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm that accelerates optimal transport by exploiting intrinsic symmetries induced by finite group actions. The core of our approach is to recover the orbit decomposition and the associated algebraic structure directly from the cost matrix—without requiring prior knowledge of the group—and to reduce the original transport problem to a substantially smaller problem on the orbit space. This reduction preserves optimality while achieving a significant drop in computational complexity. We develop efficient solvers for two central classes of optimal transport: linear OT and entropy-regularized OT. Experiments on synthetic data, real-world image datasets, and molecular graph data confirm the efficiency and robustness of the method. To our knowledge, this work is the first to systematically incorporate symmetry groups into optimal transport, providing both a theoretical framework and a practical pathway to computational acceleration.

paragraphs: Optimal transport computations can contain repeated structure when their costs have symmetries. This paper develops an algorithm that uses symmetries induced by finite group actions to shrink the optimization problem. A central feature is that the method recovers the symmetry structure from the cost matrix itself, without requiring the group to be supplied in advance.

The algorithm identifies the orbit decomposition and its associated algebraic structure. These orbits organize elements related by the symmetry, allowing the original transport problem to be reduced to a much smaller problem on the orbit space. The authors show that this reduction preserves optimality while substantially decreasing computational complexity.

They develop efficient solvers for both linear optimal transport and entropy-regularized optimal transport. Experiments on synthetic data, image datasets, and molecular graph data support the method’s efficiency and robustness. The contribution provides both a theoretical reduction and practical solvers for exploiting this particular structure. Its acceleration comes from recognizing symmetries in the transport costs and solving the corresponding reduced problem without sacrificing the stated optimality.
summary.tldr: The method discovers finite-group symmetries from transport costs and solves a smaller problem while preserving optimality.

title: Optimal Transport with Symmetry Groups

abstract: Context-aided forecasting (CAF) holds promise for integrating domain knowledge and forward-looking information, enabling AI systems to surpass traditional statistical methods. However, recent empirical studies reveal a puzzling gap: multimodal models often fail to outperform their unimodal counterparts. We hypothesize that this underperformance stems partly from insufficiently verified context usefulness in existing datasets. To address these limitations, we introduce a semi-synthetic data augmentation method that generates contexts both descriptive of temporal dynamics and verifiably complementary to numerical histories. This approach enables massive-scale dataset creation, resulting in CAF-7M, a corpus of 7 million context-augmented time series windows, including a rigorously verified test set. We demonstrate that semi-synthetic pre-training transfers effectively to real-world evaluation, and show clear evidence of context utilization. Our results suggest that dataset quality is a major bottleneck in context-aided forecasting, and that verified context can substantially improve the usefulness of CAF training data.

paragraphs: Context-aided forecasting supplements numerical histories with information such as domain knowledge or forward-looking context. Although this could improve predictions, multimodal models often fail to outperform models using only one modality. The authors hypothesize that part of this gap comes from datasets whose accompanying context has not been sufficiently checked for usefulness.

They introduce a semi-synthetic augmentation method that creates context describing temporal dynamics while verifying that it adds information beyond the numerical history. This produces CAF-7M, a collection of seven million context-augmented time-series windows, including a rigorously verified test set. The central design choice is to make complementary information an explicit property of the data.

The paper reports that pretraining on this semi-synthetic material transfers effectively to real-world evaluation and provides evidence that models use the context. These findings suggest that dataset quality is a major bottleneck in context-aided forecasting. They support verified context as a way to improve training usefulness while preserving the authors' qualified explanation: insufficiently useful context is proposed as part of the problem.
summary.tldr: CAF-7M supplies verified complementary context for forecasting, with results suggesting that data quality helps explain weak multimodal performance.

title: Overcoming the Modality Gap in Context-Aided Forecasting

abstract: Recent AI regulation has largely focused on algorithmic components such as recommender models, ranking systems, and profiling mechanisms. At the same time, cultural and digital policy agendas increasingly frame discovery as a key objective, aiming to promote exposure diversity and cultural representation. We argue that these outcomes cannot be effectively governed through algorithm-centric approaches alone. Discovery does not arise from individual algorithms in isolation, but from interactions among models, interfaces, user behavior, economic incentives, and cultural norms. We introduce the Cultural Expressions Discovery Circuit (CEDC), an interdisciplinary framework that models discovery as an emergent socio-technical process. Through this lens, we illustrate how certain regulatory approaches struggle to align with broader cultural objectives. Furthermore, we highlight how socio-technical analysis can help inform both technical research and the governance of cultural expressions in online platforms.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether regulating recommendation, ranking, and profiling algorithms is enough to shape what people discover online. Cultural policy increasingly seeks diverse exposure and representation, but the authors argue that these outcomes depend on more than algorithmic components. Discovery emerges through the combined effects of models, interfaces, user behavior, business incentives, and cultural norms.

The authors introduce the Cultural Expressions Discovery Circuit to describe those interactions. This interdisciplinary framework treats discovery as a process produced by a wider social and technical system. Its purpose is to connect the mechanisms through which content reaches people with the broader cultural objectives that policy is trying to advance.

Using that perspective, the paper illustrates why some regulatory approaches struggle to achieve their cultural aims. Governing an individual model can leave other influences on discovery outside the scope of intervention. The authors argue that examining the whole process can inform both technical research and governance. The contribution is a framework for understanding the connection between platform design and cultural outcomes, rather than a reported test of a particular regulatory solution.
summary.tldr: Governing cultural discovery online requires accounting for interfaces, behavior, incentives, and norms alongside recommendation algorithms.

abstract: Exponential Family PSR (EFPSR) models capture stochastic dynamical systems by representing state as the parameters of an exponential family distribution over a short-term window of future observations. They are appealing from a learning perspective because they are fully observed (meaning expressions for maximum likelihood do not involve hidden quantities), but are still expressive enough to both capture existing models (such as POMDPs and linear dynamical systems) and predict new models. While learning algorithms based on maximizing exact likelihood exist, they are not computationally feasible. We present a new, computationally efficient, learning algorithm based on an approximate likelihood function. The algorithm can be interpreted as attempting to induce stationary distributions of observations, features and states which match their empirically observed counterparts. The approximate likelihood, and the idea of matching stationary distributions, may have application in other models.

paragraphs: Exponential Family Predictive State Representations describe a stochastic dynamical system through a distribution over a short window of future observations. The parameters of that distribution serve as the state. This representation is attractive for learning because maximum-likelihood expressions do not require hidden quantities, while the model family can capture POMDPs, linear dynamical systems, and additional models.

The computational obstacle is that existing algorithms based on exact likelihood are not feasible to run efficiently. This paper introduces a learning algorithm built around an approximate likelihood. The change makes learning computationally efficient while preserving the predictive-state formulation as the underlying way of representing the system.

The algorithm also has a useful interpretation: it attempts to produce stationary distributions of observations, features, and states that match their empirical counterparts. In plain terms, it seeks agreement between the model's stable statistical behavior and the patterns observed in data. The authors suggest that both the approximate likelihood and this distribution-matching idea may be useful in other model families.
summary.tldr: An approximate-likelihood algorithm makes learning exponential-family predictive state models computationally efficient.

title: Efficiently learning linear-linear exponential family predictive representations of state

abstract: Hashing based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has attracted much attention due to its fast query time and drastically reduced storage. However, most of the hashing methods either use random projections or extract principal directions from the data to derive hash functions. The resulting embedding suffers from poor discrimination when compact codes are used. In this paper, we propose a novel data-dependent projection learning method such that each hash function is designed to correct the errors made by the previous one sequentially. The proposed method easily adapts to both unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios and shows significant performance gains over the state-of-the-art methods on two large datasets containing up to 1 million points.
originalAbstract: Hashing based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search has attracted much attention due to its fast query time and drastically reduced storage. However, most of the hashing methods either use random projections or extract principal directions from the data to derive hash functions. The resulting embedding suffers from poor discrimination when compact codes are used. In this paper, we propose a novel data-dependent projection learning method such that each hash function is designed to correct the errors made by the previous one sequentially. The proposed method easily adapts to both unsupervised and semi-supervised scenarios and shows significant performance gains over the state-of-the-art methods on two large datasets containing up to 1 million points.

paragraphs: Hashing supports approximate nearest-neighbor search by giving data points compact codes that are inexpensive to store and compare. However, the paper identifies a weakness in common hash construction methods: random projections or principal directions can produce codes with poor discrimination when very few bits are available.

The proposed method learns projections from the data in sequence. Each new hash function is designed to correct errors made by the preceding one, so the code is built through successive corrective steps. This makes the relationship between hash functions part of the learning process and directly addresses the challenge of extracting useful distinctions from a compact representation.

The method accommodates both unsupervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios. Experiments on two large datasets, containing up to one million points, show significant gains over the state-of-the-art methods considered. These results support the value of sequential correction for compact hashing in the evaluated settings, where storage savings and fast queries must be balanced against the ability to identify useful neighbors.
summary.tldr: Learning hash projections sequentially to correct earlier errors improves compact-code nearest-neighbor search in large-dataset experiments.

title: Sequential Projection Learning for Hashing with Compact Codes

abstract: Local Coordinate Coding (LCC), introduced in (Yu et al., 2009), is a high dimensional nonlinear learning method that explicitly takes advantage of the geometric structure of the data. Its successful use in the winning system of last year's Pascal image classification Challenge (Everingham, 2009) shows that the ability to integrate geometric information is critical for some real world machine learning applications. This paper further develops the idea of integrating geometry in machine learning by extending the original LCC method to include local tangent directions. These new correction terms lead to better approximation of high dimensional nonlinear functions when the underlying data manifold is locally flat. The method significantly reduces the number of anchor points needed in LCC, which not only reduces computational cost, but also improves prediction performance. Experiments are included to demonstrate that this method is more effective than the original LCC method on some image classification tasks.

paragraphs: Local Coordinate Coding uses the geometric structure of data to support high-dimensional nonlinear learning. Its representation relies on anchor points, providing a way to describe data through local coordinates. This paper extends that representation with local tangent directions, adding information about how the data's underlying shape behaves near those anchors.

The tangent directions supply correction terms that improve the approximation of nonlinear functions when the underlying data manifold is locally flat. This geometric condition explains when the added terms have the stated benefit. By representing more of the local structure around each anchor, the method significantly reduces the number of anchor points required by the original approach.

The reduced anchor requirement matters both computationally and predictively: the paper reports lower computational cost and improved prediction performance. Experiments on some image classification tasks show greater effectiveness than the original Local Coordinate Coding method. The contribution is thus a specific refinement of a geometry-aware representation, connecting richer local information to a smaller representation and better results in the studied applications.
summary.tldr: Adding local tangent directions improves Local Coordinate Coding under local flatness and reduces anchor requirements with better reported classification results.

title: Improved Local Coordinate Coding using Local Tangents

abstract: We introduce a method for constructing a single skill capable of solving any tasks drawn from a distribution of parameterized reinforcement learning problems. The method draws example tasks from a distribution of interest and uses the corresponding learned policies to estimate the geometry of the lower-dimensional manifold on which the skill policies lie. This manifold models how policy parameters change as the skill parameters are varied. We then apply non-linear regression to construct a parameterized skill by predicting policy parameters from task parameters. We evaluate our method on an underactuated simulated robotic arm tasked with learning to accurately throw darts at any target location around it.

paragraphs: The paper aims to learn a single adjustable skill for tasks drawn from a distribution of parameterized reinforcement learning problems. A task's parameters describe what the skill should accomplish, while policy parameters determine its behavior. The challenge is to learn how changes in the task should translate into changes in the policy.

The method first samples example tasks and learns a policy for each. It then uses those policies to estimate a lower-dimensional manifold on which the skill's policies lie. This manifold captures the geometry of how policy parameters vary as the requested skill changes. Nonlinear regression turns that relationship into a predictor from task parameters to policy parameters.

The authors evaluate the approach with an underactuated simulated robotic arm learning to throw darts at target locations around it. This setting makes the intended reuse concrete: target location parameterizes the requested behavior. The contribution is a procedure for constructing a parameterized skill from learned examples, using the lower-dimensional organization of policies to connect tasks and behaviors.
summary.tldr: The method learns a mapping from task parameters to policy parameters by estimating the lower-dimensional structure of example policies.
